RESPIRATORY__Tar Staining:
Tar staining is the yellow-brown discolouration of the fingers and nails of the smoking hand — deposited tar from cigarette smoke, not nicotine (nicotine is colourless; ‘nicotine staining’ is a misnomer).
  • A marker of heavy, long-term smoking — its real value is as a prompt.
  • Act on it: quantify the smoking, look for smoking-related disease (lung cancer, COPD, vascular disease, bladder cancer) and offer cessation.
  • First make sure the yellow is tar — not jaundice, carotenaemia or yellow nail syndrome.
🚨Tar staining is a clue, not a disease — the danger is missing what it points to. In a heavy smoker actively seek lung cancer (clubbing, weight loss, haemoptysis — a change in cough warrants an urgent chest X-ray / 2-week-wait), COPD, ischaemic heart & peripheral vascular disease and bladder cancer (painless haematuria). Every encounter is an opportunity for smoking-cessation advice.

1Characterise it
🔍What it is & the misnomer
  • Yellow-brown staining of the fingers & nails of the dominant smoking hand (often index / middle finger)
  • Caused by tar (particulate matter) — not nicotine, which is colourless (‘nicotine staining’ is a misnomer)
  • A marker of heavy, cumulative smoking — its value is as a prompt
🚩What it should trigger
  • Look for lung cancer: clubbing, weight loss, haemoptysis, a changed cough → urgent CXR / 2-week-wait
  • COPD, ischaemic heart & peripheral vascular disease, and bladder cancer (painless haematuria)
  • Use the moment for smoking-cessation advice
🚬The smoking assessment
  • Quantify pack-years (packs/day × years) and current use / readiness to quit
  • Look for other signs: clubbing, cyanosis, a CO₂-retention flap, cachexia and a tobacco smell
  • Offer very brief advice + support: NRT, varenicline or bupropion, and a referral
🟡Differential of yellow fingers / nails
  • Jaundice — generalised, with yellow sclerae (check the eyes)
  • Carotenaemia — yellow palms and soles, sclerae spared (high carotene diet)
  • Fungal nail (onychomycosis) and henna / occupational dyes
💛Yellow nail syndrome — the exam differential
  • Thick, slow-growing yellow nails (all nails) with lymphoedema
  • and respiratory disease: pleural effusions, bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis
  • A classic triad — distinct from smoking-related tar staining
🩺Confirm & act
  • A clinical / visual diagnosis — confirmed by the smoking history and distribution
  • Its worth is the prompt: take a smoking history, examine for smoking-related disease, and deliver cessation advice
Two moves: first make sure the yellow is tar (fingers / nails of the smoking hand) and not jaundice (check the sclerae), carotenaemia (palms / soles) or yellow nail syndrome; then treat the sign as a flag for heavy smoking — hunt for disease and offer cessation.

RESPIRATORY__Barrel Chest:
A barrel chest is an increased antero-posterior (AP) chest diameter — the chest looks rounded, with the AP:transverse ratio approaching 1 (normal ~0.7).
  • It is the inspection sign of chronic hyperinflation / air trapping, most often COPD / emphysema.
  • Confirm with the associated hyperinflation signs: reduced expansion (see Reduced Chest Expansion), a hyper-resonant percussion note (see Abnormal Percussion Note) and quiet breath sounds.
  • Separate true air trapping from a structural chest (kyphosis, ageing).
🚨When it reflects obstructive lung disease, a barrel chest usually marks advanced disease: these patients decompensate into type 2 respiratory failure / CO₂ narcosis during exacerbations — give controlled oxygen (88–92%) (see CO₂ Retention Signs). They are also at high risk of a pneumothorax: sudden worsening with new unilateral hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds in a hyperinflated chest can be hard to spot — a tension pneumothorax still needs immediate decompression.
📷

1Characterise it
🔍What it is & how to assess it
  • Increased AP diameter — the AP:transverse ratio approaches 1 (normal ~0.7)
  • Horizontal ribs, a widened subcostal angle and a reduced cricosternal distance (<3 finger-breadths)
  • A sign of chronic hyperinflation / air trapping — look for the other hyperinflation signs
🚩What a barrel chest warns of
  • Advanced chronic lung disease → exacerbations bring type 2 failure / CO₂ narcosis (controlled O₂ 88–92%)
  • High pneumothorax risk: sudden worsening + new unilateral hyper-resonance / reduced breath sounds
  • → a tension pneumothorax still needs immediate decompression
🫁The commonest cause — COPD / emphysema
  • Smoker with chronic air trapping; hyper-resonant, quiet breath sounds, prolonged expiration
  • Pursed-lip breathing, accessory-muscle use, and Hoover’s sign (lower ribs move IN on inspiration)
🧒Other obstructive causes
  • Severe / poorly-controlled chronic asthma (especially in children)
  • Cystic fibrosis (young patient, finger clubbing, copious purulent sputum, recurrent infections)
🦴Structural mimics & contributors
  • Thoracic kyphosis / osteoporotic vertebral collapse increases the AP curvature
  • Ageing (‘senile’ hyperinflation, costal-cartilage calcification) and pectus deformities — not air trapping
🩺Associated signs & confirm
  • Reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, loss of cardiac / hepatic dullness, quiet breath sounds
  • Chest X-ray: flat diaphragms, >6 anterior ribs, a narrow heart; spirometry: an obstructive pattern with a raised residual volume / TLC
A barrel chest is air trapping made visible: the increased AP diameter goes with hyper-resonance, quiet breath sounds and reduced expansion. Ask is this obstructive lung disease (COPD, asthma, CF) or a structural chest (kyphosis, ageing)? The added signs and spirometry decide.

RESPIRATORY__Facial & Neck Swelling:
Facial & neck swelling spans a benign lump to an airway or oncological emergency.
  • Is the airway threatened? — lip / tongue swelling, stridor, drooling.
  • Unilateral / localised (a gland, node or abscess) or bilateral / diffuse (oedema)?
  • Distended neck & chest-wall veins with facial plethora? — the signature of superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. The respiratory flagship here is SVC obstruction from a mediastinal tumour.
  • See also Stridor for the upper airway.
🚨Airway first. Rapid lip / tongue swelling with urticaria, wheeze or stridor is anaphylaxis / angioedema — give IM adrenaline and call for anaesthetic help. Floor-of-mouth swelling with fever, drooling and trismus is Ludwig’s angina (a deep-neck-space infection) — secure the airway and give IV antibiotics. SVC obstruction with stridor, marked oedema or cerebral signs is also an emergency.
📷

1Characterise it
🔍How to approach it
  • Airway threatened? lip / tongue swelling, stridor, drooling, voice change → treat first
  • Localised (a gland, node, abscess) vs bilateral / diffuse (oedema)
  • Distended neck & chest-wall veins + facial plethora → think SVC obstruction
🚩Airway & oncological emergencies
  • Lip / tongue swelling + urticaria / wheeze / stridor → anaphylaxis / angioedema — IM adrenaline
  • Floor-of-mouth swelling + fever + drooling + trismus → Ludwig’s angina — airway + IV antibiotics
  • SVC obstruction with stridor / cerebral oedema — urgent oncology / imaging
🩸SVC obstruction — the respiratory one
  • Facial, neck and arm swelling + plethora / cyanosis, worse bending forward / lying
  • Distended non-pulsatile neck & chest-wall veins; a positive Pemberton’s sign (raising the arms → facial congestion)
  • → a mediastinal mass: lung cancer (esp. small cell), lymphoma, thymoma, or a central-line thrombus
💧Bilateral / diffuse facial oedema
  • Angioedema (allergic, ACE-inhibitor, or hereditary C1-esterase deficiency — often no urticaria)
  • Nephrotic syndrome (periorbital oedema, frothy urine), hypothyroidism (myxoedema)
  • Cushing’s (moon face, central obesity, striae)
📍Localised swellings
  • Parotid (mumps, sialadenitis, a tumour), submandibular gland / stone, a dental abscess
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy (infection, lymphoma, metastasis), cellulitis, a thyroid goitre
🩺Assess & confirm
  • Airway first; then examine the veins (non-pulsatile), Pemberton’s sign, lymph nodes, thyroid and dip the urine
  • CT chest (SVC obstruction / mediastinal mass) or CT neck (deep infection); tissue diagnosis for a tumour
Three questions triage it: is the airway safe? (anaphylaxis, Ludwig’s), are the neck / chest-wall veins distended with plethora? (SVC obstruction), and is it localised or diffuse? A positive Pemberton’s sign points firmly to SVC obstruction.

RESPIRATORY__Snoring & Witnessed Apnoeas:
Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas (a bed-partner reporting pauses, gasping or choking) is the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) — repeated upper-airway collapse in sleep.
  • The key split: simple snoring (no apnoeas, no daytime symptoms) versus OSA (apnoeas + excessive daytime sleepiness).
  • Separate obstructive apnoea (effort continues) from central apnoea (effort ceases — see Abnormal Breathing Patterns) and obesity hypoventilation (daytime CO₂ retention — see CO₂ Retention Signs).
  • Score it and confirm with a sleep study.
🚨Excessive daytime sleepiness is a safety issue: ask about falling asleep while driving — patients must stop driving and inform the DVLA until treated (vocational drivers especially). Watch for obesity hypoventilation with type 2 respiratory failure (morning headache, cyanosis, a raised daytime CO₂) and for cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension from long-standing untreated OSA.

1Characterise it
🔍What to establish
  • Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas / gasping / choking (a bed-partner account is key)
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, poor concentration
  • Simple snoring (no apnoeas, no daytime symptoms) vs OSA (apnoeas + daytime sleepiness)
🚩Safety-critical & serious
  • Falling asleep while driving → stop driving and inform the DVLA until treated
  • Obesity hypoventilation — morning headache, cyanosis, a raised daytime CO₂ (type 2 failure)
  • Cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension from long-standing untreated OSA
😴OSA — the picture & risk factors
  • Obstructive: respiratory effort continues against a collapsed pharynx (paradoxical chest / abdomen)
  • Obesity, male, middle age, a large neck circumference, alcohol / sedatives at night
  • Retrognathia / micrognathia, large tonsils, nasal obstruction narrow the airway
❤️Consequences & associations
  • Resistant / hard-to-control hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke and ischaemic heart disease
  • Type 2 diabetes / metabolic syndrome, pulmonary hypertension, and road-traffic accidents
🔀Mimics & other causes
  • Central sleep apnoea — apnoeas with NO effort (heart failure, opioids, Cheyne-Stokes)
  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (daytime hypercapnia)
  • Hypothyroidism and acromegaly (macroglossia); and simple snoring
🩺Assess, score & confirm
  • Epworth Sleepiness Scale (subjective sleepiness) and the STOP-BANG risk questionnaire
  • A sleep study (polysomnography or home oximetry) gives the apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI)
  • Then CPAP (moderate–severe), weight loss, a mandibular device (mild) and avoiding alcohol / sedatives
Two questions frame it: are there apnoeas and daytime sleepiness (OSA, not simple snoring), and does respiratory effort continue during the apnoea (obstructive) or cease (central)? Then ask whether the daytime CO₂ is raised (obesity hypoventilation).

RESPIRATORY__CO₂ Retention Signs:
CO₂ retention (hypercapnia) is the clinical picture of a high arterial PaCO₂ — the hallmark of type 2 (ventilatory) respiratory failure.
  • Rising CO₂ causes vasodilatation: a bounding pulse, warm peripheries, headache.
  • As it climbs — CNS depression: a flapping tremor, then drowsiness and coma (CO₂ narcosis).
  • Recognise the signs, confirm with an ABG, decide acute vs chronic, and treat the cause — usually a lung, pump or drive problem.
  • Read it with the effort (see Increased Work of Breathing) and the pattern (see Abnormal Breathing Patterns).
🚨CO₂ narcosis — drowsiness, confusion then coma with a rising CO₂ and a respiratory acidosis — is a medical emergency: support ventilation with NIV or intubation. In a known CO₂ retainer (COPD), uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can worsen the hypercapnia — titrate to 88–92%, but never leave a critically hypoxic patient without oxygen. Beware the tiring patient whose rising CO₂ means impending ventilatory failure.
📷

1Characterise it
🔍The signs of CO₂ retention
  • Vasodilatation: a bounding pulse, warm peripheries, a flushed face and headache (often worse in the morning)
  • CNS: a coarse flapping tremor (asterixis / CO₂ retention flap), drowsiness and confusion
  • Papilloedema in severe / prolonged hypercapnia (cerebral vasodilatation raises ICP)
🚩CO₂ narcosis — the emergency
  • Drowsiness → confusion → coma with a rising CO₂ and a respiratory acidosis
  • Support ventilation with NIV or intubation; treat the cause
  • In a retainer, uncontrolled O₂ worsens it — target 88–92% (but never leave a patient critically hypoxic)
🫁Airway & lung causes
  • COPD (much the commonest), a tiring severe asthma attack
  • Obesity hypoventilation / obstructive sleep apnoea — morning headache, daytime somnolence
💪Pump (ventilatory) failure
  • Neuromuscular weakness — Guillain-Barré, MND, myasthenia (a weak cough, a falling FVC)
  • Chest-wall disease — kyphoscoliosis, severe obesity
💊Reduced respiratory drive
  • Opioids / sedatives / anaesthetics (slow, shallow breathing — pinpoint pupils with opioids → naloxone)
  • a very high CO₂ further blunts the drive (a vicious cycle), and brainstem / CNS lesions
🩺Confirm it & date it on the ABG
  • PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa defines hypercapnia; with a low PaO₂ it is type 2 failure
  • Acute: high CO₂ + low pH (respiratory acidosis, normal bicarbonate)
  • Chronic: high CO₂ + raised bicarbonate (renal compensation) → a near-normal pH
Two axes tell the story: how high the CO₂ and how depressed the patient (vasodilatation → a bounding pulse and flap; CNS depression → drowsiness → narcosis), and acute vs chronic on the gas (a low pH means an acute or decompensated rise; a raised bicarbonate means chronic retention).

RESPIRATORY__Abnormal Percussion Note:
Percussion tells you what lies under your finger: air, fluid or solid. Read the note first, then let the other signs name the cause.
  • Resonant — normal.
  • Hyper-resonant — too much air (pneumothorax, COPD).
  • Dull — solid / airless lung (consolidation, collapse, mass).
  • Stony dull — fluid (a pleural effusion).
  • Always compare side-to-side and combine with breath sounds, vocal resonance and tracheal position (and the movement — see Reduced Chest Expansion).
🚨A hyper-resonant, silent hemithorax with the trachea pushed AWAY and hypotension is a tension pneumothorax — decompress immediately, before any chest X-ray. In trauma, a stony-dull, silent hemithorax with shock is a massive haemothorax — large-bore drainage and resuscitation. A febrile, unwell patient with a stony-dull effusion after pneumonia may have an empyema needing urgent drainage.

1Characterise it
🔍How to percuss & the four notes
  • Press a finger flat on the chest and strike its middle phalanx with the other middle finger; compare side-to-side
  • Percuss the front, axillae and back over matching zones (do not percuss over the scapulae)
  • Resonant = normal; hyper-resonant = air; dull = solid; stony dull = fluid
🚩The emergencies behind the note
  • Hyper-resonant + silent + trachea away + shocked → tension pneumothorax — decompress now
  • Stony dull + silent + shocked after trauma → massive haemothorax — drain & resuscitate
  • Stony dull + febrile / unwell after pneumonia → empyema — urgent drainage
💧Stony dull → fluid
  • Stony dull + reduced breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance → a pleural effusion
  • A large effusion pushes the trachea away; a haemothorax (trauma) or empyema (infected) percuss the same
🧱Dull → solid / airless lung
  • Dull + bronchial breathing + increased vocal resonance + crackles → consolidation
  • Dull + reduced breath sounds + trachea TOWARDS → lobar collapse
  • Dull over a mass (lung cancer) or an area of fibrosis
🎈Hyper-resonant → too much air
  • Hyper-resonant + absent breath sounds → a pneumothorax (trachea away if tension)
  • Bilateral hyper-resonance + quiet breath sounds + barrel chest → COPD / emphysema (or a large bulla)
🎯Normal dullness & pitfalls
  • Normal cardiac dullness (left lower sternal edge) and hepatic dullness (right lower zone)
  • Loss of cardiac / hepatic dullness → hyperinflation (COPD) or a pneumothorax
  • Compare like-for-like and combine with breath sounds, vocal resonance & the trachea — never percuss alone
Note first, then localise. Stony dull = fluid (effusion); dull = solid (consolidation, collapse, mass); hyper-resonant = air (pneumothorax, COPD). Then the breath sounds, vocal resonance and tracheal direction separate the causes within each group.

RESPIRATORY__Reduced Chest Expansion:
Reduced chest expansion is an inspection / palpation sign of underlying lung, pleural or chest-wall disease.
  • The cardinal rule: the side that moves less is the abnormal side.
  • Unilateral (one side) — localise it with the percussion note, breath sounds and tracheal position.
  • Bilateral (symmetrical) — COPD, fibrosis, ankylosing spondylitis, neuromuscular weakness.
  • Assess by placing your hands with the thumbs meeting in the midline and comparing how far each thumb travels.
  • Read it with the effort of breathing (see Increased Work of Breathing).
🚨A tension pneumothorax is the emergency: absent expansion on one side + a hyper-resonant, silent chest + the trachea pushed AWAY + hypotension / distress → decompress immediately (needle / finger thoracostomy) before any imaging. A massive haemothorax or effusion can compromise the same way. And bilateral reduced expansion with a falling FVC in neuromuscular weakness (Guillain-Barré / MND) signals impending ventilatory failure.

1Characterise it
🔍What it is & how to assess it
  • The side that moves less is the abnormal side — the pathology is under the reduced movement
  • Place your hands with the thumbs meeting in the midline and watch how far each thumb travels
  • Test anteriorly (upper lobes) and posteriorly (lower lobes); normal is ~5 cm. First split unilateral vs bilateral
🚩Tension pneumothorax & massive effusion
  • Absent expansion + hyper-resonant (pneumothorax) or stony dull (effusion / haemothorax)
  • + trachea pushed AWAY + hypotension / distress → a clinical emergency
  • → decompress / drain immediately, before any imaging
🫁Unilateral — combine with percussion & breath sounds
  • Stony dull + reduced breath sounds → pleural effusion
  • Hyper-resonant + absent breath sounds → pneumothorax
  • Dull + bronchial breathing + crackles → consolidation; dull + trachea TOWARDS → collapse
🎯Tracheal deviation — the localiser
  • Pushed AWAY by a tension pneumothorax or a massive effusion
  • Pulled TOWARDS a lobar collapse, a pneumonectomy or upper-lobe fibrosis
  • A central trachea with unilateral signs → consolidation or a small effusion / pneumothorax
🫁Bilateral (symmetrical) reduced expansion
  • COPD / hyperinflation (barrel chest), pulmonary fibrosis / ILD (fine crackles, clubbing)
  • Ankylosing spondylitis (chest expansion <5 cm, a fused spine), neuromuscular weakness (low FVC)
  • Kyphoscoliosis and severe obesity (a restrictive chest wall)
🤕Painful & splinting causes
  • Rib fractures, flail chest (a paradoxically moving segment), pleurisy and post-operative pain
  • The patient splints the painful side to guard it; and a raised hemidiaphragm (phrenic-nerve palsy)
Movement first, then localise. The reduced side is the abnormal side. For a unilateral reduction, the percussion note and tracheal direction name it: dull → effusion / consolidation / collapse; hyper-resonant → pneumothorax; trachea away → a big effusion / tension; trachea towards → collapse.

RESPIRATORY__Tachypnoea:
Tachypnoea is a raised respiratory rate (>20/min in an adult; normal 12–20).
  • The single most sensitive early sign of deterioration — often the first vital sign to change in sepsis, PE and acidosis — yet the most neglected.
  • It is about the rate, not the effort (see Increased Work of Breathing) or the rhythm (see Abnormal Breathing Patterns).
  • The differential spans every system, so work through it structurally — and never call it “just anxiety” until the sinister causes are excluded.
🚨A raised respiratory rate is a red flag until proven benign — it drives the NEWS2 score and predicts arrest. Exclude PE, sepsis, a metabolic acidosis (DKA / lactate) and hypoxia before attributing it to anxiety or pain. And beware the exhausted patient whose rate is now falling: a “normalising” rate with a rising CO2 or drowsiness is pre-arrest, not recovery (see Increased Work of Breathing).

1Characterise it
🔍What tachypnoea is & why it matters
  • Rate >20/min (normal 12–20) — the most sensitive early warning sign of deterioration
  • Count over a full 15–30 s and do not tell the patient you are counting (they alter it)
  • Judge the rate here, the effort separately (Increased Work of Breathing) and the rhythm (Abnormal Breathing Patterns)
🚩The sinister causes not to miss
  • PE, sepsis, a metabolic acidosis (DKA / lactate) and hypoxia / pneumonia
  • The tiring patient whose rate is falling with a rising CO2 / drowsiness → pre-arrest
  • → a raised rate is never “just anxiety” until these are excluded
🫁Respiratory causes
  • Asthma / COPD (wheeze), pneumonia (fever, crackles), PE (pleuritic, hypoxia)
  • Pneumothorax (hyper-resonant), effusion (stony dull), pulmonary fibrosis / ILD (fine crackles, clubbing)
❤️Cardiac & haematological causes
  • Pulmonary oedema (acute heart failure) — orthopnoea, crackles, pink frothy sputum
  • Shock / hypovolaemia and anaemia (compensating for reduced oxygen carriage) — pallor, fatigue
🧪Metabolic & endocrine causes
  • Metabolic acidosis → a compensatory Kussmaul pattern: DKA, sepsis / lactate, uraemia, salicylate
  • Fever, pain, thyrotoxicosis and pregnancy (progesterone raises the drive)
🧠Neurological & functional causes
  • Anxiety / panic (hyperventilation) — a diagnosis of exclusion with a normal chest, tingling and carpopedal spasm
  • CNS respiratory drive / stimulants / salicylate; and physiological tachypnoea (exercise, altitude)
A raised rate is a number, not a diagnosis: ask is the patient hypoxic? (a lung or cardiac cause), is the chest clear? (think a metabolic acidosis, anaemia or anxiety), and is the rate rising or falling? (a falling rate in a distressed patient is tiring / pre-arrest).

RESPIRATORY__Abnormal Breathing Patterns:
Abnormal breathing patterns are read from the rate, depth and rhythm of breathing — the shape of the respiratory cycle, not the effort behind it (for laboured breathing see Increased Work of Breathing).
  • Several patterns are named, each pointing to a cause: Cheyne-Stokes (heart failure / CNS), Kussmaul (metabolic acidosis), ataxic (Biot’s) and apneustic breathing (brainstem), and agonal gasping (cardiac arrest).
  • First exclude the peri-arrest and brainstem patterns, then let the pattern localise the cause.
🚨Agonal (gasping) breathing — slow, irregular gasps — is a sign of cardiac arrest: start CPR and call the arrest team. Ataxic (Biot’s), apneustic or an irregular slowing pattern with a falling GCS signal brainstem failure / raised intracranial pressure (coning) — get urgent senior and neuro help. A slow, shallow pattern with pinpoint pupils and drowsiness is opioid toxicity — give naloxone.
📷

1Characterise it
🔍How to describe a breathing pattern
  • Rate: normal 12–20/min; tachypnoea >20, bradypnoea <12
  • Depth (tidal volume): deep / normal / shallow; and rhythm: regular, periodic (cyclical) or irregular (ataxic)
  • Time the cycle and watch for apnoeas; then judge effort separately (see Increased Work of Breathing)
🚩Peri-arrest & brainstem patterns — must not miss
  • Agonal / gasping breathing (slow irregular gasps) → cardiac arrest — start CPR / ALS
  • Ataxic (Biot’s) or apneustic breathing + falling GCS → brainstem damage / raised ICP (coning)
  • → call for senior and neuro help now; protect the airway
🌊Cheyne-Stokes breathing
  • Cyclical crescendo–decrescendo depth with regular apnoeic pauses
  • → heart failure, stroke / CNS lesions, opioids, altitude and the end of life
🫁Kussmaul breathing
  • Deep, sighing, rapid but effortless breathing with a clear chest
  • → a metabolic acidosis: DKA, uraemia (kidney failure), sepsis / lactic acidosis
  • This is tachypnoea without increased work — check glucose, ketones, U&E and a gas
🐌Hypo- vs hyperventilation
  • Slow / shallow (hypoventilation) → opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils → naloxone), sedatives, CO2 narcosis, raised ICP (late), neuromuscular
  • Fast / deep (hyperventilation) → anxiety / pain, PE, metabolic acidosis (compensation), sepsis, salicylates
😮‍💨Dysfunctional & sleep-related patterns
  • Sighing / erratic breathing with a normal exam, peri-oral tingling and carpopedal spasm → hyperventilation (anxiety) syndrome
  • Periodic breathing with apnoeas during sleep → obstructive sleep apnoea (covered separately)
Read three things before naming a pattern: rate (fast / slow), depth (deep / shallow) and rhythm (regular / cyclical / irregular). A cyclical pattern with apnoeas is Cheyne-Stokes; a deep effortless pattern is Kussmaul; an irregular / gasping pattern is brainstem failure or arrest.

RESPIRATORY__Increased Work of Breathing:
Increased work of breathing is the patient in respiratory distress — breathing that is visibly laboured, not just fast.
  • Not the same as tachypnoea: a raised rate can be a deep, effortless compensation for a metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing in DKA / sepsis), whereas true increased work recruits the accessory muscles and causes recession, tracheal tug and nasal flaring.
  • First recognise the exhausted (tiring) patient heading for arrest.
  • Then decide effort vs metabolic drive, find the cause, and grade the respiratory failure. See also Stridor for the upper airway.
🚨The tiring patient is a pre-arrest emergency: a falling respiratory rate, a silent chest, drowsiness / confusion, cyanosis, bradycardia and paradoxical (see-saw) breathing mean impending respiratory failure — call for senior help and support ventilation (oxygen, NIV or intubation). Do not be reassured by a “settling” rate or a quieter chest in a patient who is exhausted — it can mean the airflow, not the disease, is failing.

1Characterise it
🔍What increased work of breathing looks like
  • Accessory-muscle use (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes), tracheal tug, nasal flaring
  • Intercostal / subcostal / sternal recession, grunting and head-bobbing (infants), pursed-lip breathing
  • Tripod posture and an inability to speak in full sentences
🚩The exhausted (tiring) patient — pre-arrest
  • Falling respiratory rate, a silent chest, drowsiness / confusion, cyanosis, bradycardia
  • Paradoxical (see-saw) breathing → impending respiratory arrest
  • → call for senior help, support ventilation (O2 / NIV / intubation)
🧪Effort, or a metabolic drive? (WOB vs tachypnoea)
  • Laboured, accessory muscles + recession → an airway / lung problem
  • Deep, rapid but effortless with a clear chest → metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul: DKA, sepsis / lactate)
  • So tachypnoea is not always increased work — check glucose, ketones and an ABG / lactate
🫁Airway & lung causes
  • Wheeze → asthma / COPD / anaphylaxis; stridor → upper airway (see Stridor)
  • Fever + crackles → pneumonia; hyper-resonant → pneumothorax; stony dull → effusion
  • Pleuritic + hypoxia + VTE risk → PE
💪Cardiac, neuromuscular & CNS causes
  • Crackles + orthopnoea + pink frothy → pulmonary oedema (acute heart failure)
  • Weak, shallow, paradoxical breathing + bulbar signs → Guillain-Barré / myasthenia (measure FVC, not just sats)
  • Abnormal patterns (Cheyne-Stokes) → CNS / brainstem or heart failure
🩺Grade it & check for respiratory failure
  • RR, SpO2, ability to speak, and the work-of-breathing signs above
  • ABG: Type 1 (low PaO2, normal / low CO2) vs Type 2 (low PaO2 + high CO2 — tiring / COPD)
Two judgements come before the diagnosis: is the patient tiring (falling rate, silent chest, drowsy = pre-arrest), and is this true effort (accessory muscles, recession → airway / lung) or an effortless metabolic drive (Kussmaul → acidosis)? Tachypnoea and increased work are not the same.

RESPIRATORY__Chronic Sputum Production:
Chronic sputum production is the story of a mucus-making airway.
  • First define it — a productive cough on most days for months — then read the sputum (volume, colour, purulence, blood, smell) and the pattern.
  • Smoker + mucoid daily cough = chronic bronchitis / COPD.
  • Copious daily purulent sputum + recurrent infections = bronchiectasis (think cystic fibrosis in the young).
  • Foul, large-volume sputum + swinging fever = lung abscess.
  • A change in a smoker’s sputum, blood or weight loss = cancer or TB until excluded. See also Cough and Haemoptysis.
🚨A change in the character of a chronic cough in a smoker, new haemoptysis, or weight loss needs an urgent chest X-ray and 2-week-wait referral for lung cancer; consider TB with night sweats, weight loss and risk factors. Foul, putrid sputum with a swinging fever points to a lung abscess (often after aspiration). In a child, recurrent infections with failure to thrive is cystic fibrosis until excluded.

1Characterise it
🗓️Define it — is it chronic bronchitis?
  • A productive cough on most days for ≥3 months a year, over ≥2 consecutive years (the clinical definition)
  • Usually a smoker — part of the COPD spectrum; mucoid sputum turning purulent in exacerbations
🪣Read the sputum — volume, colour, purulence
  • Mucoid (clear / white) → chronic bronchitis, asthma
  • Purulent (yellow / green) → infection; copious daily purulent → bronchiectasis / CF
  • Foul, large-volume → anaerobes (lung abscess); blood-streaked → cancer / TB / bronchiectasis
🫁Copious daily purulent → bronchiectasis
  • Recurrent chest infections, clubbing, coarse crackles, and the classic “three-layer” sputum
  • Confirm with high-resolution CT (dilated, thick-walled airways — the ‘signet-ring’ sign)
👶Young or lifelong → CF & PCD
  • Cystic fibrosis — recurrent infections (Pseudomonas, Staph), steatorrhoea, poor growth, infertility; sweat test
  • Primary ciliary dyskinesia / Kartagener — bronchiectasis + situs inversus + infertility + sinusitis
🔍Colour & smell shortcuts
  • Rusty → pneumococcal pneumonia; foul / putrid → anaerobic (abscess / bronchiectasis)
  • Blood-streaked → cancer, TB, bronchiectasis (see Haemoptysis); black → smoke / coal dust
🚩Red flags
  • New haemoptysis, weight loss, or a persistent change in a smoker’s cough / sputum → lung cancer (urgent CXR / 2WW)
  • Night sweats + weight loss → TB; foul sputum + swinging fever → lung abscess
Two things decide it: who (a smoker → chronic bronchitis / COPD; the young → CF) and what the sputum looks like (mucoid → bronchitis; copious purulent → bronchiectasis; foul → abscess; blood-streaked → cancer / TB). A changed cough in a smoker is cancer until proven otherwise.

RESPIRATORY__Pleuritic Chest Pain:
Pleuritic chest pain — sharp pain that is worse on deep inspiration, coughing or movement — localises to the pleura, pericardium or chest wall.
  • Exclude the killers first: a pulmonary embolism and a pneumothorax (tension is an immediate emergency), then pneumonia and pericarditis.
  • Only when those are cleared is it safe to settle on a musculoskeletal or viral cause.
  • And “pleuritic” does not exclude a heart attack or aortic dissection. For crushing, central, non-pleuritic pain, see Chest Pain.
🚨Sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness and hypoxia is a PE or a pneumothorax until proven otherwise. A tension pneumothorax — a deviated trachea, distended neck veins and hypotension — needs immediate needle decompression, NOT a chest X-ray. Don’t be falsely reassured that a “sharp, catching” pain rules out ACS or aortic dissection, especially in diabetics, women and the elderly.

1Characterise it
🔍Is it truly pleuritic?
  • Sharp, worse on deep inspiration, coughing or movement → pleura, pericardium or chest wall
  • NOT the crushing central pressure of ACS or the tearing pain of dissection
  • But these can mimic or coexist — keep them in mind, especially if atypical
🩸First & commonest killer — PE
  • Pleuritic + breathless ± haemoptysis, tachycardia, hypoxia
  • VTE risk: surgery, immobility, malignancy, OCP / pregnancy, prior VTE
  • Often few signs and a normal CXR → Wells score → D-dimer / CTPA
🫁Pneumothorax?
  • Sudden pleuritic + breathless, hyper-resonant + reduced breath sounds
  • Tall thin young person, COPD, or trauma
  • Tension: deviated trachea + distended neck veins + hypotension → immediate needle decompression
🤒Infection — pneumonia / pleurisy?
  • Fever, productive cough, focal crackles / bronchial breathing / dullness
  • A pleural rub and raised inflammatory markers → CXR consolidation
❤️Pericarditis?
  • Sharp, worse lying flat / better sitting forward, a pericardial rub, viral prodrome
  • ECG: saddle-shaped ST elevation + PR depression (widespread)
  • Watch for a pericardial effusion / tamponade
🧱Chest wall & mimics (once killers excluded)
  • Reproducible on palpation → costochondritis / rib fracture
  • Dermatomal pain ± vesicles → herpes zoster (shingles); young + epidemic myalgia → Bornholm
  • Reconsider ACS / aortic dissection if the picture is atypical
Pleuritic pain is a pleura / pericardium / chest-wall problem, but the discipline is to exclude PE and pneumothorax first — both can be lethal with a near-normal examination. Reproducibility on palpation points to the chest wall, but only after the killers are cleared.

RESPIRATORY__Stridor:
Stridor — a harsh, high-pitched sound from turbulent flow through a narrowed upper airway (larynx / trachea) — is a red-flag sign of airway obstruction, not a diagnosis.
  • It is usually inspiratory (above the cords) and must not be confused with wheeze (lower airway, expiratory).
  • The first job is never the diagnosis — it is the airway: is it critical?
  • Then the differential splits by age (child vs adult) and onset (sudden vs progressive).
  • One golden rule saves lives: in suspected epiglottitis, do NOT examine the throat or distress the child.
🚨Signs of a critical airway — exhaustion, drowsiness, cyanosis, drooling and tripod positioning, or a softening stridor with worsening distress (a tiring airway) — mean impending complete obstruction: call a senior anaesthetist and ENT now, give oxygen, and do not leave the patient. Anaphylaxis needs IM adrenaline immediately. In suspected epiglottitis, keep the child calm on a parent’s lap, do not lie them down or examine the throat, and secure the airway in theatre. Suspect an inhalation injury (facial burns, soot, singed nasal hairs, hoarse voice) and intubate early, before swelling closes the airway.

1Characterise it
🚨First — is the airway critical?
  • Exhaustion, drowsiness, cyanosis, or a softening stridor with rising distress (a tiring airway) → impending obstruction
  • Drooling, tripod position, unable to speak / swallow → call a senior anaesthetist + ENT now, don’t leave
  • Give oxygen; prepare for a difficult airway / surgical airway
🔊Stridor, wheeze or stertor?
  • Stridor: harsh, high-pitched, usually inspiratory → upper airway (larynx / trachea)
  • Inspiratory = supraglottic; biphasic / expiratory = glottic / subglottic / tracheal
  • Wheeze = expiratory, lower airway (asthma / COPD); stertor = snoring-like, nasopharyngeal
👶Child or adult? (changes the differential)
  • Child: croup (commonest), epiglottitis, inhaled foreign body, laryngomalacia (infant)
  • Adult: anaphylaxis / angioedema, laryngeal tumour, post-intubation stenosis, vocal-cord palsy
⚡Acute or progressive?
  • Sudden → inhaled foreign body, anaphylaxis, inhalation burn
  • Over hours + fever → croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis
  • Over weeks → tumour, subglottic stenosis, goitre, bilateral vocal-cord palsy
🔍Read the associated features
  • Barking cough + coryza, worse at night, looks well-ish → croup
  • Drooling, tripod, toxic, high fever, NO cough, muffled voice → epiglottitis
  • Urticaria + angioedema + exposure ± hypotension → anaphylaxis
  • Choking episode, previously well → inhaled foreign body; hoarse + smoker + weight loss → laryngeal tumour
🚫The golden rules — don’t make it worse
  • Suspected epiglottitis: do NOT examine the throat or lie the child flat → keep calm with a parent, theatre for the airway + IV antibiotics
  • Nebulised adrenaline buys time (croup, severe oedema); IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis
  • Inhalation injury → intubate early, before oedema closes the airway
Stridor is a symptom of a narrowing airway, so the sequence is airway first, diagnosis second. Inspiratory stridor localises above the cords; the patient’s age and the speed of onset then narrow the cause — and the one move that harms is examining the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis.

RESPIRATORY__Cough:
Cough is one of the commonest reasons to see a doctor, and the single most useful question is “how long?”
  • Acute (<3 weeks) is usually infective — a viral URTI, or pneumonia if unwell.
  • Chronic (>8 weeks) in a non-smoker with a normal chest X-ray is nearly always one of the big three — upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip), asthma or GORD — and don’t forget an ACE inhibitor.
  • Then read the sputum, timing and red flags: a chronic cough in a smoker, or with haemoptysis, weight loss or night sweats, means cancer or TB until excluded.
🚨A cough lasting more than 3 weeks — especially in a smoker or with haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats or a hoarse voice — needs an urgent chest X-ray and a 2-week-wait referral for suspected lung cancer; think TB with fevers, night sweats and risk factors. Don’t miss a sudden cough with choking (inhaled foreign body, especially a child), an acutely breathless cough with pink frothy sputum (pulmonary oedema), or cough with pleuritic pain and haemoptysis (PE).

1Characterise it
⏱️How long has it lasted? (the master key)
  • <3 weeks (acute) → usually infective — viral URTI, acute bronchitis, or pneumonia if unwell
  • 3–8 weeks (subacute) → often post-infective (post-viral, pertussis)
  • >8 weeks (chronic) → the big three, an ACE inhibitor, or a red-flag cause
💧Dry or productive — read the sputum
  • Purulent / coloured → infection; copious daily purulent → bronchiectasis
  • Pink, frothy → pulmonary oedema; rusty → pneumococcal pneumonia
  • Dry → asthma, ILD, ACE inhibitor, GORD, post-viral
  • Blood (haemoptysis) → cancer, TB, PE, bronchiectasis
🌙When does it happen, and what triggers it?
  • Nocturnal + wheeze, atopy / triggers → asthma
  • Worse lying flat / after meals + acid brash → GORD
  • Throat-clearing, postnasal drip, blocked nose → upper airway cough syndrome
  • Nocturnal + orthopnoea + pink frothy → heart failure
💊Ask about ACE inhibitors & the environment
  • Dry cough weeks–months after starting an ACE inhibitor → drug cough (settles on stopping)
  • Occupational, bird or mould exposure → occupational asthma / hypersensitivity pneumonitis
🎯Chronic + non-smoker + normal CXR → the big three
  • Upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip)
  • Asthma / cough-variant asthma
  • GORD
  • They often coexist — treat each in turn
🚩Red flags — cancer, TB, foreign body
  • Smoker, >3 weeks, haemoptysis, weight loss, hoarse voice → lung cancer → urgent CXR / 2WW
  • Night sweats, weight loss, haemoptysis, risk factors → TB
  • Sudden choking cough (especially a child) → inhaled foreign body
Two questions do most of the work: how long (acute infective vs chronic big-three) and dry or productive (dry → asthma / ILD / ACE inhibitor / GORD; productive → infection / COPD / bronchiectasis). And always take a drug history — an ACE-inhibitor cough is common, dry and reversible.

RESPIRATORY__Foundations of Respiratory:
Overview — Mechanics of Ventilation
Ventilation = moving air in and out of the lungs — a mechanical process driven by pressure gradients created by changing the volume of the thorax.
The organising principle: air flows down pressure gradients (Boyle's law — ↑volume → ↓pressure → air flows in). Breathing changes thoracic volume; the lung's elastic recoil + the chest wall's outward pull set up the forces to overcome.
Why it matters: underpins obstructive vs restrictive disease, pneumothorax, work of breathing, and COPD/asthma/fibrosis behaviour — cross-ref lung volumes/spirometry, COPD, asthma, pneumothorax, respiratory failure.
The Pressures Involved — breathing is pressure differences
Pressure What it is Key point
AtmosphericOutside air (reference, = 0)Air flows in when alveolar P < this
Alveolar (intrapulmonary)Inside the alveoliNegative in inspiration (draws air in), positive in expiration
IntrapleuralIn the pleural spaceNegative at rest (~−5 cmH₂O at FRC) — the "vacuum" holding the lung open; can turn positive in forced expiration or tension pneumothorax
TranspulmonaryAlveolar − intrapleuralThe distending pressure keeping alveoli open
The intrapleural negative pressure is the key concept: the lung tends to collapse inward (elastic recoil), the chest wall tends to spring outward — these opposing pulls create a negative intrapleural pressure that keeps the lung expanded.
This is why a pneumothorax collapses the lung: air entering the pleural space abolishes the negative pressure → the lung recoils shut.
The Mechanics of a Breath
Inspiration (active)
  • Diaphragm contracts + descends (the main muscle, ~⅔ of the work) + external intercostals lift the ribs ("bucket handle")
  • → thoracic volume ↑ → intrapleural pressure more negative → alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric → air flows in
  • Accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) recruited in exertion/distress — the clinical sign of ↑work of breathing
Expiration (passive at rest)
  • Muscles relax → elastic recoil pulls the lung back → thoracic volume ↓ → alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric → air flows out
  • Forced expiration is active: internal intercostals + abdominal muscles (exercise, COPD)
Compliance — how stretchy the lung is
Compliance = change in volume per unit change in pressure (how easily the lung expands). It changes oppositely in the two big disease categories:
Compliance Disease Mechanism
↑ compliance (too stretchy, poor recoil)Emphysema (COPD)Destroyed elastic tissue → lungs over-distend, air trapping
↓ compliance (stiff, hard to inflate)Pulmonary fibrosis, oedema, ARDSStiff/fibrotic or fluid-filled lung
Surfactant's role: produced by type II pneumocytes, it reduces alveolar surface tension → prevents collapse + increases compliance → less work to inflate. Surfactant deficiency in prematurity → neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (stiff lungs, alveolar collapse).
Surface Tension & Laplace's Law — why surfactant matters
  • Alveoli are fluid-lined → surface tension tends to collapse them
  • Laplace's law: pressure tending to collapse an alveolus ∝ tension / radius → small alveoli have higher collapsing pressure → would empty into large ones
  • Surfactant solves this: it lowers surface tension more in small alveoli → stabilises them, prevents collapse, and equalises pressures across different-sized alveoli
Resistance & the Work of Breathing — the obstructive side
  • Airway resistance governs flow (like the vascular Poiseuille r⁴ point — radius dominates): bronchoconstriction, mucus, or airway narrowing ↑ resistance → ↑work of breathing
  • The obstructive disease link: asthma (bronchospasm), COPD (airway narrowing + collapse) → ↑airway resistance → expiratory flow limitation (air trapping; expiration is the problem → prolonged expiratory phase + wheeze)
  • Work of breathing = overcoming (a) elastic forces (elastic work is high in fibrosis — low compliance/stiff lung) + (b) resistive forces (airway resistance — high in asthma/COPD); raised in both disease types but for different reasons
Clinical Relevance — obstructive vs restrictive
Concept Mechanics explanation
Obstructive (COPD/asthma)↑airway resistance + (emphysema) ↑compliance/air trapping → trouble getting air OUT (expiratory limitation)
Restrictive (fibrosis)↓compliance (stiff lung) → trouble getting air IN
PneumothoraxAir in pleural space → loss of negative intrapleural pressure → lung recoils + collapses
Accessory muscle use / tracheal tugClinical sign of ↑work of breathing (distress)
Neonatal RDSSurfactant deficiency → ↓compliance + alveolar collapse
PEEP / CPAPApplied positive pressure keeps alveoli open (counteracts collapse)
⭐ Key Points
Driving force
Breathing = pressure gradients from changing thoracic volume (Boyle's law); air flows in when alveolar P < atmospheric.
Intrapleural pressure
Negative at rest (lung recoils in, chest wall springs out) — holds the lung open; can turn positive in forced expiration/tension pneumothorax; lost in pneumothorax → collapse.
The breath
Inspiration = active (diaphragm + external intercostals); expiration = passive at rest (elastic recoil), active when forced.
Compliance
Volume change per pressure: ↑ in emphysema (floppy), ↓ in fibrosis/oedema (stiff).
Surfactant
Type II pneumocytes ↓surface tension → ↑compliance + stabilises alveoli (Laplace); deficiency → neonatal RDS.
Airway resistance
Radius-dependent; ↑ in asthma/COPD → expiratory flow limitation + air trapping.
The big split
Obstructive = trouble getting air OUT (↑resistance); restrictive = trouble getting air IN (↓compliance).
Overview — Lung Volumes & Spirometry
Lung volumes quantify how much air the lungs hold and move; spirometry measures them to characterise lung disease.
The organising principle: the mechanics from the previous note (compliance, airway resistance) translate into measurable volumes and flow rates — and the single most useful output is the FEV1/FVC ratio, which separates obstructive from restrictive disease.
Why it matters: how COPD, asthma and fibrosis are diagnosed and monitored — cross-ref mechanics of ventilation, COPD, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, restrictive disease.
Lung Volumes & Capacities
Volumes are single; capacities are sums of volumes.
Volume Definition
Tidal volume (TV)Air moved in a normal quiet breath (~500 mL)
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)Extra air that can be inhaled beyond TV
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)Extra air that can be exhaled beyond TV
Residual volume (RV)Air left after maximal expiration — keeps alveoli open; cannot be measured by spirometry
Capacity (= sum) Definition
Inspiratory capacity (IC)TV + IRV
Functional residual capacity (FRC)ERV + RV — air left after a normal expiration (resting end-expiratory point)
Vital capacity (VC)IRV + TV + ERV — max air moved in one breath
Total lung capacity (TLC)VC + RV — everything the lungs can hold
The "can't measure" point: RV, FRC, and TLC include residual volume → spirometry can't measure them (you can't blow out the air that stays behind) → they need body plethysmography or helium dilution.
Spirometry — the Key Measurements
Measure Definition
FVC (forced vital capacity)Total volume forcibly exhaled after a maximal breath in
FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 s)Volume exhaled in the first second
FEV1/FVC ratioThe single most important value — proportion exhaled in 1 second (normally >0.7 / >70%)
The Obstructive vs Restrictive Fork — the whole point of spirometry
Obstructive Restrictive
ProblemAirflow limitation (↑resistance) — trouble getting air OUTReduced expansion (↓compliance) — trouble getting air IN
FEV1↓↓↓
FVC↓ or normal↓↓
FEV1/FVC ratio<0.7 (LOW) — the hallmark≥0.7 (normal/high) — the hallmark
Lung volumes↑ RV, ↑ TLC (air trapping/hyperinflation)↓ all volumes (small stiff lungs)
ExamplesCOPD, asthma, bronchiectasisPulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis; chest-wall/neuromuscular (obesity, kyphoscoliosis, MND)
The one rule: FEV1/FVC <0.7 = obstructive; FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 with a reduced FVC suggests restriction — but spirometry alone cannot confirm it. A low FVC with a preserved ratio can also be gas trapping in severe obstruction, or poor effort, so true restriction needs a reduced TLC on lung volumes.
The logic: obstruction = high airway resistance → slow expiration → FEV1 drops more than FVC → ratio falls; restriction = stiff small lungs → FEV1 and FVC drop proportionally → ratio preserved. Air trapping in obstruction → ↑RV + ↑TLC (the COPD "barrel chest").
Reversibility — Asthma vs COPD
Bronchodilator reversibility testing: give salbutamol and repeat spirometry. Note: current NICE/BTS/SIGN guidance leads asthma diagnosis with FeNO and blood eosinophils, with bronchodilator reversibility as a supportive test.
Asthma
Reversible obstruction → FEV1 improves significantly (≥12% + 200 mL) → variable/reversible airflow limitation.
COPD
Largely irreversible → little improvement → fixed airflow limitation.
A core part of distinguishing the two obstructive diseases (cross-ref asthma/COPD).
Flow-Volume Loops & PEFR
  • Flow-volume loop (flow vs volume during a forced breath) — the shape is diagnostic:
    • Obstructive: scooped-out/concave expiratory limb (COPD/asthma)
    • Restrictive: tall narrow loop (small volumes, preserved flows)
    • Upper airway obstruction: flattened loop
  • Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR): the fastest expiratory flow — a simple bedside/home measure; used to monitor asthma (diurnal variability, treatment response)
Other Useful Measures
  • Transfer factor (TLCO/DLCO) — gas transfer capacity (CO uptake): ↓ in emphysema + fibrosis (loss of functioning alveolar-capillary surface), ↑ in alveolar haemorrhage (extra haemoglobin to bind CO) — ties to the gas exchange note
  • FRC is the physiologically important "resting" volume — where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall pull (from the mechanics note)
Clinical Relevance
Concept Spirometry explanation
COPD diagnosisPost-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 (fixed); severity graded by FEV1 % predicted
AsthmaObstructive (↓ratio) but reversible; PEFR for monitoring
Pulmonary fibrosisRestrictive (↓FVC, normal/high ratio, ↓TLC, ↓TLCO)
Air trapping/hyperinflation↑RV + ↑TLC in COPD (barrel chest)
Neuromuscular/chest-wall diseaseRestrictive picture with normal lungs (the bellows fail, not the lung)
Transfer factorDistinguishes causes — ↓ in emphysema/fibrosis, ↑ in pulmonary haemorrhage
⭐ Key Points
Volumes vs capacities
Volumes (single) vs capacities (sums); RV, FRC, TLC include residual volume → NOT measurable by spirometry (need plethysmography/helium dilution).
The key value
FEV1/FVC ratio (normal >0.7).
Obstructive
FEV1/FVC <0.7 (↓↓FEV1, ↑RV/TLC air trapping) — COPD, asthma; trouble getting air OUT.
Restrictive
FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 (↓↓FVC, ↓TLC) — fibrosis, chest-wall/neuromuscular; trouble getting air IN.
Reversibility
Asthma reverses with bronchodilator (≥12% + 200 mL); COPD doesn't (fixed).
Monitoring & shape
PEFR monitors asthma; flow-volume loop shape is diagnostic (obstructive = scooped).
Transfer factor (TLCO)
↓ emphysema + fibrosis, ↑ alveolar haemorrhage.
Overview — Gas Exchange & Diffusion
Gas exchange = transfer of O₂ from alveoli into blood and CO₂ from blood into alveoli, across the alveolar-capillary membrane.
The organising principle: gases move by passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients — driven by the partial-pressure difference and governed by the membrane's properties (Fick's law).
Why it matters: explains the two types of respiratory failure, why fibrosis/oedema/emphysema cause hypoxia, and the basis of the transfer factor — cross-ref mechanics + spirometry, V/Q matching, respiratory failure, pneumonia, fibrosis, the O₂-dissociation curve.
The Alveolar-Capillary Membrane
📷 Image placeholder — Cross-section of the alveolar–capillary membrane (alveolar epithelium → fused basement membranes → capillary endothelium) with O₂ and CO₂ diffusing across.
  • Gas exchange occurs across the extremely thin respiratory membrane: alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocytes) + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium — only ~0.5 µm thick
  • Designed for diffusion: huge surface area (~70 m²), very thin, richly perfused — optimised for rapid gas transfer
  • The membrane is what fails in disease: thickening (fibrosis, oedema) or loss of surface area (emphysema, pneumonia) impairs diffusion
Fick's Law of Diffusion — the governing equation
Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × partial-pressure gradient × solubility) / membrane thickness.
Factor ↑Diffusion Impaired in
Surface areaLarger = more transferEmphysema (alveolar destruction), pneumonectomy
Membrane thicknessThinner = fasterFibrosis, pulmonary oedema (thickened/fluid-filled)
Partial-pressure gradientBigger = more transferAltitude (↓inspired O₂), hypoventilation
Gas solubilityMore soluble = faster(explains the CO₂ vs O₂ difference below)
Clinical payoff: every diffusion-impairing disease works through one of these — fibrosis/oedema = ↑thickness, emphysema = ↓surface area → both reduce the transfer factor (TLCO).
CO₂ vs O₂ — the key asymmetry
  • CO₂ is ~20× more soluble than O₂ → it diffuses far more readily
  • The consequence: in diffusion-limited disease (fibrosis), O₂ transfer fails before CO₂ transfer → hypoxia occurs early, CO₂ retention is late → early lung disease causes hypoxia with a normal or low CO₂
  • CO₂ removal is ventilation-dependent (it diffuses easily, so its clearance depends on how much you breathe), whereas O₂ uptake is more diffusion-dependent — this underlies the two types of respiratory failure
Partial Pressures & the Gradients
Alveolus Venous (arriving) Arterial (leaving)
O₂~13.3 kPa (100 mmHg)~5.3 kPa~11–13 kPa — a little below alveolar because of the normal physiological shunt (this is the A–a gradient)
CO₂~5.3 kPa (40 mmHg)~6.1 kPa~5.3 kPa (equilibrated)
  • O₂ diffuses alveolus → blood (down its gradient); CO₂ diffuses blood → alveolus (down its gradient)
  • Equilibration is normally complete well before blood leaves the capillary (lots of reserve) — so diffusion problems only show under stress (exercise) until severe
  • The alveolar gas equation (concept): alveolar O₂ depends on inspired O₂ minus the CO₂ being added — the basis for the A–a gradient
The A–a Gradient & Types of Respiratory Failure
The alveolar-arterial (A–a) gradient = difference between alveolar O₂ and arterial O₂; it tells you whether the problem is in the lung (gas exchange) or in ventilation. Normal A–a ≈ <2 kPa, widening with age.
Type 1 respiratory failure Type 2 respiratory failure
DefinitionHypoxaemia — PaO₂ <8 kPa (60 mmHg), normal/low CO₂Hypoxaemia + hypercapnia — PaO₂ <8 kPa + PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa
MechanismGas exchange failure (V/Q mismatch, diffusion defect, shunt)Ventilatory failure (not moving enough air)
A–a gradientRaised (lung problem — O₂ can't cross)Normal (if pure hypoventilation — bellows fail, lung fine)
CausesPneumonia (consolidation → behaves as a shunt), PE, pulmonary oedema, fibrosis, asthma (early — a tiring asthmatic moves to Type 2)COPD (severe), respiratory muscle weakness, opioid overdose, chest-wall disease
The CO₂ logic: in Type 1 the highly-soluble CO₂ still clears (often blown off → low CO₂), only O₂ fails; in Type 2, ventilation itself fails → CO₂ accumulates. Raised A–a gradient = the problem is in the lung; normal A–a with hypoxia = hypoventilation (or low inspired O₂).
Causes of Hypoxaemia — the five mechanisms
Mechanism A–a gradient Responds to O₂? Example
V/Q mismatch (commonest)RaisedYesPneumonia, PE, COPD
Shunt (blood bypasses ventilated alveoli)RaisedPoorly (the hallmark)Consolidation, ARDS, cardiac shunt

HypoventilationNormalYesOpioid overdose, neuromuscular

The shunt point: a true shunt doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ (the blood never contacts ventilated alveoli) — distinguishes it from V/Q mismatch.
Hypoxaemia vs Hypoxia — the four types (high-yield)
These are not the same word. Hypoxaemia = a low PaO₂ in the blood. Hypoxia = inadequate oxygen at the tissues. The five mechanisms above all cause hypoxaemia — but a patient can be profoundly hypoxic with a completely normal PaO₂ and SpO₂. Getting oxygen to a mitochondrion needs four things to work: enough O₂ in the blood, enough haemoglobin to carry it, enough flow to deliver it, and a cell able to use it. Each failure has its own name.
TypeThe failurePaO₂ / SpO₂Examples
HypoxaemicNot enough O₂ gets into the bloodLowThe five mechanisms above — V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defect, hypoventilation, low inspired O₂
AnaemicBlood is fully saturated but there is too little (or unusable) haemoglobin to carry O₂Normal PaO₂; SpO₂ normal in anaemia and falsely normal in CO poisoning — but characteristically stuck near 85% in methaemoglobinaemia (a “saturation gap”), unresponsive to oxygenAnaemia, haemorrhage, carbon monoxide poisoning, methaemoglobinaemia
Stagnant (circulatory)Oxygenated blood is not being delivered — flow is the problemNormalShock of any cause, cardiac failure, limb ischaemia, cardiac arrest
HistotoxicDelivery is fine but the cell cannot use the O₂NormalCyanide (blocks cytochrome c oxidase), carbon monoxide again, sepsis (mitochondrial dysfunction)
⭐ The reason this matters at the bedside: three of the four types leave the PaO₂ and SpO₂ entirely normal. A saturation of 99% with a lactate of 6 is not a contradiction — it is anaemic, stagnant or histotoxic hypoxia, and the pulse oximeter is blind to all three. This is also why oxygen alone does not fix them: you cannot oximeter your way out of shock, and giving O₂ to an anaemic patient adds only the tiny dissolved fraction. Treat the cause — transfuse, restore perfusion, give hydroxocobalamin.
🔬 The venous oxygen clue. In stagnant hypoxia, sluggish flow gives the tissues a long time to strip oxygen out → the venous O₂ saturation is low and the arteriovenous difference is wide. In histotoxic hypoxia (cyanide) the cells cannot extract O₂ at all → the venous O₂ saturation is high and the arteriovenous difference is narrow, alongside a lactic acidosis. A high venous saturation in a shocked, acidotic patient should make you think of cyanide (cross-ref toxicology).

⭐ Key Points
Hypoxaemia ≠ hypoxia
Hypoxaemia = low PaO₂ in the blood; hypoxia = not enough O₂ at the tissues. A patient can be profoundly hypoxic with a normal PaO₂ and SpO₂.
Four types of hypoxia
Hypoxaemic (low PaO₂) · anaemic (anaemia, CO) · stagnant (shock) · histotoxic (cyanide). Only the first shows on the oximeter — and only the first is fixed by oxygen.
The process
Passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane (type I pneumocytes).
Fick's law
Diffusion ∝ (surface area × gradient × solubility) / thickness → fibrosis/oedema = ↑thickness, emphysema = ↓surface area.
CO₂ vs O₂
CO₂ ~20× more soluble → in diffusion defects, hypoxia comes first, CO₂ retention late; CO₂ clearance is ventilation-dependent.
Type 1 failure
Hypoxaemia alone (gas exchange problem, raised A–a gradient) — pneumonia, PE, fibrosis.
Type 2 failure
Hypoxaemia + hypercapnia (ventilatory failure, normal A–a gradient if pure) — COPD, neuromuscular, opioids.
Five causes of hypoxaemia
V/Q mismatch, shunt (doesn't correct with O₂), diffusion defect, hypoventilation, low inspired O₂.
TLCO
The diffusion-capacity measure (↓ fibrosis + emphysema).
Overview — Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve
Once O₂ diffuses into the blood, it is carried bound to haemoglobin. The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve describes how saturated Hb is at any given oxygen partial pressure (PO₂).
The organising principle: the curve is sigmoid (S-shaped), not linear — and that shape is functionally brilliant. It lets Hb load O₂ fully in the lungs (flat top) yet unload it readily in the tissues (steep middle). Shifts in the curve fine-tune O₂ delivery to where it is needed.
P50 = the PO₂ at which Hb is 50% saturated (normal ~3.5 kPa / 26–27 mmHg) — the standard index of shifts: right shift = ↑P50 (lower affinity), left shift = ↓P50 (higher affinity).
Why it matters: explains why SpO₂ can stay normal until PaO₂ falls dangerously, why CO poisoning is lethal, and how acidosis/exercise improve O₂ delivery to tissues — cross-ref gas exchange (previous subtab), CO₂ transport (next), anaemia, CO poisoning.
Oxygen Carriage in Blood — the context
  • O₂ is carried two ways: ~98.5% bound to haemoglobin (1 Hb carries 4 O₂) and ~1.5% dissolved in plasma
  • The implication: O₂ delivery depends overwhelmingly on Hb concentration + Hb saturation, not dissolved O₂ → which is why anaemia reduces O₂ delivery even with a normal PaO₂/SpO₂ (less Hb to carry it)
  • Oxygen content ≈ (Hb × SaO₂ × 1.34) + dissolved — the carriage equation (concept-level)

Conversely, giving extra O₂ to an already-saturated patient adds little (you are on the plateau).

The Bohr effect (the key one): actively metabolising tissue produces CO₂, acid, and heat → shifts the curve right → Hb unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed most (working muscle) — an elegant feedback. The lungs do the reverse (blow off CO₂ → left shift → loading).
Mnemonic: "right = release" (a right shift releases O₂); a right shift is generally good for tissue delivery.
The High-Yield Special Cases — left shifts that matter clinically
Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
  • Left-shifted (higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA) → lets the fetus pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (fetal Hb grabs O₂ that maternal Hb releases)
Carbon monoxide (the lethal one)
  • CO binds Hb with ~250× the affinity of O₂ → forms carboxyhaemoglobin, and left-shifts the curve (the remaining O₂ is held more tightly, released less) → a double hit: less O₂ carried and less released to tissues
  • The CO/SpO₂ trap: pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb → SpO₂ reads falsely normal in CO poisoning → need co-oximetry (cross-ref CO poisoning/toxicology)

Overview — CO₂ Transport
CO₂ produced by tissue metabolism must be carried in the blood to the lungs for excretion — and it is transported three ways, dominated by conversion to bicarbonate.
The organising principle: most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), generated inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase — which is why CO₂ transport and acid-base balance are the same chemistry (CO₂ + water ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ bicarbonate + H⁺).
Why it matters: the bridge between respiratory physiology and acid-base balance — it explains respiratory acidosis/alkalosis, the bicarbonate buffer, and CO₂ retention in respiratory failure — cross-ref O₂ dissociation curve (previous subtab), acid-base balance, respiratory failure, COPD.
The Three Forms of CO₂ Transport — the spine
Form Proportion Mechanism
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)~70% (the majority)CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (in red cells, via carbonic anhydrase)
Carbamino compounds (bound to Hb)~23%CO₂ binds the globin part of haemoglobin (not the haem — so does not compete with O₂)
Dissolved~7%Dissolved in plasma (more than O₂, as CO₂ is more soluble)
The key point: unlike O₂ (which is mostly Hb-bound), CO₂ is mostly carried as bicarbonate — and that conversion is the link to acid-base.
The Bicarbonate Mechanism — the core chemistry (high-yield)
📷 Image placeholder — CO₂ transport in the red cell — dissolved, carbamino and bicarbonate pathways, carbonic anhydrase, and the chloride (Hamburger) shift.
In the tissues (where CO₂ is high), inside the red blood cell:
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺
(the central equation — memorise this)
  • Driven by carbonic anhydrase (the enzyme that makes this fast — concentrated in red cells)
  • CO₂ diffuses into the red cell → carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid → dissociates into HCO₃⁻ + H⁺
  • HCO₃⁻ exits the cell into plasma (the main transport form), in exchange for Cl⁻ entering — the "chloride shift" (maintains electrical neutrality)
  • The H⁺ is buffered by haemoglobin inside the cell (Hb is a good buffer)
In the lungs, it all reverses: low CO₂ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ recombine → CO₂ → diffuses out into the alveoli → exhaled.
The Haldane Effect — the CO₂ counterpart to the Bohr effect
Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ better than oxygenated Hb (deoxy-Hb is a better buffer for H⁺ and binds more carbamino-CO₂).
The functional elegance (pairs with the Bohr effect)
  • In tissues: Hb releases O₂ (becomes deoxygenated) → now carries CO₂ more readily → picks up CO₂ where it is produced
  • In lungs: Hb binds O₂ (becomes oxygenated) → releases CO₂ → dumps CO₂ where it is exhaled
The two effects work together: Bohr = CO₂/acid promotes O₂ unloading (tissues); Haldane = O₂ promotes CO₂ unloading (lungs) — a reciprocal system optimising both gases at both ends.
The Link to Acid-Base — the most important conceptual payoff
The central equation CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ means CO₂ directly determines blood [H⁺] / pH:
Change Equation shift Result
↑CO₂ (hypoventilation/retention)shifts right↑H⁺ → ↓pH → respiratory acidosis
↓CO₂ (hyperventilation)shifts left↓H⁺ → ↑pH → respiratory alkalosis
This is why the lungs are a rapid pH regulator: changing ventilation changes CO₂ → changes pH within minutes (the respiratory compensation for metabolic disturbances) — cross-ref acid-base.
The Henderson-Hasselbalch concept: pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control the CO₂, the kidneys control the HCO₃⁻.
CO₂ and the Control of Breathing — why CO₂ drives ventilation
  • CO₂ is the main stimulus to breathe (via central chemoreceptors sensing CSF pH, which tracks CO₂) — rising CO₂ → ↑ventilation → blows off CO₂
  • The COPD caveat (high-yield): in chronic CO₂ retainers, the chemoreceptors become desensitised to CO₂ and the drive shifts partly to hypoxia ("hypoxic drive") → why high-flow O₂ can reduce respiratory drive in some CO₂-retaining COPD patients (target SpO₂ 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, 94–98% otherwise; the mechanism is more nuanced than pure hypoxic drive — O₂ is still given, never withheld — see the Control of Breathing subtab)

Overview — Control of Breathing
Breathing is automatic (you do not think about it) yet adjustable (you can override it, and it adapts to demand) — controlled by a brainstem rhythm generator modulated by chemical and mechanical feedback.
The organising principle: the system works by negative feedback — chemoreceptors sense blood gases/pH, the brainstem sets the rhythm, and ventilation adjusts to keep CO₂ (and pH) constant. The dominant signal is CO₂, not O₂.
Why it matters: explains the CO₂/hypoxic drive, why opioids cause respiratory depression, Cheyne-Stokes/Kussmaul breathing, and the COPD oxygen-target controversy — cross-ref CO₂ transport (previous subtab), acid-base, respiratory failure, COPD, opioid toxicity.
The Respiratory Centres — the brainstem rhythm generator

  • The output travels via the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5 — "keeps the diaphragm alive") to the diaphragm + intercostal nerves to the intercostals

The central chemoreceptor mechanism (high-yield): CO₂ (not H⁺) crosses the blood-brain barrier easily → in the CSF it forms carbonic acid → H⁺ (the CO₂ transport chemistry again) → the ↑CSF [H⁺] stimulates the central chemoreceptors → ↑ventilation → blows off CO₂ → corrects it. So the central receptors sense CO₂ via CSF pH.
The dominance of CO₂: under normal conditions, CO₂ is by far the most powerful stimulus to breathe — tiny rises in PaCO₂ produce large increases in ventilation. O₂ is a backup that only drives breathing when it falls dangerously low.
The Hierarchy of Drive: CO₂ vs O₂ — the high-yield concept
  • Normally: CO₂ (via central chemoreceptors) is the dominant drive — the system defends PaCO₂ tightly
  • O₂ (hypoxic drive, via peripheral chemoreceptors) is the backup — only becomes a significant driver when PaO₂ falls below ~8 kPa
The COPD "hypoxic drive" caveat (the classic exam controversy): in chronic CO₂ retainers (severe COPD), the central chemoreceptors become desensitised to chronically high CO₂ → the patient relies more on the hypoxic drive. Giving high-flow O₂ can theoretically remove that drive → hypoventilation → worsening CO₂ retention → this is why the target SpO₂ is 88–92% in anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure — COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular or chest-wall disease — not only in those already proved to retain. Everyone else gets 94–98%. The risk sets the target, pending a gas (BTS): if the gas comes back with a normal PaCO₂, move the target up to 94–98%. Controlled oxygen, never no oxygen.
(Modern understanding — and this is the ranking to learn. Oxygen raises CO₂ mainly by V/Q mismatch: high-concentration O₂ releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so blood floods back into units that cannot clear CO₂. Second is the Haldane effect — oxygenated haemoglobin carries less CO₂. Loss of hypoxic drive is real but the smallest of the three (BTS). If it were purely about drive, the fix would be to withhold oxygen — it is not.)

Overview — Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) Matching
Gas exchange needs both air reaching the alveoli (ventilation, V) and blood reaching the capillaries (perfusion, Q) — and the two must be matched for efficient exchange.
The organising principle: the ideal is V/Q ≈ 1 (ventilation matched to perfusion); the two extremes are dead space (ventilation without perfusion, V/Q → ∞) and shunt (perfusion without ventilation, V/Q → 0) — and most lung disease causes hypoxia through V/Q mismatch.
Why it matters: V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia, and the dead-space/shunt distinction explains PE vs pneumonia, and why shunt does not correct with oxygen — cross-ref gas exchange (the A–a gradient + 5 causes of hypoxaemia), PE, pneumonia, respiratory failure.
The Two Components — the spine
  • Ventilation (V): the rate air reaches the alveoli (~4 L/min at rest)
  • Perfusion (Q): the rate blood reaches the pulmonary capillaries (~5 L/min = cardiac output)
  • The ratio V/Q ≈ 0.8 overall (close to 1) — the target for efficient gas exchange; matching matters more than the absolute values
The Two Extremes — dead space vs shunt (the conceptual core)
Dead space Shunt
V/Qhigh (→ ∞)low (→ 0)
ProblemVentilation without perfusion — air reaches alveoli but no blood to exchange withPerfusion without ventilation — blood reaches alveoli but no air to exchange with
Analogy"wasted ventilation""wasted perfusion"
Classic causePulmonary embolism (clot blocks perfusion)Consolidation/collapse (alveoli filled/airless but still perfused) — pneumonia, ARDS, atelectasis
Corrects with O₂?Yes (the ventilated areas can take up more O₂)NO (blood never contacts ventilated alveoli — the hallmark)
The shunt point (high-yield): a true shunt is the one cause of hypoxaemia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen — because the shunted blood never meets ventilated alveoli, so adding O₂ to the alveoli cannot reach it. This distinguishes shunt from V/Q mismatch and diffusion defects (which do respond to O₂).
Types of dead space: anatomical (the conducting airways — trachea/bronchi, ~150 mL, never reach alveoli) + alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g. PE) = physiological dead space.
Alveolar ventilation is the number that matters — not minute ventilation. Only the air that reaches alveoli takes part in gas exchange; the ~150 mL sitting in the conducting airways is wasted every single breath. So:
V̇A = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate
and, because CO₂ clearance depends entirely on this, PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation (for a given rate of CO₂ production). Halve the alveolar ventilation and the PaCO₂ doubles.
🧮 Why rapid shallow breathing fails — the calculation worth doing once. Two patients, identical minute ventilation of 6 L/min:
  • 500 mL × 12/min → (500 − 150) × 12 = 4.2 L/min alveolar
  • 250 mL × 24/min → (250 − 150) × 24 = 2.4 L/min alveolar
The same 6 L/min on the observation chart, but the shallow breather is achieving little over half the effective ventilation — because the fixed 150 mL of dead space eats a far larger fraction of every small breath. This is why respiratory rate alone is a poor measure of ventilation, why an exhausted patient with a rising rate can still be retaining CO₂, and why increasing tidal volume clears CO₂ far more effectively than increasing rate.
🔗 The clinical payoff: this is the physiology behind the ominous “normalising” CO₂ in acute severe asthma. The patient starts hyperventilating (low CO₂), then tires: tidal volumes fall, breathing becomes rapid and shallow, alveolar ventilation collapses even as the rate climbs, and the CO₂ drifts back up through “normal”. A normal CO₂ in a severely breathless asthmatic is not reassurance — it is a patient on the way to Type 2 failure (cross-ref asthma, respiratory failure).
Regional V/Q Variation in the Normal Lung — the gravity effect (high-yield)
📷 Image placeholder — West's zones of the lung — how ventilation, perfusion and the V/Q ratio vary from apex to base under gravity.
Even a normal upright lung has a V/Q gradient from apex to base, because gravity affects blood (perfusion) more than air (ventilation):
Region Ventilation Perfusion V/Q Net effect
Apex (top)lowermuch lowerhigh V/Q (~3)relatively over-ventilated (dead-space-like)
Base (bottom)highermuch higherlow V/Q (~0.6)relatively over-perfused (shunt-like)
  • Both V and Q increase down the lung, but perfusion increases more (gravity pulls blood to the base) → so V/Q is high at the apex, low at the base
  • The clinical payoff: this regional variation explains disease distribution — e.g. TB favours the apex (high O₂, high V/Q, relatively poor blood/immune cell delivery)
Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction — the lung's auto-correction (high-yield + unique)
The principle: unlike the systemic circulation (where hypoxia causes vasodilation), the pulmonary circulation responds to alveolar hypoxia with vasoconstriction — hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV).
The purpose: it diverts blood away from poorly-ventilated (low-V/Q) alveoli toward well-ventilated ones → improves V/Q matching → optimises oxygenation.
The clinical consequences
  • It is the lung's mechanism to minimise shunt (redirects perfusion to ventilated areas)
  • Chronic global hypoxia (e.g. COPD, altitude) → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart strain (cor pulmonale)
How V/Q Mismatch Causes Hypoxaemia — the synthesis
  • V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia (cross-ref gas exchange note's 5 causes)
  • The lung cannot fully compensate because of the shape of the oxygen-dissociation curve (cross-ref): high-V/Q areas are already on the flat plateau (cannot load extra O₂ to make up for the low-V/Q areas), but low-V/Q areas drop steeply → the net effect is hypoxaemia (the elegant link to the dissociation curve)
  • CO₂ is less affected (more soluble, and ventilation can compensate) → which is why V/Q mismatch tends to cause Type 1 failure (hypoxia with normal/low CO₂)

Overview — Acid-Base Balance (Respiratory & Framework)
The body tightly controls blood pH (normal 7.35–7.45; PaO₂ 10–13 kPa on air; PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa / 35–45 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L; base excess ±2 mmol/L) — even small deviations impair enzyme/protein function, so pH is defended by buffers (instant), the lungs (minutes), and the kidneys (hours-days).
The organising principle: pH is set by the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control CO₂, the kidneys control HCO₃⁻. Every acid-base disorder is a problem with one of these, ± compensation by the other.
Why it matters: the framework for interpreting any ABG, and for understanding respiratory failure, DKA, vomiting, COPD, and salicylate poisoning — cross-ref CO₂ transport (the chemistry), control of breathing (compensation), renal acid-base (the renal side), respiratory failure, your clinical acid-base note.
The Central Chemistry — the foundation
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (carbonic anhydrase)
Henderson-Hasselbalch concept: pH ∝ HCO₃⁻ / CO₂ (renal numerator / respiratory denominator)
  • ↑CO₂ → ↑H⁺ → ↓pH (acidosis); ↓CO₂ → ↑pH (alkalosis)
  • ↑HCO₃⁻ → ↑pH (alkalosis); ↓HCO₃⁻ → ↓pH (acidosis)
The Three Lines of Defence — the timescales
Defence Speed Mechanism
BuffersinstantBicarbonate (main extracellular), haemoglobin, proteins, phosphate — soak up H⁺ immediately
Respiratory (lungs)minutesChange ventilation → change CO₂ → change pH (fast compensation)
Renal (kidneys)hours-daysExcrete H⁺ / reabsorb + generate HCO₃⁻ (slow but complete — cross-ref renal acid-base)
The principle: buffers buy time, the lungs respond fast (but only adjust the CO₂/respiratory component), the kidneys respond slowly (but powerfully adjust HCO₃⁻ and are the only route to excrete fixed acid).
The Four Primary Disorders — the core framework
Disorder Primary change pH Cause examples
Respiratory acidosis↑CO₂ (hypoventilation)↓COPD, opioids, neuromuscular, airway obstruction
Respiratory alkalosis↓CO₂ (hyperventilation)↑Anxiety, PE, altitude, early salicylate, pain
