Metabolic alkalosis↑HCO₃⁻↑Vomiting, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism
The naming logic: "respiratory" = the problem is CO₂ (the lung); "metabolic" = the problem is HCO₃⁻ (everything else); "acidosis/alkalosis" = the direction of pH.
Compensation — how the other system corrects (high-yield)
The principle: if one system causes the problem, the other compensates to pull pH back toward normal — but never fully overcorrects (compensation does not overshoot):
Primary disorder Compensation
Metabolic acidosisRespiratory — hyperventilate to blow off CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing in DKA) — fast
Metabolic alkalosisRespiratory — hypoventilate to retain CO₂ — limited (cannot stop breathing)
Respiratory acidosisRenal — retain HCO₃⁻ (slow, days — e.g. chronic COPD)
Respiratory alkalosisRenal — excrete HCO₃⁻ (slow)
Acute vs chronic respiratory disorders: the kidney takes days to compensate → so a chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD) has a raised HCO₃⁻ (renal compensation has happened), whereas an acute one does not — the HCO₃⁻ tells you the chronicity (high-yield ABG point).
Respiratory compensation is fast (minutes); renal is slow (days) — which is why metabolic problems get quick respiratory compensation, but respiratory problems take days for renal compensation.
Interpreting an ABG — the practical synthesis (high-yield method)
📷 Image placeholder — ABG interpretation flowchart / acid–base map plotting the four primary disorders and their expected compensation.
A stepwise approach
  • 0. The patient and the FiO₂ — what oxygen are they on? A PaO₂ is meaningless without it: hypoxaemia on high-flow oxygen is far worse than the same number on air. Then is the PaO₂ adequate? (normal 10–13 kPa on air; <8 kPa = respiratory failure)
  • 1. pH — acidotic (<7.35) or alkalotic (>7.45)?
  • 2. CO₂ — is it the cause? (↑CO₂ with low pH = respiratory acidosis; ↓CO₂ with high pH = respiratory alkalosis)
  • 3. HCO₃⁻ — is it the cause? (↓HCO₃⁻ with low pH = metabolic acidosis; ↑HCO₃⁻ with high pH = metabolic alkalosis)
  • 4. Compensation — is the other value shifting to correct? (and does pH suggest acute vs chronic / mixed)
  • 5. (Metabolic acidosis) → anion gap — high vs normal (cross-ref your electrolytes/anion-gap note)
The "matching" rule: if CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ move in opposite directions relative to pH → think a mixed disorder; if they move together (one primary, one compensating) → single disorder with compensation.
The Anion Gap — the key metabolic-acidosis subdivision (cross-ref)
Anion gap = (Na⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) (normal ~8–12 mmol/L) — separates the causes of metabolic acidosis:
  • Raised anion gap: added acid — lactate, ketones (DKA), sulphate/phosphate (uraemia), toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate) — MUDPILES (Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron/INH, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates)
  • Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic): HCO₃⁻ loss — diarrhoea, RTA, Addison's
(Full detail in your clinical electrolytes/acid-base note — this is the physiological cross-reference.)
Clinical Relevance — the payoff
Scenario Acid-base picture
COPD (chronic)Respiratory acidosis + renal compensation (↑HCO₃⁻)
DKAHigh-anion-gap metabolic acidosis + Kussmaul (respiratory compensation)
VomitingMetabolic alkalosis (loss of gastric H⁺)
Anxiety/PERespiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation)
Salicylate poisoningMixed — early respiratory alkalosis + later high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (cross-ref toxicology)
Type 2 respiratory failureRespiratory acidosis (CO₂ retention)
DiarrhoeaNormal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ loss)
⭐ Key Points
The ratio
pH ∝ HCO₃⁻ (renal) / CO₂ (respiratory); normal pH 7.35–7.45.
3 defences
Buffers (instant) → lungs (minutes, CO₂) → kidneys (days, HCO₃⁻ + the only route to excrete fixed acid).
4 disorders
Respiratory (CO₂ problem) vs metabolic (HCO₃⁻ problem), each acidosis or alkalosis.
Compensation
Metabolic acidosis → respiratory (Kussmaul, fast); respiratory acidosis → renal (↑HCO₃⁻, slow/days); never overcorrects.
Chronicity marker
Chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD) → raised HCO₃⁻ (renal compensation = the marker of chronicity).
ABG method
pH → CO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → compensation → anion gap (if metabolic acidosis).
Anion gap
Raised (added acid — DKA, lactate, toxins) vs normal (HCO₃⁻ loss — diarrhoea, RTA).
Salicylate = mixed
Respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis.
RESPIRATORY__Asthma:
Overview Banner

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterised by reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperreactivity. The single most important word is reversibility — this is what distinguishes asthma from COPD (obstruction that is not fully reversible).

Chronic Asthma
The disease — managed long-term with a stepwise ladder
Acute Asthma
The exacerbation — a severity-stratified emergency
Same disease, two faces. Chronic and acute asthma are inseparable — understanding the chronic disease explains the acute emergency.
Cross-ref COPD: Asthma = reversible obstruction. COPD = obstruction that is not fully reversible (persistent). Always compare these two.
Pathophysiology Illustration
Pathophysiology

Best described as chronic eosinophilic bronchitis. The process is Th2-driven:

🧬
Allergen exposure
Triggers Th2 response → IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 release
→
🔴
IgE / Mast cell degranulation
IgE cross-linking → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins
→
💨
Three components of narrowing
Smooth muscle contraction + wall inflammation/oedema + mucus plugging
Airway Remodelling (chronic): Repeated inflammation → fibrosis of the airway wall → the irreversible component that develops over time. This is why undertreated asthma eventually acquires a fixed element — overlap with COPD.
Types of Asthma
Allergic / Atopic (most common)
  • IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity
  • The atopic march: eczema → allergic rhinitis / hayfever → asthma
  • Hygiene hypothesis: reduced childhood infections → upregulated Th2 → ↑ allergic disease
Occupational Asthma
  • The screening question: "Are your symptoms the same, better or worse on days away from work?" — ask it in adult-onset asthma, poorly controlled established asthma, or reappearance of childhood asthma
  • High molecular weight agents: flour (bakers), latex, grain dust — IgE-mediated
  • Low molecular weight agents: isocyanates (spray painters), colophony, chemicals — non-IgE
  • Diagnostic key: PEF diary — symptoms better on days off / holidays, worse at work
  • Document the diagnosis, give the patient written confirmation and refer to an occupational lung disease service. The patient may be eligible for Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit. With the patient’s consent the employer is informed, and the employer then has the RIDDOR duty to report it to the HSE — the doctor does not notify the employer directly
Aspirin-Induced (Samter's Triad)
  • COX-1 inhibition by aspirin/NSAIDs → ↑ leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
  • Samter's Triad: asthma + aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyps
  • Classic exam question — know all three components
  • LTRAs (montelukast) particularly useful in this subtype
Exercise-Induced
  • Cold, dry air during exercise → airway cooling → mast cell degranulation
  • Symptoms peak 5–10 minutes after stopping exercise
  • In a known asthmatic, exercise symptoms usually mean inadequate control — review adherence and inhaler technique and step up the ICS-formoterol (MART) regimen first
  • A pre-exercise dose of the ICS-formoterol reliever is the reliever of choice (a SABA alone only in isolated exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in someone without asthma); montelukast is an add-on option
Triggers
  • Viral respiratory infections (commonest trigger in children)
  • Cold air / exercise
  • Allergens: house dust mites, pets, pollen, mould
  • Cigarette smoke / air pollution
  • Night / early morning (diurnal cortisol dip)
  • Strong emotions / stress
  • Beta-blockers (bronchospasm — contraindicated)
  • NSAIDs / aspirin (leukotriene surge)
Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthma (bronchospasm) — even topical timolol eye drops; cardioselective agents only with caution/specialist input. Use with extreme caution in COPD; avoid in asthma.
Clinical Features
Classic Symptoms
  • Episodic symptoms with diurnal variation (worse at night / early morning)
  • Dry cough, wheeze, SOB, chest tightness
  • Bilateral polyphonic wheeze on auscultation (expiratory)
  • Atopic history (eczema, hayfever, rhinitis)
  • Symptom-free intervals between episodes
Red Flags — Consider Alternative Diagnosis
  • Productive cough (not typical of asthma)
  • Unilateral wheeze — focal lesion / foreign body
  • No response to treatment despite good technique
  • Wheeze only with colds (viral-triggered only — may be viral wheeze, not asthma)
  • Haemoptysis, significant weight loss, clubbing
  • Onset >40 years with smoking history — consider COPD
Airway Remodelling in Chronic Asthma
Investigations — Objective Diagnostic Tests
📷 Image placeholder — How FeNO testing works — eosinophilic airway inflammation raising exhaled nitric oxide, with the diagnostic cut-offs (≥50 ppb adults 17+, ≥35 ppb children 5–16) marked.
NICE emphasis: Do not diagnose asthma on symptoms alone. First-line objective tests in adults (17+) are FeNO and blood eosinophil count (in children 5–16 the sequence starts with FeNO alone); if these are non-diagnostic, use bronchodilator reversibility spirometry then PEF variability.
📊
Spirometry
Obstructive pattern: FEV1/FVC <70%. The baseline picture of airflow obstruction.
🔄
Bronchodilator Reversibility
FEV1 ↑ ≥12% AND ≥200 mL post-SABA (salbutamol). The hallmark of asthma — reversibility.
💨
FeNO (Fractional exhaled NO)
Marker of eosinophilic inflammation. ≥50 ppb (adults ≥17) or ≥35 ppb (children 5–16) = significant eosinophilic airway inflammation.
🩸
Blood Eosinophil Count
First-line with FeNO in current UK guidance — either test being positive is diagnostic. A count raised above the lab reference range confirms asthma.
📈
PEF Variability
≥20% variability diurnally or over time. Especially useful in occupational asthma (work vs holiday diary).
Exam memory: Reversibility = FEV1 ↑ ≥12% + ≥200 mL post-SABA. FeNO ≥50 ppb (adults) / ≥35 ppb (children 5–16). FEV1/FVC <70%.
📷 Image placeholder — Serial peak-flow (PEF) diary: twice-daily readings over 2 weeks showing morning dipping (diurnal variability >20%) and, for occupational asthma, readings that fall on working days and recover on days off / holidays.
Drug Classes — Mechanism & Key Side Effects
Drug Role Mechanism Key Point / SE
SABA (salbutamol — "blue") Reliever — but never prescribed without an ICS (still the acute-attack bronchodilator) β₂ agonist → bronchodilation Tremor, ↑HR; hypokalaemia at high dose
ICS (beclometasone — "brown") Preventer — daily Corticosteroid → ↓ airway inflammation Oral candidiasis → rinse mouth after every dose; hoarseness; adrenal suppression at high dose
LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) Add-on bronchodilator Long-acting β₂ agonist Never used alone without ICS — increases asthma-related mortality without steroid cover
LAMA (tiotropium) Add-on bronchodilator Muscarinic antagonist → bronchodilation Dry mouth; caution in glaucoma and BPH
LTRA (montelukast) Add-on Leukotriene receptor antagonist → ↓ bronchoconstriction + inflammation Particularly effective in aspirin-induced and exercise-induced asthma; neuropsychiatric SEs (mood changes)
MART (ICS + fast LABA combined — e.g. budesonide/formoterol) Preventer + reliever in one inhaler ICS reduces inflammation; formoterol provides fast bronchodilation Foundation of modern BTS/NICE/SIGN guidance: the maintenance dose and the reliever both come from this one inhaler. Not the same as AIR — same inhaler, as needed only, no maintenance dose
📷 Image placeholder — Inhaler colour-coding reference: blue reliever (salbutamol SABA), brown/beige preventer (beclometasone ICS), purple/green combination (ICS-LABA / MART) — with a spacer device and the “rinse mouth after ICS” reminder.
The Stepwise Ladder — BTS/NICE/SIGN Approach
📷 Image placeholder — Flowchart of the BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma treatment ladder — from low-dose ICS + as-needed formoterol (MART) up through medium-dose MART to specialist add-ons/biologics.
The headline change: every rung is built on ICS-formoterol. A SABA reliever without ICS is no longer recommended for anyone — if a patient is reluctant to take an ICS, address the reluctance rather than falling back on SABA alone.
AIR vs MART — do not confuse them: AIR (anti-inflammatory reliever) = low-dose ICS-formoterol taken as needed only, no maintenance dose. MART = the same inhaler taken as a regular maintenance dose and as the reliever.
1️⃣
Step 1 — AIR
Low-dose ICS-formoterol as needed only (anti-inflammatory reliever). No maintenance dose. This replaces SABA monotherapy for everyone. Exception: if the patient is already highly symptomatic at presentation (regular symptoms, night waking) or presents with an exacerbation, start straight at low-dose MART — and step down to AIR later if control is achieved.
→
2️⃣
Step 2 — Low-dose MART
The same ICS-formoterol inhaler now taken as a regular maintenance dose as well as the reliever.
→
3️⃣
Step 3 — Moderate-dose MART
Step up the maintenance component of the same MART inhaler to a moderate dose. There is no separate “ICS + LABA” rung.
→
4️⃣
Step 4 — Check the phenotype, then add on
Still uncontrolled on moderate-dose MART → check FeNO and blood eosinophils. If either is raised → refer to specialist. If neither is raised → trial an LTRA (montelukast) or a LAMA (tiotropium) added to moderate-dose MART for 8–12 weeks, and refer if no benefit.
→
5️⃣
Step 5 — Specialist tier
High-dose ICS-based therapy; biologics (anti-IgE for allergic, anti-IL5 for eosinophilic phenotypes); maintenance oral prednisolone at the lowest effective dose. The MBBS-level point is the referral trigger, not the choice of agent.
Beta-blockers in asthma: non-selective agents are contraindicated — including topical preparations (e.g. timolol eye drops for glaucoma). They block β₂ receptors → bronchospasm. If there is genuinely no alternative, only a cardioselective agent, under specialist supervision.
Severity Assessment
Parameter Moderate Severe Life-Threatening
PEF 50–75% best/predicted 33–50% <33%
Speech Normal sentences Cannot complete sentences —
RR <25/min ≥25/min —
Pulse <110 bpm ≥110 bpm Bradycardia / arrhythmia / hypotension
SpO₂ — — <92%
Other features — — Silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion, confusion; PaO₂ <8 kPa
Killer Pearl 1 — Normal PCO₂ = life-threatening; RAISED PCO₂ = near-fatal.
In acute asthma the patient should be hyperventilating and blowing off CO₂ → PCO₂ is normally LOW. A normal or rising PCO₂ means they are exhausting — impending respiratory arrest.
Killer Pearl 2 — Near-fatal asthma:
Raised PCO₂ ± requiring ventilation. Decide early about ITU — a tight bronchospastic chest is very difficult to intubate.
Admit if: Life-threatening features · Severe not responding to initial Rx · Near-fatal asthma history · Pregnancy · Already on oral steroids · Night-time presentation
Acute Management — Mnemonic: O SHIT ME
📷 Image placeholder — Severity chart of acute asthma — moderate vs acute-severe vs life-threatening vs near-fatal, with the PEF %, SpO₂, PaCO₂ and clinical thresholds for each tier.
🅾️
O — Oxygen
Oxygen is for the hypoxaemic patient — 15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask in a severe/life-threatening attack, then titrate down to SpO₂ 94–98%. NB: unlike COPD, do NOT restrict O₂ in acute asthma.
💨
S — Salbutamol (SABA)
Nebulised 2.5–5 mg, back-to-back every 15–30 min if severe. Driven by O₂ nebuliser in severe/life-threatening. Repeated β₂ agonist plus systemic steroid causes hypokalaemia — check U&Es and replace potassium.
💊
H — Hydrocortisone / prednisolone
Hydrocortisone IV 100 mg OR prednisolone 40–50 mg PO. Continue for at least 5 days, or until recovery (no taper needed for a short course). Reduces airway inflammation — reduces relapse rate.
🌀
I — Ipratropium bromide (SAMA)
Nebulised 0.5 mg added to salbutamol in severe / life-threatening. Anticholinergic bronchodilator — synergistic with SABA.
🧪
T — Theophylline / Aminophylline IV
IV aminophylline infusion — specialist use, narrow therapeutic window, requires levels. Reserved for refractory severe/life-threatening.
🧲
M — Magnesium sulphate IV
1.2–2 g IV over 20 min in life-threatening / severe not responding. Smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation. Safe and effective.
🏥
E — Escalate / Intubate
Early ITU referral if life-threatening. Intubation is high-risk (dynamic hyperinflation, difficult ventilation) — decide early, before arrest.
Discharge criteria: Clinically stable for 12–24 hours off nebulisers and oxygen · PEF >75% best/predicted · Inhaler technique checked and corrected · Written asthma action plan provided · GP follow-up arranged.
⏱️ Follow-up has a timeframe — and it is short.
  • GP or asthma nurse review within 2 working days of discharge — a NICE quality statement in its own right, not a courtesy
  • Hospital specialist / respiratory nurse review at about one month after an admission for acute asthma
⭐ An attack is a control failure, not just an event. If the asthma was well controlled on the current regimen, the patient would not be in front of you. So an exacerbation needing emergency treatment is evidence the maintenance treatment has failed — and discharging someone on the same inhalers that just failed them is the mistake. Before they leave, always:
  • Review the ladder — consider stepping up maintenance treatment
  • Check adherence — ask about prescription refills; over-use of SABA and under-use of ICS is the classic pattern that precedes a fatal attack
  • Watch them use the inhaler — poor technique looks exactly like treatment failure; add a spacer
  • Identify the trigger for this attack, and give a written personalised asthma action plan
🔎 When “asthma” is not responding to treatment. Before escalating the ladder again, work through this:
  • Adherence and inhaler technique first — by far the commonest reason. Check refill frequency and watch them use the device
  • ABPA — suspect in any poorly controlled or steroid-dependent asthmatic: brown mucus plugs, eosinophilia, total IgE >1000, central bronchiectasis (see the ILD and bronchiectasis notes)
  • EGPA (Churg–Strauss) — asthma + marked eosinophilia + pANCA, often with nasal polyps, neuropathy or rash (see the vasculitis note)
  • Inducible laryngeal obstruction / vocal cord dysfunction — inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze, normal gases, no response to bronchodilators
  • Untreated co-morbidity — allergic rhinitis, GORD, obesity, ongoing smoking or occupational exposure
Asthma in Pregnancy
🤰 The rule is the opposite of most people’s instinct: carry on with everything. The risk of undertreated asthma far exceeds any risk from the drugs. Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy is associated with pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, low birth weight and perinatal mortality — and the fetus tolerates maternal hypoxia badly. Treatment is the same as for the non-pregnant woman.
💊 Chronic asthma — continue it all
  • ICS, LABA, LTRA and SABA are all continued — the safety of inhaled corticosteroids in pregnancy is well established
  • Oral prednisolone is given when indicated — the benefits outweigh the risks; never withhold it because a woman is pregnant
  • Medication is continued through labour and while breastfeeding
  • Counsel actively — women commonly stop their preventer themselves on finding out they are pregnant, which is the usual route to a crisis
🚨 Acute asthma in pregnancy
  • Treat exactly as in the non-pregnant patient — same drugs, same doses, same oxygen targets (94–98%)
  • Pregnancy is itself an indication to admit (already in the admit list above) — the threshold is lower, not the treatment
  • Give steroids, salbutamol, ipratropium and magnesium as you otherwise would
  • Involve obstetrics and monitor the fetus — but do not let that delay treating the mother
📊 The course is unpredictable: roughly a third worsen, a third improve and a third are unchanged during pregnancy — so every pregnant asthmatic needs monitoring rather than an assumption either way.
⭐ High-Yield Exam Pearls
Follow-up has a clock
GP or asthma nurse within 2 working days of discharge; hospital specialist at about one month after an admission.
An attack = a control failure
Never discharge on the same regimen that just failed. Step up, check adherence and technique, identify the trigger, give a written action plan.
Pregnancy — carry on with everything
Continue ICS, LABA, LTRA and oral prednisolone; treat acute asthma exactly as in the non-pregnant. Undertreated asthma is the bigger risk to the fetus.
Normal / rising PCO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening (should be blowing off CO₂; normalising = exhaustion)
Silent chest = peri-arrest — not "improving". No wheeze because no air movement.
Near-fatal = raised PCO₂ ± requiring ventilation
Severity numbers: PEF 33–50% = severe · PEF <33% = life-threatening · SpO₂ <92% = life-threatening
Reversibility = FEV1 ↑ ≥12% + ≥200 mL post-SABA — the hallmark
FeNO ≥50 ppb (adults) / ≥35 ppb (children 5–16) = eosinophilic inflammation
FEV1/FVC <70% = obstructive spirometry
Do not diagnose on symptoms alone — NICE requires objective tests
Beta-blockers absolutely contraindicated (including topical) → bronchospasm
ICS → rinse mouth after every dose → prevents oral candidiasis and hoarseness
LABA must NEVER be used alone without ICS → mortality risk
Modern guidance: ICS-formoterol (MART) as foundation — not SABA monotherapy
Acute mnemonic: O SHIT ME (O₂, Salbutamol, Hydrocortisone, Ipratropium, Theophylline, Magnesium, Escalate)
Samter's Triad = asthma + aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyps (COX-1 → ↑leukotrienes)
Occupational asthma → PEF diary comparing work vs days off / holidays
Asthma = reversible (vs COPD = not fully reversible / persistent obstruction) — always compare
Atopic march: eczema → hayfever/rhinitis → asthma
Discharge: PEF >75%, stable 12–24h, inhaler technique checked, action plan given
RESPIRATORY__Chronic Obstructive Pulmona:
Overview Banner

COPD is an umbrella term for emphysema + chronic bronchitis + small airway disease. The defining feature is poorly reversible, progressive airflow limitation — the key word is not fully reversible / persistent (vs asthma's reversible).

Chronic COPD
The disease — managed long-term with a stepwise inhaler ladder
Acute Exacerbation (AECOPD)
The emergency — oxygen logic is everything
Cross-ref Asthma: COPD = not fully reversible / persistent, smoker, older, no diurnal variation, no significant reversibility (BDR <12%). Asthma = reversible, atopic, younger, diurnal variation, reversible (BDR >12% + 200 mL). These two are examined as a pair.
Pathophysiology Illustration
Aetiology & Pathophysiology
Causes
  • Smoking — the major cause: inflammation → protease release → parenchymal destruction + inactivates α1-antitrypsin
  • Occupational dust/pollutants (coal, silica, cadmium)
  • Biomass fuels (developing world)
  • Air pollution
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency — early-onset COPD (<40 yrs), ± FHx, non/minimal smoker; panacinar emphysema affecting lower lobes. Autosomal codominant (SERPINA1, chromosome 14) — severe disease is usually the PiZZ genotype; heterozygotes (PiMZ) are mildly affected. Also causes liver disease — neonatal cholestasis, and cirrhosis/HCC in adults — so check LFTs. Smoking accelerates it dramatically.
Mechanisms
  • Chronic bronchitis: mucus gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia → productive cough ≥3 months/yr × 2 yrs
  • Emphysema: protease-mediated destruction of alveolar walls → loss of elastic recoil → air trapping → hyperinflation
  • Small airway disease: inflammation and fibrosis of bronchioles → fixed obstruction
The Two Classic Phenotypes
Pink Puffer (emphysema-predominant)
  • Breathless, not cyanosed, thin, cachexic
  • Pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscles
  • Barrel chest, hyperinflated
  • Maintains near-normal PaO₂ by hyperventilating
Blue Bloater (chronic bronchitis-predominant)
  • Cyanosed, oedematous, overweight
  • CO₂ retainer — bounding pulse, flap (asterixis), warm peripheries, drowsy
  • Cor pulmonale: raised JVP, peripheral oedema
  • O₂ therapy must be controlled (target 88–92%) to avoid worsening hypercapnia
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side of the two classic phenotypes: the pink puffer (thin, barrel-chested, pursed-lip breathing, near-normal PaO₂) versus the blue bloater (cyanosed, oedematous, CO₂ retainer with cor pulmonale).
COPD vs Asthma
Feature COPD Asthma
SmokerAlmost alwaysPossible but not defining
Onset <35Rare (consider α1-AT deficiency)Common
AtopyUncommonCommon (atopic march)
Dominant cellsNeutrophils, macrophages, CD8+Eosinophils, CD4+
Diurnal variationUncommonCommon (worse at night/morning)
Bronchodilator response<12% (no significant reversibility)>12% + 200 mL
Steroid responseVariable (ICS only if asthmatic features)Good
Symptoms
Typical Symptoms
  • Chronic productive cough (smoker's cough) — purulent in infective exacerbation
  • Progressive breathlessness — the dominant symptom, graded by MRC scale
  • Wheeze
  • Weight loss, muscle wasting, depression (extra-pulmonary)
MRC Dyspnoea Scale
  • 1 — Breathless only with strenuous exercise
  • 2 — Short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a hill
  • 3 — Walks slower than contemporaries on level ground due to breathlessness
  • 4 — Stops for breath after walking ~100m on level ground
  • 5 — Too breathless to leave the house / breathless when dressing
Signs of Severe COPD
Respiratory Signs
  • Barrel chest (increased AP diameter from hyperinflation)
  • Loss of cardiac and hepatic dullness to percussion
  • Pursed-lip breathing (creates back-pressure → slows airway collapse)
  • Use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes)
  • Prolonged expiratory phase
  • Wheeze and ↓ breath sounds throughout
Signs of CO₂ Retention (Blue Bloater)
  • Bounding pulse (CO₂-mediated vasodilation)
  • Asterixis / flap (CO₂ narcosis)
  • Warm peripheries, plethoric face
  • Drowsiness, confusion
  • Cyanosis (central + peripheral)
  • Cor pulmonale: raised JVP, ankle oedema, RV heave
Managing cor pulmonale in COPD. Treat the COPD, not the right heart: optimise inhaled therapy, push smoking cessation, and assess for LTOT (the intervention that slows progression of the pulmonary hypertension). Control the oedema symptomatically with a diuretic. Do not use ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, alpha-blockers or digoxin to treat cor pulmonale caused by COPD — digoxin only if there is co-existing atrial fibrillation (NICE).
Spirometry — Diagnostic
Diagnosis requires spirometry: a POST-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 in someone with symptoms and risk factors, with no significant reversibility — this is the key contrast with asthma (where reversibility is >12% + 200 mL). The ratio is fixed at 0.7 and is not age-adjusted, so interpret it against the clinical picture: consider another diagnosis in an older person with a low ratio but no COPD symptoms, and do not dismiss COPD in a symptomatic younger person whose ratio is just above 0.7.
NICE Severity of Airflow Obstruction by post-bronchodilator FEV1 % Predicted

Stage (NICE / GOLD) Severity FEV1 % Predicted
IMild — only diagnose COPD at this stage if symptoms are present≥80%

Other Investigations
🩻
CXR
Hyperinflation, flat hemidiaphragms, bullae, long narrow heart, increased retrosternal air space.
🩸
FBC
Secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia (↑RBC mass as compensation). Also check for anaemia.
💨
ABG
Type 2 respiratory failure (↑PaCO₂, ↓PaO₂) in severe disease. Essential in acute exacerbation.
🫁
TLCO (transfer factor)
↓ in emphysema (loss of alveolar surface area). Helps distinguish from asthma (TLCO normal).
🧬
α1-antitrypsin
Check in early onset (<40 yrs), non-smoker, or FHx. Panacinar emphysema, lower lobe predominance.
❤️
ECG / Echo
Cor pulmonale: peaked P waves (P pulmonale), right axis deviation. Echo: RV hypertrophy, pulmonary HTN.
Foundational
  • Smoking cessation — the only intervention shown to slow the rate of decline in FEV1, and first priority in all patients. Smoking cessation and LTOT (in chronic hypoxaemia) are the two interventions that improve survival; everything else is symptom control.
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation — offer to anyone who views themselves as functionally disabled by COPD (usually MRC grade 3+), and to everyone recently admitted with an exacerbation (start within 4 weeks of discharge). Improves exercise capacity and QoL and reduces admissions. Not suitable if unable to walk, unstable angina, or recent MI (NICE).
  • Annual influenza vaccine + one-off pneumococcal vaccine
  • BMI optimisation, nutrition, exercise
Inhaler Stepwise Ladder
📷 Image placeholder — Flowchart of the NICE COPD inhaler ladder — SABA/SAMA → the asthmatic-features fork (LABA+ICS vs LABA+LAMA) → triple therapy.
1️⃣
Step 1 — PRN reliever
  • SABA (salbutamol) or SAMA (ipratropium) as needed.
  • When a LAMA is started later, STOP the SAMA (duplicate antimuscarinics) — the SABA stays on as the reliever at every step.
  • For mild, intermittent symptoms.
→
2️⃣
Step 2 — THE FORK: does the patient have asthmatic / steroid-responsive features?
Prior asthma/atopy · ↑ blood eosinophils · Significant FEV1 variability · Diurnal PEF variation
YES → asthmatic features present

LABA + ICS (e.g. salmeterol/fluticasone)
ICS reduces exacerbation risk in this group

NO → no asthmatic features

LABA + LAMA (e.g. formoterol + tiotropium)

Step 3 — Triple therapy
LABA + LAMA + ICS. Offer it outright after 1 severe (hospitalising) or 2 moderate exacerbations in a year on dual therapy. If it is being added for day-to-day symptoms alone, it is a 3-month trial — step back to LABA + LAMA if there is no benefit (NICE).
Add-On Therapies (Severe / Frequent Exacerbators)
Add-On Drug Options
  • Mucolytics (carbocisteine) — chronic productive cough; reduces sputum viscosity
  • Prophylactic azithromycin — for a patient who does not smoke (ex-smokers count) and is on optimised therapy, vaccination and pulmonary rehab but still has typically 4 or more exacerbations a year with sputum production, prolonged exacerbations, or exacerbations needing hospitalisation; check ECG for QT prolongation + LFTs before starting and recheck both within a month, then review at 3 months and at least 6-monthly
  • Oral theophylline — narrow therapeutic window; used only when inhaled therapy is insufficient
LTOT — Long-Term Oxygen Therapy
  • PaO₂ <7.3 kPa on air, confirmed on two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart when clinically stable on optimal therapy → LTOT (at least 15 hrs/day)
  • PaO₂ 7.3–8 kPa + one of: polycythaemia, peripheral oedema, pulmonary HTN
  • Do not offer to current smokers — fire risk; also assess compliance
  • Reduces pulmonary HTN progression + improves survival
Acute Exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD)
Triggers
  • Haemophilus influenzae — commonest bacterial trigger
  • Rhinovirus — commonest viral trigger
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Air pollution, cold weather
Features & Admission Criteria
  • Worsening breathlessness and cough
  • ↑ Sputum volume + colour change (purulence)
  • Admit if: unable to cope at home, severe symptoms, cyanosis, confusion, SpO₂ <90%, acidosis, significant comorbidity
🚨 Not every deterioration in a COPD patient is an exacerbation. The label is easy to reach for and it is the reason these diagnoses get missed — a breathless COPD patient is assumed to be exacerbating until someone looks. Always ask what else could do this:
  • Pneumothorax — the classic miss. COPD lungs are full of bullae, and a ruptured bulla causes a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax that presents exactly as “my breathing is worse”. It is poorly tolerated on top of bad lungs and needs a chest drain more often than a primary one (see the pneumothorax note). This is why the CXR matters.
  • Pulmonary embolism — COPD patients are high risk, and the breathlessness gets attributed to the COPD. Suspect it if the picture is breathlessness and hypoxia without wheeze, sputum change or fever.
  • Left ventricular failure — the same smoking history causes both, and LVF wheezes too (“cardiac asthma”). Look for orthopnoea, raised JVP, a gallop rhythm and bilateral crackles.
  • Pneumonia — consolidation is a different diagnosis with a different antibiotic course and severity score, not an exacerbation with dirty sputum.
  • Lung cancer — identical risk factors. Weight loss, haemoptysis or a persistent focal abnormality means investigate, not treat again.
A CXR, ECG and ABG in anyone admitted with a “COPD exacerbation” is what separates these — and the CXR is doing more work than most people credit it with.
Management of AECOPD
📷 Image placeholder — Controlled oxygen in a CO₂ retainer — a 24–28% Venturi mask with the 88–92% target range, illustrating why high-flow O₂ worsens hypercapnia.
THE exam concept — Controlled Oxygen
  • Target SpO₂ 88–92% in known/suspected CO₂ retainers, delivered by a 24–28% Venturi mask.
  • CO₂ retainers may rely on hypoxic drive to breathe. High-flow O₂ abolishes this drive → ↓ respiratory rate → worsening hypercapnia → respiratory acidosis → arrest.
  • Modern physiology: O₂-induced hypercapnia is driven mainly by V/Q mismatch (release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) and the Haldane effect; loss of hypoxic drive is a smaller contributor — but controlled O₂ still applies.
  • The other half of the rule: never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient for fear of CO₂ retention — hypoxia kills first. If SpO₂ is below 88%, give more oxygen, not less: step the Venturi up to reach 88–92% and repeat the ABG at 30–60 minutes. If the CO₂ then climbs with acidosis on adequate oxygen, the answer is NIV, not oxygen withdrawal. A critically ill COPD patient (peri-arrest, shock, unrecordable saturations) is resuscitated with high-flow O₂ like anyone else until the gas is back (BTS).
This is the single most-tested point in COPD.
🫁
Controlled O₂
  • 24–28% Venturi mask → target SpO₂ 88–92%.
  • Titrate up/down.
  • If SpO₂ falls below 88%, increase the oxygen — never withhold it. Recheck the ABG at 30–60 min.
💨

  • Drive the nebuliser with AIR (not O₂) in CO₂ retainers — but keep nasal cannulae at 1–2 L/min running underneath so the patient does not desaturate during the neb.
💊

  • Reduces inflammation, accelerates recovery.
  • IV hydrocortisone if unable to swallow.
🦠

  • Amoxicillin, doxycycline, or clarithromycin first-line (co-amoxiclav if higher risk of treatment failure).
  • Only if evidence of bacterial infection (purulence, CRP rise, consolidation).
🧪

  • Only if refractory to nebulisers.
  • Narrow therapeutic window — requires levels.
🌬️
NIV (BiPAP) — Type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis
  • Indicated for type 2 respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis — pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.5 kPa — persisting despite ~1 hour of maximal medical therapy and controlled oxygen.
  • pH 7.25–7.35 can be managed on a respiratory ward; pH <7.25 still needs NIV, but in HDU/ICU with a low threshold for intubation.
  • BiPAP pressures are set and titrated by the NIV team against repeat ABG. NIV reduces the need for intubation and reduces mortality.
🛑 Decide the ceiling of care before you start NIV — not when it fails.
  • NIV is a bridge. The question it forces is: if this does not work, is this patient for intubation? Answer it on admission, with the patient wherever possible while they can still take part — not at 2am with a failing gas.
  • Base the decision on premorbid function, exercise tolerance, frailty, home oxygen use, previous admissions and the patient’s own wishes — not on the pH alone.
  • For many people with severe COPD, NIV is itself the ceiling — a planned, legitimate decision, not a failure.
  • Document it (ReSPECT / treatment escalation plan) so the night team is not deciding from scratch.
🕊️ Severe COPD is a terminal illness, and is under-recognised as one. Prognosis in advanced disease is worse than in many cancers, yet these patients are far less likely to be offered palliative input. Consider it when there are repeated admissions, an FEV₁ that keeps falling, home oxygen, cachexia, MRC grade 5 or a failure to recover between exacerbations.
  • Low-dose oral morphine is effective for refractory breathlessness once reversible causes are treated — it reduces the sensation of breathlessness without hastening death at these doses
  • A handheld fan, breathing-control techniques and anxiety management genuinely help — breathlessness and panic feed each other
  • Advance care planning — preferred place of care, treatment escalation, and involving the palliative team early rather than in the last days
After the Exacerbation — Discharge & Follow-Up
The admission is the opportunity, and it is routinely wasted. An exacerbation needing hospital is a marker of poor control and a predictor of the next one — roughly a third of patients are readmitted within 90 days. What happens at discharge changes that more than anything given during the admission.
🏃 Pulmonary rehabilitation — the big one
  • Refer everyone admitted with an exacerbation, to start within 4 weeks of leaving hospital
  • The single most effective intervention for exercise capacity, quality of life and readmission — it outperforms most of the drugs
  • Exercise training plus education, diet and self-management support
  • Consistently under-referred — the commonest reason a patient does not get it is that nobody asked
📦 Rescue pack — with the caveat
  • A home supply of prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days ± an antibiotic, with a written exacerbation action plan
  • Antibiotics only if the sputum turns purulent — not for breathlessness alone
  • ⚠️ Only appropriate if the patient can reliably distinguish an exacerbation from their usual day-to-day variation, and only alongside education
  • An unsupervised rescue pack drives repeated inappropriate steroid and antibiotic courses — review use at every appointment and ask them to tell you when they take one
✅ Before they leave, also: reinforce smoking cessation (still the only thing that alters the disease course, and never too late), check influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, watch them use their inhaler and consider a spacer, review whether the inhaler ladder needs stepping up, reassess the need for LTOT once stable (never assess it during the acute episode — recheck the ABG at least 4–6 weeks later), and arrange early follow-up.

RESPIRATORY__Tuberculosis:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis — an acid-fast bacillus with upper-lobe predilection (high O₂ at the apices favours growth). The organising thread: everything splits by latent vs active — it determines both testing and treatment. Disease arc: primary → latent → reactivation (secondary) → ± extrapulmonary / miliary.
Pathology & Natural History
📷 Image placeholder — Primary vs post-primary (reactivation) TB — Ghon focus → Ghon complex in primary disease, and apical cavitation in reactivation, on a lung schematic.

Primary TB: inhaled bacilli → Ghon focus (lung parenchymal lesion) + ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy = Ghon complex. Histology: caseating granuloma — central caseous necrosis + epithelioid macrophages + Langhans giant cells. Mechanism: type IV hypersensitivity (cell-mediated).

Immunocompetent Host
Ghon focus heals & calcifies → latent TB: contained, asymptomatic, non-infectious. Reactivates if immunity wanes.
Immunocompromised Host
Failure to contain → haematogenous spread → miliary TB (disseminated “millet-seed” lesions in any organ).
Secondary (reactivation) TB: immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, malnutrition, age) reactivates dormant bacilli → lung apex → cavitation + haemoptysis.
Extrapulmonary sites — high-yield eponyms:
CNS → TB meningitis (most serious)  |  Spine → Pott's disease  |  Cervical nodes → scrofula  |  GI → ileocaecal TB  |  Renal → sterile pyuria
📷 Image placeholder — Histology of a caseating granuloma: central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis rimmed by epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate Langhans giant cells, with a surrounding lymphocyte cuff.
Risk Factors
Close contact with active TB High-prevalence origin (Asia, Africa, E Europe, Latin America) HIV / immunosuppression Homelessness / prison IVDU / alcohol excess Malnutrition Healthcare workers
Clinical Features
Primary TB
Usually asymptomatic. Occasionally erythema nodosum or a mild flu-like illness.
Active / Reactivation TB
  • Systemic: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, malaise
  • Pulmonary: chronic productive cough (>3 wks), haemoptysis
Extrapulmonary
Site-specific: back pain (Pott's), neck lump (scrofula), meningism (TB meningitis), haematuria / sterile pyuria (renal).
Diagnosis
📷 Image placeholder — Diagnostic algorithm for suspected TB — how sputum smear/NAAT, culture, Mantoux and IGRA fit together for active vs latent disease.

Latent TB Screening

Mantoux (Tuberculin Skin Test)
Intradermal PPD → read at 48–72 h; measure induration (not erythema); ≥5 mm = positive, regardless of BCG history. BCG does not change the threshold — it reduces specificity (false positives), which is why IGRA is preferred in the BCG-vaccinated.

False negatives: miliary TB, HIV, sarcoid, lymphoma, very young, severe malnutrition, live vaccines.
IGRA (Interferon-γ Release Assay)
Blood test measuring IFN-γ response to TB antigens. More specific than Mantoux — not affected by BCG vaccination. Preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals.

Both tests are for latent infection only. Neither distinguishes latent from active disease, and neither excludes active TB — both can be negative in miliary disease and immunosuppression. If active TB is suspected, the answer is sputum and imaging, not a skin or blood test.

Active TB Investigations

Test Findings / Notes
CXRUpper-lobe cavitation (reactivation); unilateral (ipsilateral) hilar lymphadenopathy (primary); diffuse “millet-seed” nodules (miliary)
Sputum smear ×3Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on Ziehl-Neelsen stain → bright red; rapid but less sensitive
Sputum cultureGold standard (most sensitive); liquid MGIT culture usually positive in 1–3 weeks, solid Löwenstein-Jensen up to 6–8 weeks — and either must be held the full period before a negative is reported
NAAT / PCRRapid (24–48 h); detects mycobacterial DNA + rifampicin resistance (GeneXpert)
LP / CSFFor suspected miliary or CNS TB — lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose
BloodsFBC (often normal; may show anaemia of chronic disease / monocytosis), LFTs (baseline before drugs), U&Es, HIV test

Active TB — RIPE Regimen

2️⃣
2 months — RIPE (intensive phase)Rifampicin + Isoniazid (with pyridoxine) + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol
↓
4️⃣
4 months — RI (continuation phase)Rifampicin + Isoniazid (with pyridoxine)
↓

6 months totalBaseline LFTs in all; serial LFTs if the baseline is abnormal or there are risk factors, and whenever symptoms develop
Ethambutol runs for the 2-month intensive phase — it is there to cover possible isoniazid resistance, so it can be dropped as soon as full susceptibility is confirmed. Check visual acuity and colour vision before starting, and check renal function (it is renally cleared; toxicity is dose-related).
⏳ 6 months is the standard — but not for the central nervous system. Active CNS TB (including TB meningitis) is treated for 12 months: 2 months of RIPE followed by 10 months of rifampicin + isoniazid. Everything else — pulmonary, lymph node, bone and joint including spinal, pericardial, disseminated — is the standard 6 months. (Disseminated/miliary TB with CNS involvement is treated as CNS TB for 12 months.) If you only remember one exception, make it this one: the note’s own “most serious” extrapulmonary site is the one with a different duration.
⚡ Do not wait for the culture. Culture is the gold standard but takes up to 6–8 weeks, and TB does not pause while it grows. Start treatment on clinical and radiological suspicion once you have sent smears, NAAT and cultures — then adjust when sensitivities return. Waiting two months for confirmation before treating is the error the “gold standard” label invites.

Latent TB

3 months isoniazid (with pyridoxine) + rifampicin OR 6 months isoniazid (with pyridoxine) alone Choose the 6-month isoniazid-only option where rifampicin interactions matter — e.g. HIV on antiretrovirals Generally offered under 65 — above that, isoniazid hepatotoxicity outweighs the benefit

Adjunctive Steroids — Two Sites Only

The counterintuitive one: we give immunosuppression in an infection. In these two sites it is the inflammatory response itself that causes the damage — vasculitis, exudate and hydrocephalus in the CNS, and fibrous constriction in the pericardium — so damping it down improves outcome.
🧠 CNS TB / TB meningitis
  • Dexamethasone or prednisolone, started with the anti-TB regimen — not later
  • High dose initially, then withdrawn gradually over 4–8 weeks
  • Reduces mortality in tuberculous meningitis — this is why it is a NICE recommendation, not an optional extra
  • Remember the treatment itself also runs for 12 months here
🫀 Pericardial TB
  • Oral prednisolone 60 mg/day in adults, started with the anti-TB regimen
  • Withdrawn gradually 2–3 weeks after starting treatment
  • Aim is to reduce the risk of constrictive pericarditis and the need for pericardiectomy
  • Anti-TB treatment is the standard 6 months
🚫 Not for anything else. Steroids are not given routinely for pulmonary, lymph node or bone TB. And do not confuse this with the paradoxical reaction below — that is a recognised worsening a few weeks into treatment which does not mean the drugs are failing.

Drug-Resistant TB — Why the NAAT Result Matters

🧬 MDR-TB = resistance to at least both rifampicin and isoniazid — the two drugs that carry the whole regimen. GeneXpert reports rifampicin resistance within hours because the two resistances travel together, so rifampicin resistance is used as the rapid surrogate marker for MDR-TB. That is the reason the NAAT result matters and why it is worth having in 24–48 hours rather than waiting weeks for the culture.
⚠️ Suspect resistance if
  • Previously treated for TB — especially an interrupted or incomplete course
  • Contact with a known resistant case
  • From a high-prevalence country for resistance (e.g. Eastern Europe, parts of Asia and Africa)
  • Failure to improve, or still smear-positive after 2 months of treatment
  • HIV co-infection
🏥 What changes
  • Specialist / MDR-TB service referral — never managed on the standard regimen
  • Second-line agents and a much longer course, guided by full sensitivities
  • Directly observed therapy and strict infection control — prolonged negative-pressure isolation
  • Enhanced contact tracing, because contacts are exposed to a resistant strain

Practical / Public Health

Notifiable Disease
Active TB is notifiable — latent TB is not. The attending clinician notifies the local health protection team on clinical suspicion, without waiting for culture (within 3 days; by phone within 24 h if urgent) → contact tracing of close contacts (UKHSA).
DOT
Directly Observed Therapy — part of enhanced case management, for those at risk of non-adherence: street homeless, in or recently in prison, drug or alcohol misuse, previous non-adherence or previous TB treatment, serious mental health or cognitive impairment, denial of diagnosis. And for everyone with MDR-TB, whatever their adherence history. Video-observed therapy is an accepted alternative (NICE).
Paradoxical reaction
3–6 weeks into treatment — paradoxical enlargement of nodes / worsening CXR (do not stop treatment).
Isolation
A single side room (source isolation) for suspected or confirmed infectious pulmonary TB, until 2 weeks of effective treatment. A negative-pressure room is required only for suspected/confirmed MDR-TB, or if the patient must be cared for on a ward with immunocompromised patients.
Drug Side Effects
📷 Image placeholder — Visual map linking each first-line drug to its key side effect (rifampicin→orange secretions/enzyme inducer, isoniazid→neuropathy, pyrazinamide→gout/hepatitis, ethambutol→optic neuritis).
Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are the hepatotoxic ones — ethambutol’s toxicity is ocular, not hepatic, which is why ethambutol-based regimens are used in significant liver disease. Check LFTs in everyone before starting, and monitor if the baseline is abnormal or there are risk factors (alcohol, chronic liver disease, older age), or at any point if symptoms develop. Act on the numbers: stop the hepatotoxic drugs if ALT/AST >5× the upper limit of normal, or >3× ULN with jaundice or hepatitis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, RUQ pain) — then specialist reintroduction, one drug at a time, once LFTs settle. Rifampicin induces liver enzymes; isoniazid inhibits them (opposite effects — frequently examined).

VTE = DVT + PE — the same disease, two ends. A clot forms in the deep veins (usually legs) → embolises to the pulmonary arteries. Wells 2-level PE score — key components: Clinical DVT signs (+3) · PE most likely diagnosis (+3) · HR >100 (+1.5) · Immobilisation >3 days or surgery in the last 4 wks (+1.5) · Prior DVT/PE (+1.5) · Haemoptysis (+1) · Active malignancy (+1)
Wells >4 — PE Likely
  • → Immediate CTPA
  • Start interim anticoagulation if any delay
  • CTPA +ve → treat; CTPA −ve → consider leg USS
Wells ≤4 — PE Unlikely
  • → D-dimer first
  • D-dimer −ve → stop; consider alternative diagnosis
  • D-dimer +ve → CTPA
Haemodynamically unstable and too sick for CTPA → bedside echo (RV dilatation = strong presumptive evidence) → thrombolyse empirically. Do not delay for imaging.
📷 Image placeholder — 12-lead ECG of the classic (rare) S1Q3T3 pattern: prominent S wave in lead I, Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III, often with sinus tachycardia and T-wave inversion in V1–V4 (RV strain).
⚠️ Pregnancy — a different pathway. Wells scoring and D-dimer are not used in pregnancy or the puerperium. If there are leg symptoms, do a compression leg ultrasound first — a confirmed proximal DVT treats both. Otherwise get a CXR, then a V/Q scan or CTPA guided by its findings. Treatment-dose LMWH is started on clinical suspicion, before imaging confirms it — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated. Continue for at least 3 months and until at least 6 weeks postnatal, whichever is longer. Full RCOG GTG37b detail: see Medical Disorders in Pregnancy (Obstetrics & Gynaecology).
