ABGHypoxaemia + hypocapnia → respiratory alkalosis (blowing off CO₂ due to hyperventilation).
CXRUsually normal. Rarely: wedge infarct, Westermark's sign (oligaemia distal to clot), raised hemidiaphragm, effusion.
EchoBedside for unstable patients — RV dilatation / strain; rules out other causes (tamponade, LV failure).
Leg USSProximal DVT confirmed → sufficient to treat as VTE even without CTPA.
BloodsFBC, U&Es, LFTs, coagulation, troponin (RV stress), BNP (severity). No routine thrombophilia screen — see “Unprovoked VTE — what to work up” below for the narrow indications.
Management — Stable vs Unstable Fork
📷 Image placeholder — Management fork flowchart — haemodynamically stable (DOAC) vs unstable/massive (thrombolysis → embolectomy) PE.
Haemodynamically Stable
  • DOAC first-line. Apixaban or rivaroxaban — start immediately (no heparin lead-in), but both begin with a higher loading phase: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily; rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily (BNF)
  • Dabigatran or edoxaban — need 5 days LMWH lead-in first
  • Exceptions → LMWH bridge → warfarin (INR 2–3): established renal failure, CrCl <15 mL/min (apixaban and rivaroxaban stay first-line down to CrCl 15; dabigatran needs CrCl ≥30), and antiphospholipid syndrome, triple positive. In pregnancy and the puerperium, treatment-dose LMWH throughout — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated (NICE)
  • Warfarin is initially prothrombotic (↓ Proteins C & S first) → bridge with heparin until INR therapeutic
Haemodynamically Unstable (Massive PE)
  • Continuous IV unfractionated heparin infusion is the anticoagulant of choice — its effect can be switched off quickly if thrombolysis or surgery is needed, so not a DOAC or LMWH (NICE)
  • Thrombolysis (alteplase) — the key reperfusion intervention
  • Supportive: O₂, cautious IV fluids (RV is preload-sensitive), ICU, vasopressors
  • If thrombolysis contraindicated / fails: surgical or catheter embolectomy (IVC filter is reserved for patients who cannot be anticoagulated or recurrent PE despite anticoagulation — it does not treat the existing clot)
  • Percutaneous catheter-directed therapy in specialist centres
🏠 Disposition — a confirmed PE can go home.
  • Not every PE is admitted. If low risk — sPESI 0, PESI class I–II, or all Hestia criteria negative — consider outpatient treatment with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban, first dose before discharge). See Risk Scores & Criteria — Cardiology & VTE for the sPESI components.
  • BTS exclusion criteria — admit if any of these: HR >110 · SBP <100 mmHg · needs inotropes or critical care · needs thrombolysis or embolectomy · SpO₂ <90% on air · active bleeding or high bleeding risk · creatinine clearance <30 mL/min or severe liver disease · severe pain needing opiates · already on full-dose anticoagulation when the PE occurred · no safe home support or unable to attend follow-up.
  • Before they leave: written safety-netting advice (return immediately with worsening breathlessness, chest pain, syncope, or any bleeding — black stool, haematuria, head injury), an anticoagulant alert card, and a booked review at ~7 days — see After the Acute PE below.

Duration of Anticoagulation

Scenario Duration
Provoked PE (clear precipitant — surgery, fracture)3 months
Unprovoked PE (no identifiable cause)At least 3 months, then reassess at 3 months — the NICE default is to continue long-term unless bleeding risk is high (HAS-BLED ≥4 and unmodifiable)
Active cancer3 to 6 months, then reassess and discuss continuing, stopping or changing while the cancer remains active; a DOAC is the usual choice, taking tumour site, drug interactions and bleeding risk into account (NICE). Antiphospholipid syndrome — long-term while the risk persists. Note hereditary thrombophilia alone does not mandate indefinite treatment — a provoked VTE in a factor V Leiden carrier is still 3 months
After the Acute PE — Follow-Up & Complications
The bit that gets skipped. The duration table tells you how long to anticoagulate — this tells you what actually happens at each of those decision points. Every PE patient should leave with a follow-up plan, not just a prescription.
~7 Days Post-Discharge
  • BTS quality standard — review within about a week of discharge
  • Check adherence, tolerance and any bleeding; confirm the diagnosis still fits
  • Confirm the planned duration and who will review it
3 Months — The Fork
  • Formal reassessment: continue or stop?
  • Weigh recurrence risk against major bleeding risk
  • Ask about residual breathlessness and exercise tolerance
Annual Review — NICE
  • For anyone on long-term anticoagulation
  • Re-check the risk/benefit balance, renal and hepatic function, adherence
  • Ask again about bleeding and any new provoking factors

The 3-Month Fork — Continue or Stop?

Favours Continuing
  • Unprovoked VTE — recurrence risk stays high once treatment stops
  • Active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, recurrent VTE
  • An ongoing or irreversible risk factor; low bleeding risk
Favours Stopping
  • Provoked by a transient, now-resolved factor (surgery, cast, long-haul flight)
  • High bleeding risk — HAS-BLED ≥ 4 that cannot be modified
  • Patient preference after a genuine risk/benefit discussion
HAS-BLED in VTE.
  • NICE asks you to assess the risk of major bleeding with HAS-BLED when deciding whether to continue anticoagulation beyond 3 months for an unprovoked VTE, and to discuss stopping if the score is ≥ 4 and the risk cannot be modified.
  • Fix what is modifiable first — uncontrolled blood pressure, concurrent NSAIDs or antiplatelets, harmful alcohol intake, labile INR.
  • Do not base the decision on a predictive tool alone: it informs the conversation, it does not make the call. See Risk Scores & Criteria — Cardiology & VTE for the HAS-BLED components.

Unprovoked VTE — What to Work Up (and What Not To)

🚩 The classic trap. NICE says do NOT offer further investigations for cancer after an unprovoked VTE unless there are relevant clinical symptoms or signs — no routine CT abdomen/pelvis, no tumour markers, no blind imaging. What you do offer: a review of the history, a physical examination, and baseline bloods — FBC, renal and hepatic function, PT and APTT. Then investigate anything those turn up.
Antiphospholipid Antibodies
  • Consider testing in unprovoked VTE if stopping anticoagulation is planned
  • Positive (especially triple positive) → long-term warfarin, not a DOAC
Hereditary Thrombophilia
  • Consider only if all three: unprovoked VTE and a first-degree relative with VTE and stopping is planned
  • Do not test anyone who will continue anticoagulation — the result cannot change the plan
  • Do not test after a provoked VTE

Complications of PE

Complication What to know
Recurrent VTEHighest in the first year after anticoagulation stops, and far higher after an unprovoked event than a provoked one. New breathlessness or leg swelling → re-investigate, do not assume anxiety.
Bleeding on anticoagulationThe price of treatment — GI and intracranial bleeds matter most. Review at every visit: renal function (DOAC dosing), interacting drugs, Hb, falls risk.
Persistent breathlessnessCommon and under-recognised — roughly a third to a half are still symptomatic at 3 months (“post-PE syndrome”: deconditioning, anxiety, residual clot). Assess it properly rather than simply reassuring.
CTEPH (~2%)Organised, unresolved thrombus obstructing the pulmonary arteries months after PE — suspect it if breathlessness persists beyond 3 months, screen with echo then V/Q scan. This is WHO Group 4 pulmonary hypertension: see the Pulmonary Hypertension note for the full assessment and treatment.
Deep Vein Thrombosis
📷 Image placeholder — Anatomy of a lower-limb DVT — deep venous system with a proximal (femoral/popliteal) thrombus and the resulting unilateral leg swelling.
Features
  • Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness along the vein
  • Calf circumference >3 cm difference = significant
  • Homan's sign (unreliable — calf pain on dorsiflexion)
Diagnosis
  • 2-level DVT Wells score — ≥2 = likely, ≤1 = unlikely
  • Likely → proximal leg USS (compression USS), result within 4 hours; if that is not possible → interim therapeutic anticoagulation + D-dimer, and scan within 24 hours
  • Scan negative → do a D-dimer; if positive, stop the interim anticoagulation and repeat the scan in 6–8 days (catches a distal DVT extending proximally)
  • Unlikely → D-dimer → USS if positive
  • Proximal DVT confirmed = treat as VTE (NICE)
Management
  • Same as PE — DOAC first-line (apixaban / rivaroxaban)
  • Duration by provoked / unprovoked
  • Do not offer compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome or recurrence (NICE) — they may still be used for symptomatic leg pain or swelling
Complications
  • PE (embolisation — commonest serious complication)
  • Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers)
Exam Pearls
Virchow's triad: stasis · endothelial injury · hypercoagulability — maps all PE risk factors
Algorithm: Wells >4 → immediate CTPA; ≤4 → D-dimer → CTPA if positive
CTPA = gold standard. V/Q scan if renal impairment, contrast allergy, or pregnancy
D-dimer rules OUT, not in — raised in cancer, pregnancy, post-op, infection
ECG: usually sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 classic but rare; T-inversion V1–4 = RV strain. ABG = respiratory alkalosis (hypoxaemia + ↓PCO₂)
Stable → DOAC (apixaban / rivaroxaban start immediately). Massive / unstable → thrombolyse (alteplase)
Duration: provoked = 3 months · unprovoked = at least 3 months, then NICE default is to continue long-term unless bleeding risk is high · active cancer / APS = long-term. Hereditary thrombophilia alone does not decide duration
Apixaban / rivaroxaban: immediate start. Dabigatran / edoxaban: need 5 days LMWH lead-in first
Antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive) — do NOT use DOACs → LMWH → warfarin, INR 2–3
DVT: unilateral leg swelling + USS. Same anticoagulation as PE. Complication: PE + post-thrombotic syndrome
Unstable + can't do CTPA → bedside echo (RV dilatation) → empirical thrombolysis
Westermark's sign (CXR oligaemia), wedge infarct, normal CXR — classic PE CXR findings (CXR often normal)
Follow-up: review ~7 days post-discharge (BTS) → reassess at 3 months → annual review while on long-term anticoagulation (NICE). At 3 months use HAS-BLED in unprovoked VTE — discuss stopping if ≥ 4 and unmodifiable
Unprovoked VTE: history + examination + FBC, renal and hepatic function, PT and APTT — no further cancer investigations unless there are symptoms or signs. Thrombophilia testing only if stopping is planned
Not every PE is admitted — sPESI 0 / PESI I–II / Hestia negative → outpatient DOAC. Admit if HR >110, SBP <100, SpO₂ <90% on air, or inotropes / critical care / thrombolysis are needed. CTEPH (~2%) if breathless beyond 3 months
RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusion:
Excess fluid in the pleural space. Clinically detectable at >500 mL. On CXR: ~50 mL blunts the posterior costophrenic angle on the lateral film, ~200 mL to blunt the costophrenic angle on the PA. Massive effusion → think malignancy. The organising fork: transudate vs exudate — this single distinction drives investigation and management, decided by Light's criteria.
Transudate vs Exudate — The Spine
📷 Image placeholder — Mechanism diagram — transudate from a pressure imbalance (↑hydrostatic/↓oncotic pushing fluid across intact pleura) vs exudate from a leaky, inflamed pleura.
Transudate (protein <25 g/L) Exudate (protein >35 g/L)
MechanismPressure imbalance — ↑hydrostatic or ↓oncotic pressure pushes fluid across intact pleuraPleural damage / inflammation — ↑capillary permeability leaks protein-rich fluid
CausesHeart failure (commonest), hypoalbuminaemia (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), hypothyroidism, Meigs syndromePneumonia (parapneumonic), malignancy, TB, PE, RA / connective tissue disease, pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture
Typical appearanceClear, straw-coloured; often bilateralVariable; may be turbid, purulent, bloody; usually unilateral
Memory hooks: Transudate = “the fluid is pushed across” (systemic disease, often bilateral)  |  Exudate = “the pleura is leaky” (local disease, inflammatory)
Light's Criteria
📷 Image placeholder — Light’s criteria as a decision flowchart — the three ratios and the “any one positive → exudate” rule for a borderline protein.
Protein settles most cases on its own: <25 g/L = transudate, >35 g/L = exudate. Light’s criteria are needed only in the borderline band, 25–35 g/L (the “30 g/L” shorthand is the midpoint of that band, not a hard cut). Classify as exudate if ANY ONE of these is met. The trap: a diuresed heart failure effusion is concentrated by the diuretic and reads as a false (“pseudo-”) exudate — if the picture is clearly heart failure, check the serum − pleural fluid albumin gradient: >12 g/L means it is really a transudate.
Criterion 1 — Protein
Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5
Criterion 2 — LDH ratio
Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6
Criterion 3 — LDH level
Pleural fluid LDH > ⅔ of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Meet ANY one criterion = exudate. Must meet none of them to call it a transudate when protein is borderline.
Clinical Features
Symptoms
Small → asymptomatic. Larger: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (exudates especially), dry cough.
Examination — Key Signs
  • Stony dull percussion (distinguishes from consolidation, which is just dull)
  • Reduced / absent breath sounds
  • Reduced vocal fremitus / resonance
  • Reduced chest expansion ipsilaterally
  • Tracheal deviation away (massive effusion — mediastinal shift)
Effusion vs consolidation: both give dullness on percussion, but effusion = stony dull + absent breath sounds + reduced fremitus. Consolidation = dull + bronchial breathing + ↑vocal resonance.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Triangle of safety for pleural aspiration/chest drain — the anatomical borders (lateral pec major, anterior lat dorsi, 5th intercostal space, base of axilla).
TestFinding / Role
CXRCostophrenic angle blunting (~200 mL on PA, ~50 mL on lateral); meniscus sign; fluid in fissures; mediastinal shift (massive). Bilateral = transudate until proven otherwise.
USS chestConfirms fluid (vs consolidation); guides safe aspiration site; detects loculations
Diagnostic tap (USS-guided)First-line for an undiagnosed effusion (any effusion not clearly explained by a transudative cause). Site chosen by ultrasound at the time. Send: protein, LDH, glucose, cytology, MC&S, ± amylase — and get the containers right. pH goes into a heparinised blood gas syringe, capped, straight to a blood gas analyser — never a plain tube; air and delay falsely raise it, local anaesthetic falsely lowers it. If infection is possible, send microbiology in a sterile pot and inoculate 5–10 mL into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles — this roughly doubles the organism yield. Send the largest volume you can for cytology.
CT thoraxIf aspiration is non-diagnostic; pleural nodularity, circumferential or mediastinal thickening suggests malignancy; loculated collections. Cytology is positive in only ~60% of malignant effusions — a second sample adds a few percent, a third adds nothing. Two negative cytologies with ongoing suspicion → image-guided biopsy or local-anaesthetic thoracoscopy (diagnostic in ~90%, and talc can be given at the same sitting).
Pleural biopsyImage-guided (CT/USS) or thoracoscopic — for undiagnosed exudate, suspected malignancy or TB. Blind (Abrams) biopsy is superseded and should be avoided; the Abrams needle survives only as an exam eponym.
When NOT to tap: when the clinical picture strongly suggests a transudate — clear-cut decompensated heart failure with bilateral effusions — do not aspirate: treat the cause, and sample only if there are atypical features (unilateral, fever, pleuritic pain, disproportionate size) or failure to respond to therapy.

Fluid Appearance — Pattern Recognition

Purulent → empyema Turbid → infection / inflammation Milky / creamy → chylothorax (triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L) — but also empyema and pseudochylothorax: centrifuge it Bloodstained → malignancy, PE or a traumatic tap — a true haemothorax needs fluid haematocrit >50% of blood haematocrit Straw-coloured → transudate
Fluid biochemistry red flags: pH <7.2 in non-purulent fluid → drain (↓glucose and ↑LDH support it, they are not required)  |  ↑amylase → pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture  |  cytology positive → malignancy
🚩 Procedure safety — what goes wrong after the tap or the drain. The note teaches you how to do it; this is how it hurts people.
  • Re-expansion pulmonary oedema — the rule is symptom-led, not volume-led. Stop draining immediately if the patient develops cough, chest tightness or chest discomfort. BTS advises a maximum of 1.5 L drained in the first hour / at the first drainage, after which the remaining fluid can be drained slowly — that is a first-hour limit, not an absolute ceiling, and draining to dryness is reasonable provided no respiratory symptoms develop.
  • Higher-risk groups for re-expansion oedema: lung collapsed >7 days, younger patients, and where >3 L is drained.
  • Iatrogenic pneumothorax. Ultrasound guidance substantially reduces it — never tap “blind” off the CXR alone. A post-procedure CXR is not routine after an uncomplicated aspiration; it is indicated if air was aspirated, multiple passes were needed, or the patient becomes breathless or hypoxic.
  • Other complications: vasovagal episode, bleeding / intercostal vessel injury, site infection, drain blockage or dislodgement, and puncture of liver or spleen if the site is too low.
  • Drain mechanics (swinging, bubbling, clamping rules, removal) are covered in the Oxygenation & Respiratory Support note under Chest Drain Management — not repeated here.
Management
Transudate
Treat the underlying cause — diurese heart failure, correct hypoalbuminaemia, treat hypothyroidism. Aspiration if tense / symptomatic.
Exudate
Treat the underlying cause. Drainage if large / symptomatic (chest drain or aspiration). Send fluid for cytology / MC&S. Investigate for pneumonia, malignancy, TB.
Malignant Effusion
Recurs after aspiration. Drain, send a generous volume for cytology — positive in only ~60%, so a negative result does not exclude malignancy; repeat once, and if still negative with ongoing suspicion go to image-guided biopsy or thoracoscopy. Then choose between talc pleurodesis and an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) — the choice depends on whether the lung re-expands (see the block below).
Small / Asymptomatic
Conservative management + monitoring. Serial USS / CXR. Investigate aetiology.

Malignant Effusion — Pleurodesis vs Indwelling Pleural Catheter

The whole decision turns on one thing: pleurodesis requires the visceral and parietal pleura to appose — the sclerosant can only fuse two surfaces that are actually touching. A lung that will not re-expand cannot be pleurodesed. So check re-expansion on the post-drainage CXR before you commit to anything.
Lung re-expands
Offer a choice of talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC), guided by patient preference (BTS). Both are legitimate first-line options — pleurodesis buys a definitive result at the cost of an inpatient stay; an IPC allows drainage at home with no admission.
Non-expandable (“trapped”) lung
>25% of the lung not apposed to the chest wall after drainage. IPC is preferred — pleurodesis will fail, because the two pleural surfaces never meet. Clues: fluid re-accumulates almost immediately, chest pain during drainage, or a hydropneumothorax ex vacuo on the post-drainage film.
Correct the old teaching: the IPC is not a rescue after failed pleurodesis. BTS guidance positions it as a first-line option alongside pleurodesis when the lung expands, and as the preferred option when it does not.
Parapneumonic Effusion & Empyema
📷 Image placeholder — Staging of parapneumonic effusion — simple → complicated → empyema, with the pH/glucose/LDH thresholds that trigger drainage.
The infective spectrum. Fluid analysis defines the stage and mandates the treatment — know the thresholds.
StageFluid CharacteristicsManagement
Simple parapneumonicClear, sterile; normal pH (>7.2), normal glucose, normal LDHAntibiotics alone — resolves with treatment of pneumonia
Complicated parapneumonicInfected, non-purulent; pH <7.2 decides. Supporting: glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000, ongoing fever, a large collection, septations on ultrasound or pleural enhancement on CTChest drain (intercostal) + antibiotics
EmpyemaFrank pus — the diagnosis is made by looking at it. Do not send pus for pH: it adds nothing and damages the blood gas analyserChest drain ± intrapleural tPA (alteplase) + DNase; VATS if the drain fails
Drain on ANY ONE of: frank pus (= empyema — drain, no further tests needed)  |  organisms on Gram stain or a positive culture  |  pH <7.2 in non-purulent fluid. Glucose <2.2 mmol/L and LDH >1000 U/L are supporting, not deciding. Clear fluid with pH >7.2 and no organisms = simple effusion → antibiotics alone. It is not a triad.

After the Drain — The Pleural Infection Pathway

Antibiotics — not a CAP regimen
Pleural infection is frequently polymicrobial and anaerobic, so anaerobic cover is required — unlike the CAP regimens taught in the Pneumonia note. Options include a penicillin / β-lactamase inhibitor combination, clindamycin, metronidazole or a carbapenem.
Drainage & escalation
  • Small-bore (≤14F) drain is first-line for pleural infection — as effective as a large tube and far less painful. (The large-bore drain belongs to haemothorax, not empyema — a classic mix-up.)
  • Reassess early. If drainage has stalled and a residual collection remains, consider intrapleural tPA (alteplase) + DNase.
  • Involve thoracic surgery early (VATS ± decortication) if antibiotics, drainage and fibrinolytics all fail — do not let a septic patient drift.
⏳ Duration — the actual learning point. Treatment is prolonged: commonly around 3 weeks or more, guided by clinical response. Recommended durations genuinely vary between sources — BTS suggests around 3 weeks is probably appropriate, while other guidance quotes 4–6 weeks — so state it as prolonged and response-guided rather than a single settled figure. Contrast this with the 5–7 days you memorised for community-acquired pneumonia. Switch IV → oral once there is clinical improvement: pyrexia settled, inflammatory markers falling, radiological improvement.
Aftermath: residual pleural thickening / fibrothorax — a fibrous peel encasing the lung — produces a restrictive defect with reduced expansion on that side (see the Reduced Chest Expansion note); a minority need decortication.
Haemothorax
Causes
Trauma (rib fractures → intercostal vessel injury) — commonest; malignancy; iatrogenic (central line, post-thoracic surgery).
Flail Segment
≥2 (typically ≥3) consecutive ribs fractured in ≥2 places → loss of chest-wall rigidity → paradoxical movement (segment moves in on inspiration). Respiratory failure risk.
Management
A–E resuscitation; tranexamic acid (TXA) early; large-bore chest drain (28–40 Fr) — prevents clotting / empyema. Early VATS (48–72 h) for a retained haemothorax — clot the drain has failed to clear. Immediate thoracotomy for a massive haemothorax — >1500 mL drained immediately, or >200 mL/hour for 2–4 consecutive hours — or persistent bleeding. (These drainage and surgical thresholds come from trauma practice, not from BTS.)
Exam Pearls
Stop draining for cough, chest tightness or chest discomfort — the symptom, not a number, is the re-expansion pulmonary oedema rule. 1.5 L is the first-hour limit, not an absolute cap; draining to dryness is fine if the patient stays symptom-free.
Empyema antibiotics ≠ CAP antibiotics: anaerobic cover and a prolonged course (commonly ~3 weeks or more, guided by response) — not the 5–7 days of CAP. The drain is small-bore (≤14F).
Pleurodesis needs the pleurae to touch. Non-expandable (“trapped”) lung >25% → IPC preferred; lung re-expands → patient chooses talc or IPC. And clear-cut decompensated HF with bilateral effusions → treat, don't tap.
Transudate (<30 g/L) = pressure — HF (commonest), cirrhosis, nephrotic, hypothyroid. Exudate (>30 g/L) = pleural disease — pneumonia, cancer, TB, PE.
Light's criteria for borderline: protein >0.5, LDH >0.6, LDH >⅔ ULN → exudate if ANY one met
Massive effusion → malignancy first. Drain, send cytology, then check re-expansion on the post-drainage film: lung re-expands → talc pleurodesis OR an indwelling pleural catheter by patient choice; trapped lung → IPC preferred. The IPC is a first-line option, not a rescue.
Fluid appearance: purulent = empyema · milky = chylothorax (triglycerides >1.24 mmol/L), but spin it — empyema and pseudochylothorax also look milky · bloodstained = usually malignancy or a traumatic tap; a true haemothorax needs fluid haematocrit >50% of blood
Drain on ANY ONE: frank pus (= empyema, no further tests) · organisms on Gram stain or a positive culture · pH <7.2 in non-purulent fluid. Glucose <2.2 and LDH >1000 support the decision, they do not make it. There is no triad.
Meigs syndrome = ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion, right-sided in ~70%, resolving after tumour removal. Traditionally listed under transudates, but the fluid is often exudative — classify it on the protein, not the eponym
PE causes an exudate — not transudate. A common exam trick.
Pleural aspiration is always ultrasound-guided — the site is chosen by USS at the time (never blind off the CXR), entering immediately above the superior border of the rib below, because the neurovascular bundle runs at the inferior border of the rib above. The triangle of safety is the landmark zone for chest drain insertion: lateral border of pectoralis major (anterior), anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posterior), a horizontal line at the 5th ICS / nipple line (inferior), apex of the axilla (superior).
Haemothorax: large-bore drain to prevent clotting; TXA; early VATS (48–72 h) for a retained haemothorax, thoracotomy if bleeding is massive or ongoing
Stony dull percussion = effusion (vs dull = consolidation). Effusion also has absent breath sounds + reduced fremitus (consolidation has bronchial breathing + ↑resonance).
RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax:
Air in the pleural space → partial or complete lung collapse. The framing: classify (primary vs secondary) → assess symptoms & high-risk features → decide management with the patient (conservative / ambulatory / aspiration / drain) → never miss tension (the emergency). Cross-ref pleural effusion — same pleural space, same triangle of safety and chest drain technique; the key contrast is hyperresonant (pneumothorax) vs stony dull (effusion).
Classification & Aetiology
Primary Spontaneous
  • No underlying lung disease
  • Tall, thin, young men
  • Ruptured subpleural bleb/bulla
  • Smoking is a risk factor
  • Often a positive family history; recurrence is highest in the first year and higher in smokers
  • Good prognosis — manage conservatively if minimally symptomatic (this applies even to a larger PTX in a stable patient)
Secondary Spontaneous
  • Also connective tissue disease (Marfan’s, vascular Ehlers–Danlos), cystic lung disease (lymphangioleiomyomatosis — young women; Birt–Hogg–Dubé — renal tumours + skin fibrofolliculomas; tuberous sclerosis), and catamenial pneumothorax (thoracic endometriosis — within ~72 h of menses onset, ~90% right-sided)
  • Underlying lung disease — COPD (commonest), asthma, CF, bronchiectasis, TB, malignancy
  • Worse outcomes — lower threshold to drain
  • Admit all
Traumatic / Iatrogenic
  • Rib fractures
  • Biopsy
  • central line insertion
  • Mechanical ventilation (barotrauma)
  • Chest drain complications
Tension Pneumothorax
  • Emergency subtype — one-way valve mechanism → progressive pressure build-up
  • Can occur from any cause
  • See dedicated section below
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated CXR of a simple pneumothorax — the visible visceral pleural (lung) edge with an absent-lung-marking lucent zone peripheral to it; contrast with the normal side.
Symptoms
  • Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain ± breathlessness
  • May be minimal in primary (small)
  • Marked dyspnoea in secondary (limited reserve)
Examination — Air Signature
  • Hyperresonant percussion on affected side
  • Reduced / absent breath sounds
  • Reduced chest expansion ipsilaterally
  • Reduced vocal resonance / fremitus
Percussion contrast: Pneumothorax = hyperresonant (air)  |  Effusion = stony dull (fluid)  |  Consolidation = dull with bronchial breathing
Investigations
Erect PA CXR — First-line
  • Visible lung edge with absent peripheral lung markings
  • Measure at both the hilum and the apex: ≥2cm laterally at the level of the hilum or ≥2cm apically
  • What 2cm means now: not “small vs large, therefore aspirate vs drain” — it is the threshold at which the pneumothorax is big enough to intervene on safely
  • Any size can be drained on CT if it can be safely accessed with imaging guidance
CT Thorax
  • If bullous disease suspected (distinguishes bulla from pneumothorax — avoids dangerous needling of a bulla)
  • Also for small/atypical cases or surgical planning
Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for CXR. Treat immediately.

Management — Symptom & Risk-Driven (BTS)
📷 Image placeholder — Flowchart of the BTS pneumothorax pathway — high-risk features? → intervention; otherwise symptoms + patient preference → conservative / ambulatory device / aspiration / chest drain.
O₂ in pneumothorax: a high FiO₂ washes nitrogen out of the pleural gas and can speed reabsorption several-fold — but the evidence is weak and it is never a substitute for drainage. In practice treat the hypoxia, not the film: titrate to SpO₂ 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. known COPD). Do not give high-flow O₂ to a normoxic patient purely to shrink the pneumothorax.
Current BTS approach: rigid size cut-offs are no longer the primary driver. Management is decided by symptoms + high-risk characteristics + patient priorities (shared decision), with size a secondary factor. (There is no NICE pneumothorax guideline — BTS is the UK authority.)
High-risk characteristics — favour intervention (chest drain)
Haemodynamic compromise · significant hypoxia · bilateral pneumothorax · underlying lung disease · over 50 with a significant smoking history · haemopneumothorax.
ScenarioManagement
Minimally symptomatic, no high-risk features Conservative management — regardless of size (even a large primary spontaneous PTX in a stable, minimally symptomatic patient). Outpatient review + safety-net; repeat imaging to confirm resolution.
Symptomatic, no high-risk features Shared decision between: conservative observation · ambulatory management with a one-way valve device (e.g. pleural vent) · needle aspiration (16–18G, ≤2.5L) · chest drain — guided by patient priorities and local expertise.
High-risk features present Chest drain — provided the pneumothorax is large enough to drain safely. Ambulatory devices are not the alternative here: the ambulatory recommendation covers primary spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk features only.
Secondary spontaneous (e.g. COPD) Lower threshold to intervene — most need admission + chest drain; worse outcomes.
Outside the BTS spontaneous pathway — traumatic & iatrogenic pneumothorax.
  • BTS deliberately scopes traumatic and iatrogenic pneumothorax out of its spontaneous-pneumothorax recommendations — do not apply the table above to them.
  • Iatrogenic (post CT-guided lung biopsy, central line or pacemaker insertion, ventilation barotrauma) usually resolves rapidly and often needs no intervention — observation ± supplemental O₂ with repeat imaging; drain only if symptomatic, large, or the patient is ventilated.
  • Traumatic (rib fractures, penetrating injury) follows ATLS principles — most need a chest drain, and any haemopneumothorax needs one.
  • Key caveat — positive-pressure ventilation: any pneumothorax in a patient about to be intubated and ventilated (or put on NIV) is a different risk category — positive pressure can convert a simple pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax, so a chest drain generally goes in first.
Persistent air leak (>3–5 days) or recurrence → refer thoracic surgery for VATS pleurodesis (talc) ± bullectomy.
Recurrence & Definitive Surgery
  • Recurrence risk: after a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax, recurrence is commonly quoted at ~25–30% within the first year (published series range widely, 23–50%). Risk is highest in that first year and is higher in smokers — which is why smoking cessation is a therapeutic intervention here, not generic lifestyle advice.
  • BTS surgical trigger: consider elective surgery after a second ipsilateral pneumothorax, a first contralateral pneumothorax, or synchronous bilateral pneumothoraces.
  • Consider it earlier where recurrence prevention especially matters: at-risk occupations — professional divers, airline pilots, military personnel — or where the first presentation was a tension pneumothorax.
  • What the operation is: VATS bullectomy (resect the offending bleb/bulla) plus a pleural procedure to obliterate the space — chemical pleurodesis (talc), mechanical/abrasive pleurodesis, or pleurectomy (surgical stripping of the parietal pleura, the most durable option).
  • Read this against the Discharge Advice below: “permanently no scuba diving” is the default for the unoperated patient — but definitive surgery is the route back for someone whose livelihood depends on diving or flying. So an at-risk occupation is a reason to refer thoracic surgery early, not a reason to simply hand out the blanket ban.
Tension Pneumothorax — The Emergency
📷 Image placeholder — Mechanism of a tension pneumothorax — a one-way valve trapping air under pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum/trachea away with kinking of the great veins → obstructive shock.
Clinical diagnosis only — do NOT wait for CXR. Treat immediately or patient will arrest.
Mechanism
  • One-way valve: air enters pleura on inspiration but cannot escape → progressive ↑intrapleural pressure → mediastinal shift → kinked great vessels → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest
Clinical Signs
  • Severe respiratory distress with ↓air entry + hyperresonance on the affected side
  • Hypoxia; tachycardia → hypotension → arrest
  • In a ventilated patient: a sudden rise in airway pressures with hypotension
  • Tracheal deviation away and distended neck veins are LATE and often absent — neck veins are flat if the patient is also hypovolaemic, which most trauma patients are. Do not wait for tracheal deviation before decompressing.
Immediate Management
  1. Immediate chest decompression. In a ventilated or peri-arrest/arrested patient, finger (open) thoracostomy is preferred — needles kink, block and fail. Otherwise needle decompression with a long large-bore cannula (14G, 5–8 cm) → hiss of air confirms. A standard short cannula fails to reach the pleura in many adults — “no hiss” from a short needle does NOT exclude tension. Preferred adult site is the 4th–5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line (within the safe triangle), where the chest wall is thinnest; the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line remains an accepted alternative and is the site to use when the lateral chest wall cannot be reached.
  2. Chest drain (definitive) — insert after needle decompression
Chest Drains — Practical Safety Points
📷 Image placeholder — Chest-wall diagram of insertion sites — the triangle of safety (pec major, lat dorsi, 5th ICS) and the needle-decompression site (4th–5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line), with the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line as the alternative.
Triangle of Safety
  • Bounded by: lateral border of pectoralis major (anterior)
  • anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posterior)
  • 5th ICS / nipple line (inferior)
  • Apex of axilla (superior)
  • For a spontaneous pneumothorax use a small-bore (8–14F) Seldinger drain — as effective as a large tube and far less painful. Large-bore belongs to haemothorax.
  • Always insert above the rib (neurovascular bundle runs below)
Underwater Seal
  • Acts as a one-way valve: air/fluid exits, cannot re-enter
  • Swinging with respiration = correctly sited
  • Bubbling = active air leak
  • No swing = blocked or drain displaced
Safety Rules — Classic SBA Points
  • Never lift the bottle above the patient → retrograde flow back into pleura
  • Never clamp a bubbling drain → tension pneumothorax
  • Swinging = good; no swing = re-examine/reposition
When does the drain come out? Lung fully re-expanded on CXR and the air leak has stopped (drain no longer bubbling) → consider removal. Remove during expiration or a Valsalva manoeuvre so air cannot be drawn back into the pleural space as the tube leaves. Repeat CXR after removal, before discharge.
Do not put a fresh pneumothorax drain straight onto suction — rapid re-expansion of a large or long-standing pneumothorax can precipitate re-expansion pulmonary oedema (highest risk: young patient, large pneumothorax, late presentation). If suction is needed it is high-volume low-pressure, started late, on senior advice.

Cross-ref → full aftercare is elsewhere: ongoing chest drain management — daily checks, suction settings and the complications list — lives in LUNG FUNCTION → Oxygenation & Respiratory Support → Chest Drain Management. Go there; it is not repeated here.
Discharge Advice
  1. Smoking cessation (↓bleb formation + recurrence risk)
  2. An unresolved pneumothorax is an absolute contraindication to flying. After a spontaneous pneumothorax: no flying until at least 1 week after a CXR confirms complete resolution (BTS) — the old “6 weeks” advice is not supported. After a traumatic pneumothorax: about 2 weeks from confirmed resolution (CAA).
  3. No scuba diving — permanently, unless definitive surgery (bilateral pleurectomy) with normal post-operative lung function and thoracic CT. Trapped gas expands on ascent (Boyle’s law) → tension.
  4. Return if worsening breathlessness / chest pain
  5. Review CXR at 2–4 weeks (primary spontaneous, conservative Mx)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Primary = tall thin young man, bleb, no lung disease. Secondary = underlying lung disease (COPD commonest) — worse outcome, drain earlier.
Size measurement: lung edge to chest wall at hilum. <2cm = small; ≥2cm = large. Under current BTS guidance size is a secondary factor — conservative management also applies to a large primary pneumothorax if the patient is stable and minimally symptomatic with no high-risk features.
Hyperresonant percussion = pneumothorax. Stony dull = effusion. Don't confuse these on the SBA.
Tension = clinical diagnosis, do NOT wait for CXR. Signs: trachea away, hypotension, distended neck veins, hyperresonance.
Tension immediate Rx: needle decompression (14G) at the 4th–5th ICS, anterior axillary line (finger thoracostomy if ventilated or arrested) → then chest drain (definitive). The old 2nd ICS midclavicular site is superseded.
Triangle of safety: lateral border of pec major, anterior border of lat dorsi, 5th ICS (nipple line). Insert above the rib — neurovascular bundle runs below.
Never clamp a bubbling drain → tension. Never raise bottle above patient → retrograde flow.
Persistent air leak >3–5 days → refer thoracics: pleurodesis (talc/VATS) ± bullectomy
Diving is contraindicated after a spontaneous pneumothorax — permanently, unless treated by bilateral surgical pleurectomy with normal post-operative lung function and thoracic CT. Gas trapped at 10 m doubles in volume on ascent (Boyle’s law) → tension. No flying until at least 1 week after CXR-confirmed resolution.
CT chest if bullous disease suspected — distinguish bulla from pneumothorax before any needling.
Recurrence ~25–30% in the first year after a first primary spontaneous PTX (higher in smokers). Elective surgery — VATS bullectomy + pleurodesis or pleurectomy — after a 2nd ipsilateral or 1st contralateral PTX, or earlier in divers / pilots / military.
Pneumothorax + about to be ventilated = drain first. Positive-pressure ventilation can convert a simple pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax. Otherwise an iatrogenic PTX (post lung biopsy / central line) usually just needs observation ± O₂.
Drain removal: lung re-expanded and no longer bubbling → remove in expiration or Valsalva (stops air re-entry), then CXR after removal before discharge.
RESPIRATORY__Lung Cancer:
3rd commonest cancer in the UK; smoking = biggest risk factor. The organising fork: SCLC vs NSCLC — this single split drives staging logic, treatment choice, and paraneoplastic syndromes. Everything in this topic hangs off which histological type.

Risk Factors
  • Smoking (biggest — 90% of SCLC)
  • Asbestos (synergistic with smoking)
  • Radon gas
  • Air pollution / diesel fumes
  • Ionising radiation
  • Family history

NICE Referral Criteria
2-Week Wait Referral
Suggestive CXR finding at any age, OR unexplained haemoptysis in patients ≥40 years.
Urgent CXR (age ≥40)
Age ≥40 with ≥2 unexplained symptoms — or ≥1 if they have ever smoked: cough, SOB, fatigue, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss. Perform within 2 weeks.
Also consider: clubbing, supraclavicular/persistent cervical LN, thrombocytosis, persistent or recurrent chest infection, chest signs consistent with lung cancer.
Thrombocytosis is a classic exam clue for lung-cancer referral criteria — easy to miss.
Investigations — The Diagnostic Pathway
InvestigationRole / Finding
CXR (first-line)Hilar enlargement, peripheral opacity, pleural effusion, lobar collapse, raised hemidiaphragm. Often the first clue.
Contrast CT — chest, liver, adrenals, lower neckStaging — tumour size, nodal involvement, distant metastases. The lower neck is included because supraclavicular nodes are N3. Perform before biopsy so the biopsy can be targeted.
PET-CTMetabolic activity; identifies occult metastases not seen on CT. Offered before treatment with curative intent. A PET-avid mediastinal node is not proof of N2 — where nodal status changes the plan, confirm it histologically with EBUS-TBNA ± EUS-FNA, and consider surgical mediastinal staging if sampling is negative but suspicion stays high.
Biopsy — histological diagnosisEssential. Central/endobronchial → bronchoscopy ± EBUS. Peripheral → CT-guided percutaneous biopsy. Always needed to confirm type.
Pleural fluid cytologyMalignant cells in the effusion = M1a — stage IV. Cytology cuts both ways: a single negative sample does not exclude it (repeat aspiration or thoracoscopy before committing), and an effusion that is repeatedly cytology-negative, non-bloody and non-exudative is excluded from staging — do not let unproven fluid strip a patient of curative treatment.
BloodsFBC (thrombocytosis), bone profile (Ca²⁺), LFTs (liver mets), Na⁺ (SIADH), U&Es
SpirometryPre-operative lung function — essential before any surgical resection
Stage & Fitness — What Decides Treatment
Every lung cancer plan answers two questions: how far has it spread (stage) and how fit is this person (performance status). Histology tells you which drugs; stage + PS tell you the intent — radical (curative) vs palliative.
T — Primary tumour
T1≤3 cm
T2>3–5 cm, or main bronchus / visceral pleura
T3>5–7 cm; chest wall, phrenic nerve, or a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or invading mediastinum, heart, great vessels, carina, oesophagus or vertebra
N — Nodes
N0none
N1ipsilateral hilar / peribronchial
N2ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal
N3contralateral mediastinal / hilar, or any supraclavicular / scalene
M — Metastases
M0none
M1acontralateral lung nodule, pleural / pericardial nodules, or malignant pleural effusion
M1bsingle extrathoracic metastasis
M1cmultiple extrathoracic metastases
Stage groups
  • I — small, node-negative → surgery
  • II — bigger and/or N1 → surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy
  • III — N2/N3 or T4 → multimodal, usually not primarily resectable
  • IV — any M1 → systemic / palliative
Exam anchors: N2 (ipsilateral mediastinal) usually means stage III and chemoradiotherapy rather than the knife; N3 is not a surgical case, and M1 is not a routine surgical case — though genuinely oligometastatic disease (e.g. a solitary adrenal or brain metastasis) can still be treated radically; a malignant pleural effusion is M1a, not “a bit of fluid”.
SCLC — Limited Stage (~1 in 3)
Disease confined to one hemithorax and its regional nodes, and small enough to be encompassed within a single tolerable radiotherapy field. This is the group treated with curative intent (concurrent chemoradiotherapy).
SCLC — Extensive Stage (~2 in 3)
Anything beyond that — contralateral lung, distant metastases, or a malignant pleural/pericardial effusion. Treatment is palliative: chemotherapy ± immunotherapy, with radiotherapy for symptom control.
WHO / ECOG PSDefinitionTreatment implication
0Fully active; no restriction on pre-disease activityBroadly the radical-treatment / systemic anticancer therapy group — surgery, radical radiotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy
1Restricted in strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to do light work
2Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work; up and about >50% of waking hours
3Capable of only limited self-care; confined to bed or chair >50% of waking hoursGenerally best supportive / palliative care; toxicity outweighs benefit
4Completely disabled; no self-care; totally confined to bed or chair
PS 0–2 is the radical-treatment candidate group. In UK practice performance status decides radical vs palliative as much as stage does — a stage I tumour in a PS 4 patient is not a surgical case, and PS is the reason two people with identical scans get different plans. Always quote stage + PS together in an exam answer.
Management — SCLC vs NSCLC Fork
📷 Image placeholder — Treatment-fork flowchart — NSCLC (surgery/radical RT ± adjuvant, targeted/immunotherapy) vs SCLC (chemo ± RT; rarely surgical).
NSCLC — Localised Disease
  • Surgery first-line if localised (stages I–II ± IIIA).
  • Lobectomy preferred (FEV1 >1.5 L); pneumonectomy if needed (FEV1 >2 L); wedge/segmentectomy if poor lung function.
  • Curative radiotherapy (SABR) if surgery is contraindicated.
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II+.
NSCLC — Advanced Disease
  • Platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin / carboplatin).
  • Targeted therapy if mutation positive: EGFR inhibitors (osimertinib first-line; also gefitinib / erlotinib); ALK inhibitors (alectinib first-line; crizotinib).
  • Immunotherapy (pembrolizumab — PD-L1 high).
  • Palliative radiotherapy for bone / brain mets.
SCLC
  • Surgery almost never used — widespread at presentation.
  • Chemotherapy + radiotherapy: cisplatin + etoposide.
  • Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) — prevents brain mets.
  • Worse prognosis than NSCLC.
Palliative / Supportive
  • Endobronchial stenting / laser debulking — airway obstruction.
  • Malignant effusion — drain, send cytology, then check re-expansion: lung re-expands → talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter by patient choice; trapped lung → IPC preferred.
  • Dexamethasone — cerebral oedema from brain metastases (not the SVC obstruction answer; steroids are widely given there but the evidence is weak).
  • Endovascular stenting — severe symptomatic SVC obstruction.
  • Bisphosphonates — bone mets.
  • MDT: oncology, thoracic surgery, palliative care, respiratory.
StageTreatmentIntent
NSCLC stage I–II (± selected IIIA)Lobectomy (SABR if unfit or declines surgery); adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy for stage II+Radical
NSCLC stage III — unresectablePlatinum-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy, then consolidation durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) in eligible patients who have not progressed — in the UK this is restricted to PD-L1-positive diseaseRadical
NSCLC stage IVTest for driver mutations first: osimertinib (EGFR) or alectinib (ALK) first-line; pembrolizumab if PD-L1 high and no driver; otherwise platinum-doublet chemotherapy ± immunotherapy. Palliative RT for bone / brain diseasePalliative
SCLC — limited stageConcurrent chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin + etoposide) with curative intent. PCI (prophylactic cranial irradiation) is offered only to people with WHO PS 0–2 whose disease has not progressed on first-line treatmentRadical
SCLC — extensive stagePlatinum + etoposide ± atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1). Thoracic radiotherapy alongside PCI where appropriate after a response. Chemo-sensitive but relapses earlyPalliative
PCI is not automatic. The note-level shorthand “SCLC gets PCI” loses marks — It is restricted to WHO PS 0–2 with no progression on first-line treatment.
Pre-op spirometry thresholds: Pneumonectomy → FEV1 >2.0 L  |  Lobectomy → FEV1 >1.5 L (traditional cut-offs; formal BTS assessment uses predicted post-op FEV1 & TLCO)
Complications of Treatment
Lung cancer treatment toxicity is examined as “recognise it, name it, act on it”. The two highest-yield patterns: breathless with a dry cough weeks after thoracic radiotherapy = radiation pneumonitis, and any new organ inflammation on a checkpoint inhibitor = an immune-related adverse event. Both are treated with corticosteroids.
Treatment Key Complication(s) Recognition / Action
Surgery (lobectomy / pneumonectomy)Prolonged air leak (commonest — persistent bubbling in the drain), empyema ± bronchopleural fistula, post-pneumonectomy dyspnoea, arrhythmia (AF)Air leak → keep the drain, do not clamp. Fever + purulent drainage after resection → empyema. New AF post-thoracotomy is common — rate control + treat the cause
Thoracic radiotherapy (radical RT, SABR, chemoradiotherapy)Radiation pneumonitis — breathlessness and a dry cough weeks to months after thoracic RT; ground-glass change confined to the radiation fieldAfebrile, no purulent sputum, timing fits → corticosteroids (with a slow taper). Exclude infection, PE and progression. Late sequel = pulmonary fibrosis in the treated field
Thoracic radiotherapy — oesophagus in fieldRadiation oesophagitis — retrosternal pain and odynophagia during or shortly after mediastinal RTSoft diet, analgesic mouthwash, PPI; watch for dehydration and weight loss. Worse with concurrent chemoradiotherapy
Platinum chemotherapy (cisplatin, carboplatin)Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (high-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus), peripheral neuropathy, severe emesis; myelosuppressionCisplatin needs pre- and post-hydration and U&E monitoring; highly emetogenic → 5-HT₃ antagonist + dexamethasone ± NK1 antagonist. Carboplatin = less nephro/oto/neurotoxic but more myelosuppressive
EGFR / ALK TKIs (osimertinib, alectinib)Acneiform rash, diarrhoea, and — uncommon but serious — interstitial lung diseaseRash and diarrhoea are usually manageable (emollients, topical/oral antibiotics, loperamide). New breathlessness or cough → stop the TKI, image, and exclude ILD before blaming progression
Immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab)Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) — any organ, most often pneumonitis, colitis, thyroiditis and hepatitis (also hypophysitis, rash, nephritis)The principle: stop the drug and give corticosteroids; escalate if there is no response (e.g. infliximab for steroid-refractory colitis). Thyroiditis is the exception — replace thyroid hormone rather than steroid. Can appear weeks to months after a dose, and even after stopping
Routing: a febrile patient on chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — see the Neutropenic Sepsis note (haematology) for the 1-hour antibiotic rule. SVC obstruction, malignant spinal cord compression, hypercalcaemia and tumour lysis are covered in Oncological Emergencies.
After Treatment — Follow-up, Recurrence & Smoking Cessation
Structured Follow-up (NICE)
  • Offer an initial specialist follow-up within 6 weeks of completing treatment (NICE), then regular appointments thereafter — not waiting for symptoms to prompt a request.
  • Surveillance includes clinical review and interval CT imaging.
The Clinical Nurse Specialist
  • Offer protocol-driven follow-up led by a lung cancer clinical nurse specialist as an option.
  • The CNS is the key worker — the named point of contact between visits.
  • Coordinates care, gives information and support, and is the fast route back into the service.
Recognising Recurrence
  • Most recurrence happens in the first 2 years.
  • Warning features: new or changed cough, haemoptysis, new breathlessness or a new pleural effusion, hoarseness, unexplained weight loss.
  • New bone pain → bone mets; new headache / seizure / focal neurology → brain mets.
  • Route back: patient contacts the CNS key worker directly → urgent re-imaging and re-discussion at the lung cancer MDT — not a fresh GP 2-week-wait referral.
  • Also watch for second primaries — the risk factor has not gone away.
Smoking Cessation at Diagnosis
  • Offer NRT and cessation support to everyone who still smokes at diagnosis — continued smoking worsens surgical and radiotherapy outcomes, treatment toxicity and second-primary risk.
  • But do not postpone lung cancer surgery to allow someone to stop smoking — the delay costs more than the cigarettes.
  • Pharmacology (NRT, varenicline, cytisine, bupropion, vapes) is in the Smoking Cessation note — not repeated here.
Prognosis
Stage at diagnosis is everything.
  • Around 65% of people diagnosed at stage 1 survive 5 years or more, versus roughly 5% at stage 4.
  • SCLC splits the same way: limited-stage disease on concurrent chemoradiotherapy has a median survival of roughly 15–20 months (a minority cured); extensive-stage survival is measured in months (~10) even with chemo-immunotherapy — the worst prognosis of the lung cancers.
  • Why it matters: most UK patients still present at stage 3–4, so the 2-week-wait referral criteria and the NHS lung cancer screening programme (targeted lung health checks — invite people aged 55–74 who have ever smoked, risk-assess, then low-dose CT for those at high risk) exist to shift diagnosis leftwards — that stage shift, not a new drug, is the biggest available survival gain. Note the UK rule is age plus ever-smoked, not a pack-year threshold.
Mesothelioma
Separate entity — malignancy of pleural mesothelial cells. Strongly asbestos-linked. Very long latency: up to 45 years after exposure.
Features
Dyspnoea, chest-wall pain (pleuritic), weight loss, clubbing. A pleural effusion is the commonest presenting finding; around 30% present as a painless effusion alone. Pleural plaques on CXR (asbestos marker — may predate cancer).
Investigation
CT thorax (pleural thickening ± effusion), thoracoscopic biopsy (diagnostic), pleural fluid cytology (often non-diagnostic alone).
Prognosis & Management
Poor prognosis (median ~12 months); rarely curative. Systemic therapy is nivolumab + ipilimumab (performance status 0–1) or platinum + pemetrexed; surgery in highly selected cases; palliative MDT. Always raise compensation at diagnosis — mesothelioma is a prescribed industrial disease, with a government lump-sum scheme where the employer or insurer cannot be traced, and the death is reportable to the coroner. Take a detailed occupational history and record it.
Exam Pearls
Central = squamous + SCLC; peripheral = adenocarcinoma (adeno = commonest overall, non-smokers/women)
SCLC paraneoplastics: SIADH (↓Na) · ectopic ACTH (Cushing's, hypokalaemic alkalosis) · Lambert-Eaton (improves with use) · limbic encephalitis (anti-Hu)
Squamous → hypercalcaemia (PTHrP) — not bony mets necessarily; PTHrP mimics PTH action
SCLC = chemo + radio (surgery only in early-stage T1–2a N0 M0); NSCLC = surgery if localised. Pre-op: pneumonectomy FEV1 >2 L, lobectomy FEV1 >1.5 L (traditional cut-offs; formal BTS assessment uses predicted post-op FEV1 & TLCO)
Pancoast → Horner's (ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis): apex tumour compressing the sympathetic chain
SVC obstruction → Pemberton's sign: raise arms → worsening facial plethora — an oncological emergency. Urgent oncology discussion; stenting for severe symptoms, then treatment directed by histology and stage (see Oncological Emergencies)
2WW referral: unexplained haemoptysis ≥40 or suggestive CXR. Thrombocytosis = red flag for urgent CXR.
Biopsy essential for histology; contrast CT chest, liver, adrenals, lower neck for staging; PET-CT for occult mets
Lambert-Eaton vs myasthenia gravis: LE improves with repeated use (↑ACh), MG worsens. Both → proximal weakness.
Mesothelioma: asbestos, long latency (typically 20–40+ years), pleural plaques on CXR, pleural effusion very common (~30% present as a painless effusion alone), poor prognosis
Hoarseness in lung cancer = recurrent laryngeal nerve compression (left side more common — longer course)
Adenocarcinoma tip: look for EGFR mutation in never-smokers, women, and people of East Asian ancestry → targeted therapy with gefitinib/erlotinib
Stage tells you where, PS tells you whether
WHO/ECOG PS 0–2 is broadly the radical-treatment group; PS 3–4 → best supportive care. Quote stage + performance status together — identical scans get different plans because of PS.
The two chemoradiotherapy answers
Unresectable stage III NSCLC = platinum-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy then consolidation durvalumab (PD-L1-positive disease). Limited-stage SCLC = concurrent chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin + etoposide, then PCI — but PCI is restricted (WHO PS 0–2, no progression on first-line treatment). “All SCLC gets PCI” is the trap answer.
Two toxicity patterns worth full marks
Breathless + dry cough weeks after thoracic RT = radiation pneumonitis → steroids. Diarrhoea, breathlessness or deranged LFTs on pembrolizumab = an immune-related adverse event → stop the drug + corticosteroids, escalate if no response.
Follow-up and smoking
Specialist follow-up within 6 weeks of finishing treatment, then CNS-led protocol-driven review — the clinical nurse specialist is the key worker. Offer NRT and cessation support, but never delay lung cancer surgery to let someone stop smoking.
RESPIRATORY__Cystic Fibrosis:
Autosomal recessive — CFTR gene, chromosome 7 — a defective cAMP-regulated Cl⁻ channel. Commonest mutation: ΔF508. The mechanism that explains everything: defective Cl⁻ (and water) transport → thick, viscous secretions → blocked tubes in every exocrine organ. One channel defect → multi-system disease: lungs, pancreas, gut, reproductive tract.
Pathophysiology
🧬
CFTR mutation → defective Cl⁻ channel
↓
🚫
Impaired Cl⁻ & water secretiononto epithelial surfaces
↓
🟤
Dehydrated, thick, viscous mucus
↓
⛔
Obstruction of tubesairways, pancreatic ducts, bile ducts, vas deferens…
↓
🩺
Recurrent infections, malabsorption, infertility, organ damage
Every clinical feature traces back to this single mechanism — a tube blocked by thick secretions. The sweat gland is the exception: there CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride from the duct, so losing it makes the sweat salty — which is why the sweat test works.
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Finger clubbing — a common examination finding in cystic fibrosis, reflecting chronic suppurative lung disease.
📷 Image placeholder — Body map of multisystem CF features — respiratory, pancreatic/GI, hepatobiliary, reproductive and sweat-gland involvement.
Respiratory
Thick airway mucus → impaired mucociliary clearance → recurrent infections → bronchiectasis, clubbing, nasal polyps, sinusitis.
GI / Pancreatic
Blocked pancreatic ducts → exocrine insufficiency → malabsorption, steatorrhoea, failure to thrive; fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (ADEK); CF-related diabetes; biliary → cirrhosis.
Neonatal
Meconium ileus — the classic newborn presentation (intestinal obstruction); prolonged neonatal jaundice; failure to pass meconium.
Reproductive
Male infertility — bilateral absence of the vas deferens (azoospermia); female subfertility (thick cervical mucus). Neither means childlessness — the azoospermia is obstructive (spermatogenesis is normal) and women with CF are substantially fertile; see Living with CF.
Other
Rectal prolapse (bulky stools), short stature, delayed puberty, and salt loss in heat, fever and exercise — and act on it: extra dietary salt for everyone, with sodium chloride supplements in infants and in hot weather, fever or heavy exercise. Untreated it causes hyponatraemic, hypochloraemic dehydration with a metabolic alkalosis, which can be how an infant with CF first presents.
Colonising Organisms
Organism Context / Significance
Staphylococcus aureusEarly / childhood coloniser — most common initially
Pseudomonas aeruginosaLater coloniser — marker of disease progression. A first or new isolate is a reason to act, not to observe: attempt eradication (NICE) — systemic antibiotics (usually oral ciprofloxacin) plus a nebulised antibiotic. Once infection is chronic it can no longer be eradicated, only suppressed — long-term nebulised colistimethate is first choice (NICE), with nebulised tobramycin if that fails
Burkholderia cepaciaThe dangerous one — associated with rapid decline; B. cenocepacia in particular is a contraindication to lung transplant at most centres. Above all it is transmissible between people with CF — which is what drives segregation
Aspergillus fumigatusCan cause allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — treat with steroids ± itraconazole
Why CF services are built around keeping patients apart.
  • These organisms pass between people with CF, so two patients with CF should never meet face to face.
  • Inpatients — individual rooms with en-suite facilities (NICE).
  • Outpatient clinics — segregated by time slot and cohorted by organism.
  • CF Trust policy allows only one person with CF at an indoor event — so patients cannot attend a CF support group together.
  • The point that lands it: Burkholderia is not merely "the dangerous one" — it is a transmissible danger, and that transmissibility drives the entire service model.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — The sweat test — pilocarpine iontophoresis technique and the diagnostic chloride thresholds (≥60 positive, 30–59 intermediate, <30 normal).
Sweat Test — Gold Standard
Pilocarpine iontophoresis → sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L = positive (normal <30). Repeat if intermediate (30–59) — and refer to a specialist CF centre for extended CFTR gene analysis: an intermediate result neither confirms nor excludes CF.

False positives: malnutrition, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, eczema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. (Oedema / hypoproteinaemia instead cause a false negative.)
Newborn Screening
Heel-prick — immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT); if elevated → CFTR mutation analysis as the second screening tier, then a sweat test to confirm the diagnosis. Part of the UK newborn screening programme.
Genetic Testing
CFTR mutation analysis — identifies ΔF508 and other mutations and guides eligibility for modulators. It supports the diagnosis but does not replace the sweat test, which remains the confirmatory test.
Other
Spirometry (obstructive pattern), CXR / HRCT (bronchiectasis, hyperinflation), sputum cultures (track colonisation), faecal elastase (pancreatic insufficiency), an annual OGTT from age 10 for CF-related diabetes — HbA1c is not sensitive enough to screen for it in CF — and LFTs.
Management
MDT approach: respiratory physician, physiotherapist, dietitian, specialist CF nurse, gastroenterologist, endocrinologist, fertility specialist, psychologist.
Respiratory
  1. 1Chest physio + postural drainage (≥2×/day)
  2. 2Nebulised DNase (dornase alfa) — thins mucus
  3. 3Anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis — flucloxacillin from diagnosis to age 3, consider continuing to 6 (NICE)
  4. 4Pseudomonas → first/new isolate: attempt eradication (oral ciprofloxacin + a nebulised antibiotic); chronic infection: long-term nebulised colistimethate (NICE), tobramycin second line
  5. 5Bronchodilators + hypertonic saline
Nutritional
  1. 1High-calorie, high-fat diet
  2. 2Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) — with every meal
  3. 3Fat-soluble vitamins — ADEK supplementation
  4. 4CF-related diabetes — insulin, never metformin or a sulfonylurea; and the high-calorie, high-fat CF diet continues unchanged — do not apply standard diabetes calorie or fat restriction
GI — Distal Intestinal Obstruction Syndrome (DIOS)
DIOS is the grown-up meconium ileus. Inspissated faecal and mucus material impacts at the ileocaecal region, affecting roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 5 people with CF — mainly adults and older children. It presents with colicky right iliac fossa pain, a palpable RIF mass, abdominal distension and vomiting.
The differential trap — this is where the marks are. DIOS mimics appendicitis, simple constipation and intussusception, and the reflex "obstruction → theatre" answer is wrong. In someone with CF, RIF pain with a palpable mass is DIOS until proven otherwise, and it is treated medically; an unnecessary laparotomy is a serious insult to a patient with poor lung reserve.
  1. 1Rehydrate — oral or IV fluids
  2. 2Oral or enteral water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) — usually tried first (NICE)
  3. 3Iso-osmotic macrogols (polyethylene glycol) — if that fails
  4. 4Surgery — last resort only
CFTR Modulators
Lumacaftor / Ivacaftor (Orkambi)
  • Now largely superseded by Kaftrio in eligible patients.
  • For ΔF508 homozygotes.
  • Lumacaftor = corrector (folds CFTR correctly); Ivacaftor = potentiator (keeps the channel open).
  • Increases functional CFTR at the cell surface — disease-modifying.
Elexacaftor / Tezacaftor / Ivacaftor (Kaftrio)
  • Triple therapy — highly effective for ΔF508 (one or two copies).
  • Significantly improves lung function and reduces exacerbations.
Advanced / Other
  1. 1Lung transplant (bilateral)
  2. 2Genetic counselling — AR; 25% risk in siblings
  3. 3Carrier screening for partners
Burkholderia cepacia complex (esp. B. cenocepacia) — associated with rapid decline; a contraindication to lung transplant at most centres.
Living with CF
CF is now an adult disease.
  • UK median predicted survival is now into the sixties — a projection for a baby born with CF today, not a guarantee, and not the same as the current life expectancy of adults already living with the disease.
  • Roughly 65% of the UK CF Registry is aged 16 or over (UK CF Registry).
  • Read the rest of this note with an adult in mind, not only a child.
Annual Review
Everyone with CF has an annual review by the specialist CF MDT — on top of routine reviews every 3–6 months in a stable adult, and more often in infancy (NICE) — spirometry, sputum culture, screening for CF-related diabetes, LFTs, vitamin levels, bone health and nutritional assessment. This is why the tests in the Investigations section exist: most are not one-off diagnostics but an annual monitoring cycle.
Transition to Adult Services
Transfer from paediatric to adult care requires a coordinated transition plan and a named worker (NICE). This is classically when adherence collapses — a teenager taking on sole responsibility for a treatment burden of a couple of hours a day, alongside school, exams and independence.
Fertility is managed, not simply lost.
  • In congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, spermatogenesis is normal — the azoospermia is obstructive, so surgical sperm retrieval (PESA / MESA / TESA) with ICSI allows biological fatherhood.
  • "Azoospermia means he cannot have children" is the classic wrong conclusion — obstructive vs non-obstructive azoospermia is directly examinable.
  • Women with CF are substantially fertile; pregnancy is achievable and increasingly common — pair this with the partner carrier screening listed under Advanced / Other.
Exam Pearls
AR, CFTR chromosome 7, ΔF508 commonest mutation
Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L = gold standard; newborn heel-prick = IRT
One defect → multi-system: lungs (bronchiectasis) + pancreas (malabsorption) + gut (meconium ileus) + infertility
Meconium ileus = classic neonatal presentation
Male infertility = absent vas deferens (azoospermia — testes normal); obstructive, so sperm retrieval + ICSI still allows fatherhood
Bugs: Staph (early) → Pseudomonas (later — first isolate: try to eradicate; chronic: suppress with a nebulised antibiotic) → Burkholderia cepacia complex (B. cenocepacia especially: transmissible, and a transplant contraindication at most centres)
Creon (pancreatic enzymes) with every meal + ADEK vitamins + high-calorie diet
DNase (dornase alfa) thins mucus; Orkambi / Kaftrio for ΔF508 — disease-modifying
A recognised cause of bronchiectasis
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies: A (night blindness), D (rickets / osteoporosis), E (neuropathy), K (coagulopathy)

Two people with CF never meet — individual en-suite rooms, time-segregated clinics cohorted by organism; Burkholderia is transmissible, not just dangerous
CF is now an adult disease — median predicted survival now into the sixties, ~65% of the UK registry aged 16+; annual MDT review and a planned transition with a named worker
RESPIRATORY__Interstitial Lung Disease /:
ILD = diseases causing inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium → impaired gas exchange. The unifying functional signature: restrictive spirometry — FEV1/FVC normal or ↑ (FVC falls proportionally more than FEV1), ↓FVC, ↓TLCO. Two organising anchors: the zone of fibrosis (upper vs lower) and a per-condition template (features → Ix → Mx).
Shared Features — Most ILDs
📷 Image placeholder — Finger clubbing — the loss of the nail-bed angle and bulbous fingertips seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (and other fibrotic ILD); a key bedside sign.
Clinical features
  • Progressive exertional dyspnoea
  • Dry cough
  • Fine inspiratory crackles
  • Clubbing — characteristic of fibrotic ILD (IPF, asbestosis, CTD-ILD); typically absent in sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis
InvestigationFinding
PFTsRestrictive — ↓FVC, FEV₁/FVC normal or ↑, ↓TLCO
HRCTKey diagnostic investigation (reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis)
Zonal Classification — The Master Table
📷 Image placeholder — Lung diagram splitting upper-zone (CHARTS) vs lower-zone fibrosis causes, keyed to where each characteristically deposits.
The single most-tested object in ILD. Anchor this early — the zone of fibrosis on CXR / HRCT narrows the differential immediately.
Upper Zone — CHARTS Lower Zone
C — Coal worker's pneumoconiosisIdiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)
H — Hypersensitivity pneumonitis / HistiocytosisMost connective tissue disorders (RA, systemic sclerosis, SLE) — lower zone (AS, a spondyloarthropathy, is the upper-zone odd-one-out)
A — Ankylosing spondylitisDrugs — amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin (stop the drug — the first and most important step)
R — Radiation fibrosisAsbestosis

Exceptions: HP fibrosis can be upper/mid zone in the chronic phase. Ankylosing spondylitis = upper zone — it is a spondyloarthropathy, not a true connective tissue disorder, but is often grouped with them; the true CTDs are all lower zone.
Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated HRCT of the UIP pattern — subpleural, basal honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis and reticulation.
IPF — progressive lower-zone fibrosis with no identifiable cause. Age 50–70, M > F. Poor prognosis: median survival ~3–4 years from diagnosis.
Symptoms
Progressive exertional dyspnoea (insidious onset), dry non-productive cough, fatigue, weight loss.
Signs
Bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles (“velcro crackles”), clubbing (common — roughly half to two-thirds), cyanosis in advanced disease.
Zone
Lower zone / bibasal on CXR and HRCT — the key differentiator from upper-zone ILDs.
TestFinding
HRCT (diagnostic)UIP pattern — honeycombing (subpleural cysts), reticular / linear opacities, traction bronchiectasis, subpleural and bibasal predominance. Biopsy is usually not needed when the HRCT shows a classic UIP pattern, but the diagnosis is made by consensus of the ILD multidisciplinary team (NICE), not on the scan alone; where the MDT cannot reach a confident diagnosis, BAL, transbronchial biopsy or surgical lung biopsy is considered.
PFTsRestrictive: ↓FVC, FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓TLCO (most sensitive marker of severity)
ABGHypoxaemia with normal or low CO₂ (type 1 respiratory failure)
BloodsANA, RF may be weakly positive (exclude connective tissue disease); CRP/ESR may be raised
CXRBibasal reticular shadowing (less sensitive than HRCT)

Management

Antifibrotics (Disease-Modifying)
Pirfenidone (anti-inflammatory + antifibrotic) or Nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) — slow progression; do not reverse fibrosis.
Supportive
Pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental O₂, treat comorbidities (GORD, pulmonary hypertension), palliative care.
Lung Transplant
The only curative option — for selected patients with progressive disease; whether single or bilateral is a transplant-centre decision.

Antifibrotics — What They Do, and What They Cause

Pirfenidone
  • Combined anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic action
  • Key toxicity: photosensitivity and rash — counsel on high-factor sunblock, covering up and avoiding sun exposure
  • Also nausea, anorexia and weight loss; hepatotoxicity
Nintedanib
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (PDGFR, FGFR, VEGFR)
  • Key toxicity: diarrhoea — very common and often dose-limiting; also nausea and vomiting
  • Also hepatotoxicity, increased bleeding risk and arterial thrombotic events
  • Teratogenic — women of childbearing potential need effective contraception during and after treatment, with a barrier method added to any hormonal contraceptive, since nintedanib may reduce its effectiveness (BNF)
Common to both: both are hepatotoxic and are started and monitored by the ILD specialist service. Check LFTs before starting, then monthly for the first 6 months and 3-monthly thereafter for pirfenidone (BNF), with regular monitoring on nintedanib and most intensively in the early months — and test liver function promptly, without waiting for the next scheduled check, in anyone reporting jaundice, dark urine, nausea or right-upper-quadrant pain.

UK eligibility differs between them: pirfenidone is used where FVC is 50–80% predicted, and is stopped if predicted FVC falls by 10% or more in any 12-month period; nintedanib is used at 50–80% under the same stopping rule, and is also an option when FVC is above 80% predicted (NICE). Note what the stopping rule is not — it is not “any decline”. Neither drug reverses established fibrosis and neither halts decline; both slow the rate of it, so a slow fall in FVC on treatment is expected and is not a reason to stop.
Steroids are not beneficial in IPF (unlike other ILDs) and may be harmful — do not use.

Acute Exacerbation of IPF

Definition: an acute, clinically significant, unexplained worsening of dyspnoea (typically within a month) with new bilateral ground-glass opacification superimposed on the background UIP pattern on HRCT. It is the commonest cause of acute deterioration and of death in IPF, and can be the presenting event.
Must Exclude First
  • Infection — sputum and blood cultures, viral PCR, atypical screen
  • Pulmonary embolism — CTPA (the same CT shows the ground-glass)
  • Heart failure / fluid overload — echocardiography, BNP
  • Drug-induced pneumonitis — review the drug chart
  • Aspiration — GORD is common in IPF
Management and Prognosis
  • Management is largely supportive — oxygen, treat anything found on the exclusion workup, ventilatory support where appropriate
  • High-dose corticosteroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics are used in practice despite weak trial evidence — no trial has shown a mortality benefit
  • In-hospital mortality approaching 50%, worse still in those who are invasively ventilated
  • Median survival after an exacerbation is only 3–4 months
  • Outcomes from invasive ventilation are poor enough that a ceiling-of-care and escalation discussion belongs in the answer, not as an afterthought
The exception to the “no steroids in IPF” rule. That rule — stated above — is about chronic, stable IPF, where immunosuppression was shown to increase mortality. It does not mean steroids are never given in IPF: in an acute exacerbation high-dose corticosteroids are standard practice, on admittedly weak evidence, once infection, PE and heart failure have been excluded. Name the setting — chronic vs acute exacerbation — before you answer yes or no to steroids.
Follow-Up and Disease Trajectory (IPF)
IPF is not a diagnose-and-discharge condition. NICE sets specialist review every 3–6 months, tightening to 3-monthly if the disease is progressing rapidly — the interval is set by trajectory, not by how the patient feels on the day.
What Is Tracked at Each Review
  • Symptoms — breathlessness, cough, functional limitation, weight
  • FVC and TLCO trend — the serial trend matters far more than any single value
  • Exertional desaturation on walk testing, and the oxygen requirement
  • Antifibrotic tolerance and LFTs; whether the stopping rule has been met — a 10% or greater fall in predicted FVC over 12 months, not any fall
  • Comorbidities — GORD, pulmonary hypertension, emphysema, sleep-disordered breathing
Two Timings Commonly Got Wrong
  • Transplant should be discussed 3–6 months after diagnosis — a defined timing, not “when they deteriorate”. The conversation has to happen while the patient is still fit enough to be listed.
  • Palliative care has a role from diagnosis, not only at the end of life (NICE) — breathlessness and cough control, and advance care planning, run alongside disease-modifying treatment.

Complications to Name

ComplicationThe point to make
Lung cancerRisk raised several-fold — a new or enlarging nodule in a fibrotic lower zone is cancer until proven otherwise, and is easily lost against the reticulation
Pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonaleSuspect when hypoxaemia and ↓↓TLCO are out of proportion to the FVC; raised JVP and peripheral oedema. Markedly worsens prognosis
Venous thromboembolismRisk is increased in IPF — and PE is a key differential for any acute deterioration
Acute exacerbationSee the IPF section above — the commonest cause of death; in-hospital mortality approaching 50%
Type 1 respiratory failureProgressive hypoxaemia with normal or low CO₂; the oxygen requirement climbs through the disease course
Cross-references — do not re-learn these here. LTOT thresholds are set out in the COPD note. 6MWT exertional desaturation thresholds are set out in LUNG FUNCTION → Muscle & Exercise.
When a Non-IPF ILD Starts Behaving Like IPF
The old shortcut — “IPF gets antifibrotics, every other ILD gets steroids” — is no longer true. Any fibrotic ILD can start to progress like IPF, and when it does, antifibrotics may be used for it too — in the UK that antifibrotic is nintedanib, which is approved for progressive fibrosing ILD and for systemic sclerosis-associated ILD; pirfenidone is not (NICE). So “antifibrotics are only for IPF” is wrong as an exam answer.
Which ILDs Can Do This
  • Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis — the classic example
  • Rheumatoid arthritis-ILD
  • Systemic sclerosis-ILD
  • Asbestosis and the other fibrotic pneumoconioses
What You Are Expected To Do
  • Recognise progression — worsening breathlessness, falling lung function, or more fibrosis on HRCT despite treating the cause
  • Removing the antigen in HP, and treating the underlying connective tissue disease, still come first
  • Refer back to the ILD MDT — the decision to add or switch to an antifibrotic is a specialist one
  • Immunosuppression keeps its place where inflammation is driving the disease — the two approaches are complementary
