Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)
📷 Image placeholder — ABPA schematic — Aspergillus colonising proximal bronchi, type I + III hypersensitivity, ↑IgE and central bronchiectasis.
Type I + type III hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways. Almost exclusively in asthmatics and CF patients. Causes proximal bronchiectasis.
Clinical features
  • Wheeze + worsening asthma control
  • Cough with brown mucus plugs
  • Dyspnoea
  • Recurrent pulmonary infiltrates
  • Proximal (central) bronchiectasis
A background of asthma or CF is almost always present — consider ABPA in any asthmatic with poor control despite treatment.
TestFinding
Blood eosinophilia↑ Eosinophils — key positive finding (absent in HP)

Skin prick testImmediate reaction to Aspergillus antigen

Management

1st Line — Steroids
Oral prednisolone — reduces inflammation, controls acute exacerbations. Most patients need long courses.
2nd Line — Antifungal
Itraconazole — reduces Aspergillus load, steroid-sparing. Used when steroids alone are insufficient.
Background Asthma
Optimise asthma treatment; monitor IgE levels to assess treatment response.
HP vs ABPA: HP → no eosinophilia, IgG precipitins only, avoid antigen + steroids. ABPA → eosinophilia + ↑IgE + Aspergillus RAST +ve, steroids → itraconazole.
Exam Pearls
All ILD = restrictive: FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓FVC, ↓TLCO — the unifying PFT pattern. HRCT is the key investigation for all.
Upper zone = CHARTS (Coal, HP/Histiocytosis, AS, Radiation, TB, Silicosis/Sarcoidosis)
Lower zone = IPF, CT disorders, drugs (ABM), asbestosis. Exception: AS is upper — a spondyloarthropathy, not a true CTD, but often grouped with them.
IPF: honeycombing + bibasal crackles + clubbing; antifibrotics (pirfenidone/nintedanib); poor prognosis ~3–4 years; steroids not used.
HP: organic antigen → BAL lymphocytosis, NO eosinophilia; treat: avoid antigen + steroids.
ABPA: asthma/CF + Aspergillus → eosinophilia + ↑IgE + proximal bronchiectasis; treat: steroids → itraconazole.
HP vs ABPA: eosinophilia + ↑IgE = ABPA not HP — the key distinguishing contrast.
Drug-induced fibrosis (lower zone): Amiodarone, Bleomycin, Methotrexate (“ABM”) + nitrofurantoin — and the answer to “what would you do” is always stop the drug, then steroids if severe.
Named HP vignettes: bird (droppings) · farmer (mouldy hay) · malt worker (barley / Aspergillus clavatus) · mushroom worker (actinomycetes).
The two antifibrotics by side effect: pirfenidone → photosensitivity (sunblock, cover up); nintedanib → diarrhoea; both → deranged LFTs, so liver monitoring for either.
Acute exacerbation of IPF: new bilateral ground-glass on a UIP background, having excluded infection, PE and heart failure. In-hospital mortality approaching 50%. The one setting where high-dose steroids are used — the “no steroids in IPF” rule is about chronic disease.
Antifibrotics are not IPF-only. Any fibrotic ILD that keeps progressing despite treating its cause can be considered for one — chronic HP, RA-ILD and scleroderma-ILD are the classics.
Follow-up timings: review 3–6 monthly (3-monthly if progressing rapidly); discuss transplant 3–6 months after diagnosis; palliative care from diagnosis. Watch for lung cancer (risk raised several-fold) and pulmonary hypertension.
RESPIRATORY__Sarcoidosis:
Multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown cause. The defining lesion: non-caseating granuloma (epithelioid cells + multinucleate giant cells) — non-caseating is the key contrast with TB (caseating). Epidemiology: young / middle-aged adults, F > M, more common and more severe in Black patients; also more common in northern Europeans (esp. Scandinavians), who typically have acute, self-limiting disease with a good prognosis. Commonest presentation: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL); ~50% found incidentally on CXR.
Pathology & Immunology
📷 Image placeholder — Non-caseating granuloma histology schematic — epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate giant cells surrounded by CD4⁺ T cells, with no central necrosis (contrast caseating TB).
Granuloma Composition
Non-caseating granuloma = focal epithelioid macrophages, multinucleate giant cells, CD4+ T cells. No central necrosis — the absence of caseation is the defining feature.
BAL & the Lymphocyte Paradox
↑ CD4 T cells in BAL (CD4:CD8 ratio ↑ in active disease). Paradoxically: peripheral lymphopenia + cutaneous anergy — lymphocytes are sequestered in granulomas, depressing tuberculin / Candida skin-test reactivity.
Hypercalcaemia Mechanism
Activated macrophages produce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃ (calcitriol) → unregulated ↑ Ca²⁺ absorption → hypercalcaemia ± hypercalciuria. Explains the metabolic feature without primary hyperparathyroidism.
Clinical Features — System by System
📷 Image placeholder — Cutaneous sarcoidosis — erythema nodosum (tender red shin nodules, part of Löfgren syndrome) and lupus pernio (violaceous nose/cheek plaques); high-yield recognisable signs.
SystemFeatures
Chest (commonest)Dry cough, breathlessness; the chest is often normal on auscultation despite an abnormal film (crackles are uncommon and clubbing is not a feature); BHL ± pulmonary infiltrates; often asymptomatic
SkinErythema nodosum (acute, tender nodules, shins); lupus pernio (indurated violaceous plaques on nose/cheeks — most specific sign); scar infiltration
EyesUveitis (anterior most common — red eye, photophobia, floaters); lacrimal gland enlargement; conjunctival nodules
MetabolicHypercalcaemia (macrophage 1,25-D₃ production) → polyuria, constipation, renal stones
Bone / JointArthralgia, periarthritis, bone cysts (hands/feet)
LiverGranulomatous hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, ↑ALP
NeurologyCranial nerve palsy (especially CN VII — facial palsy), meningeal involvement, pituitary/hypothalamic infiltration, peripheral neuropathy
Cardiac (rare but dangerous)Conduction defects (heart block), arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy — can cause sudden death
Named Syndromes — High-Yield Eponyms
Löfgren's Syndrome
BHL + erythema nodosum + polyarthralgia (± fever). Acute onset. Good prognosis — spontaneously resolves in most. Treat supportively — NSAIDs, not systemic steroids, unless symptoms are severe or refractory. Classic SBA: “which syndrome is associated with a good outcome?”
Heerfordt's Syndrome (Uveoparotid Fever)
Uveitis + parotid gland enlargement + facial nerve palsy (CN VII) + fever. Subacute onset; more chronic course than Löfgren's. Think: eye + parotid + face.
Differentials of Bilateral Hilar Lymphadenopathy
Sarcoidosis (commonest) Lymphoma Tuberculosis Bronchial carcinoma with nodal spread Infections (EBV, fungi)
Symmetrical BHL + erythema nodosum = essentially only sarcoidosis — near-pathognomonic, and rarely needs biopsy to confirm.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Scadding CXR staging 0–IV — four small chest films showing normal → BHL → BHL + infiltrates → infiltrates alone → fibrosis.
TestFinding / Role
Serum ACE↑ in ~60% of active sarcoidosis — supportive but not diagnostic (poor specificity; also ↑ in TB, lymphoma, diabetes). It is not a diagnostic test, and it is a poor marker of disease activity — monitoring is by symptoms, FVC/TLCO, CXR and calcium, not ACE.
Calcium↑ (hypercalcaemia) — check urinary calcium too; risk of renal stones
CXR stagingBHL ± pulmonary infiltrates ± fibrosis. Staging: 0 = normal, I = BHL only, II = BHL + infiltrates, III = infiltrates alone, IV = fibrosis
CT chestBetter parenchymal assessment; guides biopsy site (mediastinal nodes / lung)
PFTsRestrictive pattern (↓FVC, ↓TLC, FEV1/FVC normal/↑, ↓TLCO) — links to the ILD pattern
Biopsy — gold standardNon-caseating granulomas on histology; bronchoscopy ± EBUS (mediastinal nodes), transbronchial biopsy, skin / lymph-node biopsy if accessible
BAL↑ CD4:CD8 ratio (active disease); lymphocytosis
ECG / EchoBaseline screen for cardiac involvement (heart block, arrhythmias) — normal results do not exclude cardiac sarcoid; see the cardiac screening section below
Ophthalmology reviewSlit-lamp exam for uveitis — all newly diagnosed patients
Diagnosis = compatible clinical and radiological picture + biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of TB and lymphoma. Biopsy can be omitted where the presentation is classic — Löfgren's syndrome, or asymptomatic stage I BHL. ACE alone is never diagnostic.
Screening the Heart — Cardiac Sarcoidosis
Clinically apparent cardiac involvement is uncommon, but it is the involvement that kills — heart block, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death. Every newly diagnosed patient therefore gets a deliberate cardiac screen, not just a passing question.
1 — Ask, at Every Review
Palpitations, syncope or pre-syncope, and breathlessness out of proportion to lung function (symptoms far worse than the FVC / TLCO would predict). Any of these is a cardiac question until disproved.
2 — Baseline Tests
ECG ± echo at diagnosis in everyone. Add a 24-hour Holter if there are palpitations (BTS) — intermittent block and non-sustained VT are missed by a single resting strip.
3 — If Anything Is Suspicious
Cardiac MRI or FDG-PET plus cardiology referral. These are the tests that actually find granulomatous myocardial disease; the bedside tests only raise the question.
⚠️ A normal ECG and a normal echo do NOT exclude cardiac sarcoidosis — both are insensitive to patchy myocardial granulomas. Reassuring bedside tests in a patient with syncope, palpitations or unexplained breathlessness are a reason to image, not a reason to stop.
Where a device is needed for high-grade AV block in confirmed cardiac sarcoid, cardiology will usually consider an ICD rather than a plain pacemaker. The threat is ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, not simply bradycardia, so a pacemaker alone leaves that risk untreated.
For the imaging detail — cross-ref the MRI — Cardiac note (patchy mid-wall / epicardial LGE favouring the basal septum and LV free wall) and the Nuclear — PET / Oncology note (FDG-PET dietary preparation, focal or focal-on-diffuse uptake). Both are written from the opposite direction — unexplained high-grade AV block in a younger patient → work up for cardiac sarcoid — which is the same reflex read backwards.
Management
Mild — BHL Only, No Organ Dysfunction
No treatment needed — monitor with serial CXR / PFTs. ~⅔ remit spontaneously within 2 years.
Indications for Oral Steroids
Persistent pulmonary infiltrates / abnormal PFTs >6 months; hypercalcaemia; cardiac involvement; CNS/neuro involvement; eye disease not responding to topical; significant systemic symptoms. Cardiac and neurological disease are treated systemically from the outset — there is no topical step — and are managed with the relevant specialist (cardiology, neurology).
Steroid Regime
Prednisolone 20–40 mg/day in more acute disease; lower (around 10 mg/day) where disease is long-standing and indolent. Then maintenance 5–10 mg for 6–12 months before withdrawal (BTS). Add a bisphosphonate (bone protection) for long-term steroid use — but read the calcium warning below before adding calcium / vitamin D. Monitor Ca²⁺ (steroids lower it — risk of rebound on stopping).
Second Line / Severe
Methotrexate or azathioprine (steroid-sparing). End-stage pulmonary fibrosis → lung transplant.
⚠️ The bone-protection trap — calcium and vitamin D are not automatic here. With any long-term steroid the standard reflex is calcium + vitamin D alongside the bisphosphonate. Sarcoidosis is the disease where that reflex can do harm: granuloma macrophages make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃ (calcitriol) autonomously, outside normal PTH feedback (the mechanism set out under Pathology & Immunology above) — so supplements simply feed substrate into a pathway that is already unregulated.
  • Check serum calcium AND urinary calcium before prescribing calcium / vitamin D — give them only if neither is raised, and recheck after starting.
  • Hypercalciuria is commoner than hypercalcaemia (roughly 50% vs 10–20%) — a normal serum calcium on its own under-detects the problem, which is why the urine matters.
  • Patient advice: over-the-counter supplements and heavy sun exposure both increase substrate and can tip an at-risk patient into symptomatic hypercalcaemia; advise good hydration and sensible sun exposure.
Acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia management is not repeated here — cross-ref the endocrinology hypercalcaemia note.
Follow-up & Relapse
What is trackedWhy it earns its place
SymptomsCough, breathlessness, fatigue — plus a deliberate ask about palpitations, syncope and red eye at each visit
Spirometry (FVC) and TLCOThe objective marker of pulmonary progression — a falling FVC or TLCO is what actually triggers or escalates treatment
CXRSerial films for radiographic change (new infiltrates, evolving fibrosis)
Serum calcium and creatinineHypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria damage the kidney silently — calcium and renal function are checked alongside the lung tests, not instead of them
Asymptomatic Stage I — Follow-up Ends
Incidentally-found asymptomatic stage I disease (BHL only) is followed for a period with symptoms, CXR, lung function and calcium — and then discharged. It is not watched indefinitely; the point of follow-up is to catch progression, and once it has not progressed the patient goes back to primary care.
When Relapse Happens
Relapse clusters during the steroid taper and in the 2–6 months after stopping — most relapses occur while the dose is being reduced, so that is exactly when review should be tightest. Late relapse after ~3 symptom-free years is rare, which is what makes eventual discharge safe.
Relapsing disease is treated for 2 years or more (BTS/ERS) — a relapser is not managed with another short course. Recognising the taper as the danger window, and planning a long enough course for someone who has already relapsed, is the whole of good follow-up here.
Prognosis
Good Prognostic Markers
Löfgren's syndrome / acute presentation; BHL alone; asymptomatic incidental finding; European ethnicity.
Poor Prognostic Markers
Pulmonary fibrosis / pulmonary HTN; cardiac, CNS, or renal involvement; Black ethnicity (higher mortality, more severe); lupus pernio (marker of chronic disease); splenomegaly.
~60% of all patients resolve spontaneously (~⅔ of stage I disease, within 2 years). Chronic / relapsing course in ~20%. Mortality ~5% (mainly cardiac / pulmonary HTN).
Exam Pearls
Non-caseating granuloma (vs caseating = TB) — the single most important histological contrast
BHL = commonest finding; ~50% incidental on CXR. Symmetrical BHL + erythema nodosum = sarcoidosis until proven otherwise.
Löfgren's = BHL + erythema nodosum + arthralgia (good prognosis, often self-limiting)
Heerfordt's = uveitis + parotid enlargement + CN VII palsy + fever (“uveoparotid fever”)
↑ACE = supportive, NOT diagnostic (also ↑ in TB, lymphoma). Diagnosis requires biopsy + exclusion of alternatives.
Hypercalcaemia = macrophage 1,25-vitamin D₃ production (not parathyroid). Steroids treat it.
Lupus pernio = most specific skin sign; red-blue indurated nose/cheeks; marker of chronic systemic disease
Restrictive PFTs (↓FVC, ↓TLCO, normal/↑ ratio) — links to the ILD pattern
Mild BHL only → no treatment; ⅔ remit spontaneously within 2 years. Steroids for organ involvement.
Worse in Black patients; cardiac/CNS involvement = dangerous (arrhythmia, heart block, sudden death)
Normal ECG + normal echo do NOT exclude cardiac sarcoid — insensitive to patchy granulomas. Palpitations, syncope or breathlessness out of proportion to lung function → Holter, then cardiac MRI / FDG-PET. Device for high-grade AV block = usually an ICD, not a plain pacemaker.
Bone protection ≠ automatic calcium + vitamin D. Granulomas already make calcitriol autonomously — check serum AND urinary calcium first, and give supplements only if neither is raised. Hypercalciuria (~50%) is commoner than hypercalcaemia (10–20%).
Relapse clusters during the taper and in the 2–6 months after stopping. Relapsing disease is treated for ≥2 years (BTS/ERS); late relapse after ~3 symptom-free years is rare, so asymptomatic stage I disease can be followed and then discharged.
RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis:
Overview

Anaphylaxis is a severe type 1 (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction → mast cell degranulation → histamine release → airway / breathing / circulation compromise. Rapid onset is the hallmark. Note that some triggers — radiocontrast, NSAIDs, opioids, some neuromuscular blockers — produce an identical picture by direct, non-IgE mast cell activation; the emergency treatment is exactly the same.

Common Triggers
  • Foods — nuts, shellfish, egg, milk
  • Insect venom — bee/wasp stings
  • Drugs — penicillins, NSAIDs, contrast media
  • Latex
  • Idiopathic
The Framing

This is an emergency. The entire management reduces to:

Recognition → IM adrenaline

Everything else is adjunctive.

Who Is at Risk of a Severe or Fatal Reaction

Anaphylaxis is not one uniform illness. A short list of features separates the reaction that settles after a single dose of adrenaline from the one that kills — and two of them are things we control.

Risk Factors for Death
  • Co-existing asthma, especially if poorly controlled — the single biggest risk factor for fatal food anaphylaxis. Death in these patients is usually from bronchospasm, not upper-airway occlusion.
  • Delayed adrenaline — modifiable
  • Upright posture at the time of collapse — modifiable (the empty-ventricle mechanism in the algorithm below)
  • Risk of death peaks in adolescents and young adults (~10–24 years) — the age of eating out, taking risks, and leaving the auto-injector at home
Cofactors — turn a mild reaction severe
  • Exercise
  • Alcohol
  • NSAIDs
  • Intercurrent infection
  • Underlying mast-cell disease (mastocytosis — suspect if the baseline tryptase is persistently raised)
Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis — the explanation for the patient who eats wheat safely every day but reacts after a run. The food alone is tolerated; the food plus the cofactor is not. Unless you ask specifically about exercise, alcohol and NSAIDs in the hours around the reaction, the trigger looks idiopathic.
Why this drives the observation decision: the 12-hour observation criterion further down names severe asthma — this is why. The asthmatic has the least respiratory reserve to lose, so a biphasic reaction occurring after discharge is the one most likely to be fatal.
Recognition — What Makes It Anaphylaxis
📷 Image placeholder — Urticaria and angioedema — widespread wheals plus lip/tongue/periorbital swelling; the visible skin/mucosal features that usually (not always) accompany anaphylaxis.
📷 Image placeholder — Type 1 (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity mechanism — allergen cross-links IgE on sensitised mast cells → degranulation → histamine/tryptase release → vasodilatation, increased permeability, bronchospasm.
Anaphylaxis = acute onset + life-threatening A/B/C compromise, usually with skin changes.
Skin changes alone (urticaria, angioedema) without A/B/C = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.
🫁
Airway
Swelling, hoarseness, stridor — upper airway oedema threatening occlusion
💨
Breathing
SOB, wheeze (bronchospasm), hypoxia, increasing respiratory fatigue
❤️
Circulation
Hypotension, tachycardia, collapse, light-headedness, pallor
🌸
Skin (usually present, NOT required alone)
Urticaria, itching, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, eyes)
Differentials — What Else Looks Like This

The step the algorithm skips: before you decide this is anaphylaxis, know the handful of conditions that imitate it — and which of them adrenaline will not touch.

Mimic Discriminating feature Does adrenaline help?
Life-threatening asthmaWheeze, hypoxia, silent chest — usually no urticaria and no exposure. But it can be clinically indistinguishable, especially in children, and the two frequently coexist.Yes — IM adrenaline is a recognised rescue in life-threatening asthma unresponsive to standard treatment, so this is a safe mistake to make
Inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) — formerly vocal cord dysfunctionInspiratory stridor with normal saturations, sudden onset and sudden offset, often recurrent and previously investigated; no urticaria, no hypotension⚠️ No — the obstruction is paradoxical cord adduction, not oedema
ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedemaOn an ACE inhibitor, no urticaria. Lip / tongue / laryngeal swelling, often years after the drug was started, no identifiable exposure⚠️ No — it is bradykinin-mediated, not mast-cell mediated. It is still life-threatening: airway first, stop the ACE inhibitor permanently.
Vasovagal faintBradycardia (not tachycardia), pallor, sweating, rapid recovery when laid supine; no urticaria, no bronchospasmNot needed — lying the patient flat is the treatment
Panic attackBreathlessness and a subjective sense of throat tightness, but no objective airway / breathing / circulation compromise and no skin changes; saturations and BP normalNot needed
The RCUK safety rule — learn this sentence: where the diagnosis is uncertain, IM adrenaline is unlikely to cause harm — give it. The harm from withholding adrenaline in true anaphylaxis vastly outweighs the harm of giving it to a mimic. Diagnostic doubt is a reason to treat, never a reason to wait.
Angioedema without urticaria is taught elsewhere — go there. ACE-inhibitor and hereditary (C1-esterase) angioedema, including icatibant and the C4 / C1-INH work-up, belong to Urticaria / Angioedema (Dermatology) and Allergy & Immunodeficiency (Immunology / Serology). The same discriminator — on an ACE inhibitor, no urticaria — is the one that flips the diagnosis in Stridor and Facial & Neck Swelling.
Management — The Algorithm
📷 Image placeholder — Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis algorithm flowchart — recognition → IM adrenaline (repeat at 5 min) → A/B/C support → refractory pathway.
IM ADRENALINE IS THE FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT ACTION — nothing precedes it. An antihistamine comes only after stabilisation and treats skin symptoms; steroids are not part of initial treatment.
💉
IM Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) — anterolateral thigh (middle third)
  • Call for help and stop the trigger if you can — stop the drug or contrast infusion, remove the sting. Then give adrenaline; do not delay adrenaline to do it.
  • Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL).
  • Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.
  • IM not IV — IV is specialist-only (arrhythmia risk).
↓
🅾️
A/B — Airway + Breathing
  • Secure airway (call anaesthetics early if stridor).
  • High-flow O₂ via non-rebreathe.
  • Salbutamol nebuliser if wheeze.
↓
🩸
C — Circulation
  • IV access; IV fluid bolus (500–1000 mL crystalloid adult; 10 mL/kg child).
  • Monitor ECG and BP.
↓
🛏️
D — Position
  • Lie flat + raise legs (improves venous return and cerebral perfusion); pregnant → left lateral tilt.
  • Sit up only if breathing is the dominant problem.
  • Do NOT sit or stand the patient up, and do not let them walk — the change of posture alone can precipitate cardiac arrest (empty-ventricle).
↓
💊
Adjuncts — only after A/B/C stabilised, never instead of adrenaline
  • Once stable, a non-sedating oral antihistamine (cetirizine) may ease residual skin symptoms (itch/urticaria).
  • Corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended (no longer part of initial treatment (RCUK) — no evidence they prevent biphasic reactions, and they can delay discharge).
Adrenaline Doses by Age — IM, 1 mg/mL (1:1000)
📷 Image placeholder — IM adrenaline injection site — the anterolateral thigh (middle third), with auto-injector (EpiPen/Jext) technique.
Age Dose Volume (1:1000)
<6 months100–150 mcg0.1–0.15 mL
6 months – 6 years150 mcg0.15 mL
6 – 12 years300 mcg0.3 mL
>12 years / adult500 mcg0.5 mL
Refractory Anaphylaxis

Defined: respiratory/cardiovascular compromise persisting despite 2 IM adrenaline doses.

  • Continue IV fluid resuscitation (adults 500–1000 mL; children 10 mL/kg boluses)
  • Senior/expert help immediately
  • IV adrenaline infusion — specialist/ITU only (arrhythmia risk requires monitoring)
  • Consider intubation if airway deteriorating
  • If the patient takes a beta-blocker, the response to adrenaline may be blunted — continue adrenaline as normal, and IV glucagon is given on senior or specialist advice as an adjunct in refractory cases. Their reactions are more often severe and refractory, so escalate early.
After the Event
Immediate Post-Acute
  • Serum mast cell tryptase — confirms mast cell degranulation. Ideally 3 timed samples: (1) as soon as possible after treatment starts, (2) 1–2 h (no later than 4 h) after symptom onset, (3) >24 h / at convalescence (baseline)
  • Non-sedating antihistamine for persisting skin symptoms

Risk-stratified observation (RCUK) — timed from resolution of symptoms, not from arrival or from the adrenaline. It covers the biphasic reaction risk (recurrence hours later without re-exposure):

Observe When it applies
2 hGood response to a single dose given within 30 min of onset, with complete resolution + auto-injector, training and adequate supervision after discharge
6 h2 doses needed, or a prior biphasic reaction
12 hSevere — >2 doses, severe asthma, possible ongoing absorption, or a late-evening presentation

Under-16s treated for suspected anaphylaxis are admitted under a paediatric medical team (NICE), whichever observation band they fall into.

Discharge Planning
  • Two adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed (EpiPen/Jext) + technique demonstrated
  • Allergy clinic referral (all new diagnoses)
  • Written action plan + trigger avoidance advice
  • Medical alert bracelet (Medic-Alert) discussion
Auto-Injector — What the Patient Must Actually Be Told

Prescribing two devices and demonstrating the technique is not the same as telling the patient what to do on the day. This is the discharge conversation, and it is highly examinable.

The Discharge Script
  • Carry both devices at all times — and check they are in date. An expired or forgotten pen is the commonest reason a patient has no adrenaline at the moment they need it.
  • Use it early, into the outer thigh, through clothing if necessary — delayed adrenaline is one of the modifiable risk factors for death.
  • After using one, call 999 and say the word “anaphylaxis” — even if you feel better. The word itself changes the ambulance response.
  • Lie flat with the legs raised. Sit up only if breathing is the problem, and lie back down as soon as possible. Never stand up.
  • Use the second device 5 minutes after the first if you are not improving — this is why two are prescribed.
  • Always attend hospital after any use, because of the biphasic risk — never treat yourself at home and stay there.
⚠️ Carry the empty-ventricle rule out of the resus room and into the discharge advice. The algorithm above already warns never to sit or stand an anaphylactic patient up, or let them walk — a vasodilated, fluid-depleted patient who stands can empty the right ventricle and arrest. Deaths have occurred at the exact moment of standing. The street, not the resus room, is where that rule is most likely to be broken, so it has to be said to the patient in plain words: lie down, legs up, do not stand up — not even to walk to the ambulance.
The Allergy Clinic — and Venom Immunotherapy
What the Clinic Is Actually For

Referral is not paperwork — the clinic confirms the trigger, then builds the plan around the answer:

  • Confirms the trigger — skin prick testing and allergen-specific IgE
  • Supervised challenge where real doubt remains — the gold standard
  • Builds the avoidance plan and the written emergency plan around the result

Full detail, including how to interpret these tests: Allergy & Immunodeficiency.

Venom Immunotherapy — the disease-modifying treatment for venom anaphylaxis
  • For wasp / bee-sting anaphylaxis — escalating then maintenance venom injections over several years, under specialist supervision
  • Highly effective: roughly 95% protection for wasp venom and 80% for bee venom
  • It converts a patient who would otherwise carry adrenaline for life into one who is largely protected — nothing else in this topic changes the natural history
  • NICE says people who have had a systemic reaction to insect venom are referred for specialist assessment for venom immunotherapy

Note the loop this closes: bee / wasp sting opens the trigger list at the top of this note, and it is the one trigger with a treatment that can take the diagnosis away.
