RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hypertension:
PH = ↑pulmonary arterial pressure — mean PAP >20 mmHg at rest, measured on right heart catheterisation (echo screens, it does not diagnose) → right heart pressure overload → cor pulmonale → systemic venous congestion. Classified into 5 WHO groups by cause — the spine of this topic. The mechanistic thread: every feature (ECG, CXR, signs) = the right heart struggling against high pulmonary resistance.
WHO Classification — 5 Groups
📷 Image placeholder — Chest X-ray/CT of pulmonary hypertension — dilated proximal pulmonary arteries with peripheral "pruning" of vessels, plus right heart (RV/RA) enlargement.
GroupCauseExamples
1 — PAH Pulmonary arterial hypertension (primary vascular) Idiopathic; connective tissue disease (scleroderma, SLE); congenital heart disease (Eisenmenger); HIV; drugs (fenfluramine)
2 — Left heart Left heart disease — commonest cause overall LV failure (systolic or HFpEF), mitral/aortic valve disease; long-standing systemic hypertension counts only once it has caused HFpEF
3 — Lung/hypoxia Chronic lung disease / hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction COPD (commonest in this group), ILD, high altitude; OSA — but OSA alone is an uncommon cause of significant PH and any PH is usually mild
4 — CTEPH Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Unresolved organised thrombus → obstructed vessels. Follows PE, but about a quarter have no known prior PE — so a negative PE history does not exclude it
5 — Misc Multifactorial / unclear mechanisms Sarcoidosis, haematological disorders (sickle cell), metabolic, compression of pulmonary vessels
Two to anchor: Group 2 (left heart disease) = commonest cause overall. Group 1 (PAH) = the one with specific pulmonary vasodilator drug therapy.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of the RV pressure-overload cascade — ↑pulmonary vascular resistance → RV hypertrophy → RV failure (cor pulmonale) → systemic venous congestion.
↑ Pulmonary vascular resistance (any cause)
↓
RV pressure overload → RV hypertrophy
↓
RV failure (cor pulmonale)
↓
Back-pressure → systemic venous congestion (↑JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly)
This single chain explains every sign, ECG change, and CXR finding in PH.
Clinical Features
Early Symptoms
  • Exertional dyspnoea (main presenting symptom)
  • Fatigue
  • exertional syncope (fixed low cardiac output — cannot augment with exercise)
  • Chest pain
Advanced / Cor Pulmonale
  • Raised JVP
  • Peripheral oedema
  • hepatomegaly (± pulsatile liver)
  • Ascites
  • Pleural effusion
Clinical Signs
  • Loud P2 (pulmonary valve closure)
  • RV heave (parasternal)
  • Tricuspid regurgitation murmur (pansystolic, LSE, louder on inspiration)
Exertional syncope = fixed low output — the RV cannot increase output on demand (obstructed outflow). A high-yield clinical clue to PH.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — ECG of right heart strain — dominant R in V1, right axis deviation, RBBB and P pulmonale; alongside a CXR showing dilated proximal pulmonary arteries with distal "pruning".
TestFinding / Role
ECGRVH (dominant R in V1–3, deep S in V5–6); right axis deviation; RBBB; P pulmonale (peaked P in II — RA enlargement)
CXRDilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally ("pruning"); RV/RA enlargement; peripheral oligaemia
NT-proBNP↑ — right heart strain marker; correlates with severity and prognosis
Echo — key screening testEstimates pulmonary artery pressure (via TR jet velocity); RV size/function; excludes left heart disease (Group 2); guides referral to a nationally designated specialist PH centre
Right heart catheterisation — gold standard
  • Direct measurement of PAP and pulmonary vascular resistance; confirms the diagnosis.
  • Vasoreactivity testing — done only in idiopathic, heritable and drug-induced PAH, and only there does a positive result justify high-dose CCBs. It is not done in the rest of Group 1 (connective-tissue disease, congenital heart disease, HIV, portopulmonary), nor in Groups 2–5.
  • Separates pre-capillary PH (a normal wedge pressure — obstruction in the pulmonary vessels themselves; Groups 1, 3 and 4) from post-capillary PH (a raised wedge pressure — transmitted back from the left heart; Group 2).
  • Being pre-capillary does not by itself mean vasodilators are appropriate: PAH-specific drugs are for Group 1 (plus riociguat in inoperable Group 4), are not used in Group 3, and are harmful in Group 2.
PFTsIdentify Group 3 (obstructive/restrictive lung disease)
V/Q scan — screening test for CTEPHThe screening test of choice for Group 4: it is more sensitive than CTPA for chronic organised thrombus, and a normal V/Q scan effectively excludes CTEPH. Matches the PE note, which says to screen persistent breathlessness with echo then V/Q.
CTPA / conventional pulmonary angiographyUsed after a positive V/Q to define the lesions and decide operability (proximal, surgically accessible disease vs distal) — not as the screening test
Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-Scl-70, anti-dsDNA)Identify connective tissue disease (Group 1 — scleroderma, SLE)
Management
Principle: treat the underlying cause first (by WHO group). PAH-specific vasodilator drugs are for Group 1 only — not for other groups.
Treat the Cause (by group)
  • Group 2 → treat the left heart (diuretics, ACEi, valve surgery)
  • Group 3 → optimise the underlying COPD/ILD; add LTOT only if the patient meets the standard chronic hypoxaemia criteria (it ↓hypoxic vasoconstriction). LTOT is prescribed for the hypoxaemia, not for the PH itself — and there is no PAH-specific drug therapy for Group 3
  • Group 4 → lifelong anticoagulation — continued whether or not endarterectomy is performed, and note the diagnosis itself is only made after ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation — plus pulmonary endarterectomy, which is potentially curative. Operability is decided by a CTEPH MDT at an expert centre, never locally. If surgery is not possible, the specialist options are riociguat and/or balloon pulmonary angioplasty
Supportive (all groups)
  • O₂ (especially Group 3)
  • diuretics (peripheral oedema/ascites)
  • anticoagulation (lifelong and mandatory in Group 4 CTEPH; no longer routine in idiopathic Group 1 PAH — uncertain benefit)
  • Pregnancy is contraindicated — contraception must be discussed at diagnosis (see the callout below)
  • Supervised exercise
PAH-Specific Therapy (Group 1)
  • Reduce pulmonary vascular resistance:
  • Prostanoids — epoprostenol (IV), iloprost (inhaled)
  • Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) — bosentan, macitentan
  • PDE-5 inhibitors — sildenafil, tadalafil
  • sGC stimulator — riociguat (also used in inoperable Group 4 CTEPH)
  • CCBs — high-dose, and only for the small minority who are vasoreactive on right heart catheter testing, within idiopathic, heritable or drug-induced PAH. Giving them to a non-responder causes systemic hypotension, syncope and acute right ventricular failure — never start them empirically
  • Current practice: initial combination therapy (ERA + PDE-5i) for low/intermediate-risk PAH
End-Stage
  • Lung or heart-lung transplant — for refractory Group 1 PAH or Group 4 CTEPH not suitable for endarterectomy
⚠️ Pregnancy & contraception — give the instruction its reason.
  • Pregnancy is contraindicated in PAH: the physiological fall in systemic vascular resistance and rise in circulating volume cannot be met by a fixed, obstructed pulmonary circulation.
  • Maternal mortality is very high, and higher again in Eisenmenger syndrome.
  • Contraception must be discussed at diagnosis with every woman of childbearing age — not left until she asks. Several PAH drugs are also teratogenic and some interfere with hormonal contraception, so contraception is planned with the specialist centre, not assumed.
  • An unplanned pregnancy is an indication for urgent specialist PH centre referral.
Specialist Centre Care & Follow-Up
PH suspected on echo → prompt referral to a nationally designated specialist PH centre. Right heart catheterisation and the initiation of PAH-specific drugs happen only at those centres — they are not started in a general respiratory or cardiology clinic. Thereafter care is explicitly shared: the centre owns the diagnosis, the drug decisions and the risk assessment; the local team manages diuretics, oxygen, comorbidity, vaccination and acute illness.
CTEPH (Group 4) — who decides operability? Not the referring team. Every case is discussed by a CTEPH multidisciplinary team at an expert centre — surgeon, PH physician and thoracic radiologist — who decide whether the disease is surgically accessible. Remember the diagnosis is only made after ≥3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation, with anticoagulation continued lifelong regardless of whether endarterectomy goes ahead.
Follow-up is objective, not symptom-led. At every visit the specialist centre re-assesses the patient on three things, and escalates treatment if they are not doing well enough.
1 · WHO Functional Class (WHO-FC)
  • I — no limitation of ordinary physical activity
  • II — slight limitation; comfortable at rest, ordinary activity causes symptoms
  • III — marked limitation; less than ordinary activity causes symptoms
  • IV — symptoms at rest; signs of right heart failure; any activity worsens them
  • Think of it as the NYHA class of the pulmonary circulation
2 · 6-minute walk distance (6MWD)
  • Objective exercise capacity, tracked visit to visit
  • A falling walk distance is a warning sign, whatever the patient says about symptoms
  • Cross-ref → the test itself (protocol, standardised encouragement, desaturation) is taught in LUNG FUNCTION → Muscle & Exercise. Go there; it is not repeated here.
3 · BNP / NT-proBNP
  • Biochemical marker of RV wall stress
  • Falling towards normal = the right ventricle is being successfully unloaded
  • A rising level on treatment is an early warning, often before walk distance or symptoms deteriorate
Escalation rule. A patient who is still not doing well despite an ERA + PDE-5 inhibitor should have an infused prostacyclin analogue added and be referred for lung transplant assessment at the same time. Transplant work-up takes months, so it is triggered by persisting deterioration — not by the patient becoming moribund. This is the trigger for the “End-Stage — transplant” box above.
Prognosis & Palliative Care
PAH is progressive and incurable. Modern therapy slows progression and improves function; it does not reverse the pulmonary vasculopathy. Survival in idiopathic PAH is measured in years, not decades, and is markedly better in those who respond to treatment and keep responding. That is precisely why follow-up is objective and treatment is escalated rather than left alone.
Palliative care runs in parallel with active disease-targeted treatment — not after it has failed. Delivered through the specialist centre MDT, it addresses refractory breathlessness, syncope, fatigue, anxiety and advance care planning (including resuscitation decisions and what happens if transplant is declined or unavailable). Referral is not “giving up”: a patient on a prostacyclin infusion and on the transplant list can and should have palliative input alongside it. It remains substantially under-used in PH.
⭐ Exam Pearls
5 WHO groups: 1=PAH (CTD/idiopathic) · 2=left heart (commonest) · 3=lung/hypoxia (COPD) · 4=CTEPH (chronic PE) · 5=misc
Mechanism: ↑pulmonary pressure → RV strain → cor pulmonale → systemic congestion. Every sign traces to this chain.
ECG: RVH + right axis deviation + RBBB + P pulmonale — all signs of right heart strain
CXR: dilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally ("pruning") + RV/RA enlargement
Echo = screening (estimates PAP). Right heart catheter = gold standard (direct PAP measurement + vasoreactivity testing).
Treat the cause first. PAH-specific drugs (sildenafil, ERAs, prostanoids) = Group 1, the one exception outside it being riociguat in inoperable Group 4 CTEPH — don't use them in Group 2: dilating the pulmonary arteries drives more blood into a left heart that cannot take it, raising left-sided filling pressures and precipitating pulmonary oedema.
Loud P2 + exertional syncope = classic PH exam vignette. Syncope = fixed low output.
Group 4 (CTEPH): anticoagulate + consider pulmonary endarterectomy — potentially curative. Cross-ref PE.
Group 3 (COPD): optimise the lung disease; add LTOT if the chronic hypoxaemia criteria are met — it reduces hypoxic vasoconstriction. No PAH-specific drugs in Group 3.
Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) = highest PAH risk among CTDs — screen annually with echo
PH on echo → designated specialist PH centre. RHC and PAH drugs are started only there; CTEPH operability is decided by an expert-centre CTEPH MDT, and V/Q is the CTEPH screening test (a normal V/Q effectively excludes it).
Follow-up is objective: WHO-FC + 6-minute walk distance + BNP/NT-proBNP at every visit. Still deteriorating on an ERA + PDE-5 inhibitor → add an infused prostacyclin AND refer for lung transplant assessment at the same time.
Pregnancy is contraindicated in PAH — maternal mortality is very high, higher still in Eisenmenger syndrome. Contraception is discussed at diagnosis with every woman of childbearing age, and planned with the specialist centre because several PAH drugs are teratogenic.
RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sleep Apnoea:
Repeated pharyngeal airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas (≥10 sec cessation) → recurrent micro-arousals + intermittent hypoxia. Classic patient: overweight, middle-aged man (also children with enlarged tonsils). Two consequence streams: sleep fragmentation → daytime symptoms and intermittent hypoxia → cardiovascular risk.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of pharyngeal airway collapse during sleep — hypotonic dilator muscles → airway sucked closed on inspiration → apnoea → arousal → reopening; open vs collapsed airway cross-section.
1
Sleep → pharyngeal dilator muscles become hypotonic
↓
2
Airway sucked closed on inspiration → apnoea
↓
3
Struggle to breathe → brief arousal (patient unaware; hundreds/night)
↓
4
Airway reopens
↺ cycle repeats through the night
Stream 1 — Sleep Fragmentation
  • Hundreds of micro-arousals
  • Never reaches deep restorative sleep
  • → Excessive daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, mood change, morning headache
Stream 2 — Intermittent Hypoxia
  • Repeated desaturations
  • Sympathetic activation
  • → Hypertension (especially resistant), ↑MI/stroke risk, arrhythmias (AF), cor pulmonale
Risk Factors
  • Obesity (biggest modifiable RF)
  • Male sex
  • Middle age
  • Large neck circumference
  • Enlarged tonsils / adenoids (children)
  • Retrognathia / craniofacial abnormality
  • Alcohol / sedatives (↑muscle relaxation)
  • Smoking
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Acromegaly
Clinical Features
WhenFeatures
Nocturnal (partner-reported)Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, nocturnal choking / gasping, restless sleep, nocturia
DaytimeExcessive daytime sleepiness (driving, meetings), unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, poor concentration, personality change, low libido
Consequences (untreated)Resistant hypertension, cor pulmonale / RHF, AF, ↑MI / stroke risk, type 2 diabetes worsening, road traffic accidents
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Overnight oximetry / polysomnography trace showing the repetitive saw-tooth desaturation pattern of obstructive apnoeas.
InvestigationRoleDetails
Epworth Sleepiness ScaleScreeningRates dozing likelihood in 8 situations (0–3; max 24); >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness → warrants investigation. It is subjective and quantifies sleepiness only — it does not diagnose OSA, correlates poorly with the AHI, and a normal score does not exclude OSA. It cannot separate OSA from simple snoring; a sleep study does that
Polysomnography (sleep study)Reference standard — not the routine first test in the UKSleep stages, airflow, O₂ sat, respiratory effort, EEG, ECG; gives the Apnoea–Hypopnoea Index (AHI) = events/hour
Home sleep study (polygraphy / oximetry)First-line in the UKHome respiratory polygraphy is the first-line UK sleep study (airflow, oximetry, respiratory effort, ± position); overnight oximetry alone — frequent saw-tooth desaturations — is the simpler alternative where polygraphy is not available. Full polysomnography is the reference standard but is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected other sleep disorders
AHI (events/hour)Severity
<5Normal
5–14Mild OSA
15–29Moderate OSA
≥30Severe OSA
Management
📷 Image placeholder — CPAP set-up — nasal/full-face mask pneumatically splinting the upper airway open; alongside a mandibular advancement device.
Conservative (all patients)
  • Weight loss — most important modifiable factor; can resolve mild OSA
  • How much: a 5–10% reduction in body weight can meaningfully lower the AHI, and can resolve mild OSA outright
  • How it is delivered: refer to a structured or specialist weight-management service — not bare "lose some weight" advice in clinic
  • Weight-loss pharmacotherapy via specialist weight-management services where criteria are met (these drugs are licensed for weight management — OSA is one of the qualifying comorbidities, not an indication in its own right)
  • Bariatric surgery: consider at BMI ≥40, or 35–39.9 with a significant health condition that would improve with weight loss — OSA counts (NICE). Lower thresholds apply for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African and African-Caribbean family background
  • Avoid alcohol & sedatives (↑muscle relaxation)
  • Smoking cessation
  • Sleep position (lateral)
  • Treat hypothyroidism / acromegaly if present
CPAP — Mainstay for Moderate/Severe
  • Continuous Positive Airway Pressure — tight nasal/full-face mask that pneumatically splints the upper airway open
  • Used every night
  • Reliably improves sleepiness, cognition and quality of life, and modestly lowers BP (most in resistant hypertension). Randomised trials have not shown a reduction in major cardiovascular events — treat that benefit as plausible but unproven
  • NICE: offered for symptomatic OSAHS across all severities — including mild disease where lifestyle measures have failed (not moderate/severe only)
  • With coexisting obesity hypoventilation (daytime hypercapnia): where the OSAHS is severe, CPAP is first-line — not NIV. Move to NIV if CPAP fails or the daytime CO₂ does not settle
Mandibular Advancement Device
  • Oral appliance that protrudes the lower jaw → opens the oropharyngeal space
  • For mild OSA, simple snorers, or CPAP-intolerant patients
Surgery
  • Tonsillectomy — children with enlarged tonsils (often curative)
  • UPPP (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) — resects uvula/soft palate; variable results in adults
Life after CPAP is started
Adherence is the central practical problem. A machine in the cupboard treats nothing, and the benefit is dose-dependent — the conventional benchmark is ≥4 hours per night on most nights, with more hours giving more improvement in sleepiness and blood pressure. Almost all dropout happens in the first few weeks, and early failure is a solvable technical problem, not "non-compliance" — the mask, the humidifier and the pressure are all adjustable, so troubleshoot before you conclude that CPAP has failed.
Why people stopWhat it looks likeThe fix
Mask fit / leakAir blowing into the eyes, noisy leak, red pressure marks, partner disturbed; high leak figure on the downloadRe-fit and re-size; try a different interface (nasal pillows ↔ nasal mask ↔ full-face); adjust strap tension rather than over-tightening
Nasal dryness or congestionDry mouth and nose, blocked nose, nosebleeds, sore throat on waking — the commonest reason a new patient quitsHeated humidification — the NICE answer to CPAP-related upper-airway side effects; add nasal saline, and treat rhinitis; a chin strap or full-face mask if mouth leak is drying the airway
ClaustrophobiaPanics or rips the mask off within minutes of lights-outDesensitisation — hold the mask on the face while awake, then wear it with the machine running during the day, then for part of the night, building up; a smaller/less enclosing interface helps
Pressure intolerance"Too much air", cannot breathe out against it, aerophagia and bloatingRe-titration — use the ramp, expiratory pressure relief, or an auto-titrating device so the pressure is only high when it needs to be
Follow-up. Review the machine download or telemonitoring data in the first weeks, while problems are still fixable — hours used, nights used, mask leak and residual AHI. Once CPAP is optimised and the patient is established on it, NICE supports annual review.
Still sleepy despite CPAP — work through it in order
  • 1 · Is it being used? Look at the adherence download first — hours per night and nights used. Most "CPAP failure" is simply under-use.
  • 2 · Is it working? Check the residual AHI and the leak figure. A high residual AHI means the pressure or the interface is wrong — that is a titration problem, not a failed treatment.
  • 3 · Is something else causing the sleepiness? Exclude depression, shift work / simply not enough time in bed, drugs (sedatives, opioids, antihistamines, alcohol) and narcolepsy.
  • 4 · Only then — adherent, optimised CPAP with no other explanation — consider a specialist-initiated wakefulness-promoting agent as an adjunct (solriamfetol is NICE-approved for residual excessive sleepiness in OSA). It is added to CPAP, never instead of it. Modafinil is not an option here — its OSA, shift-work and idiopathic-hypersomnia indications were withdrawn; it is now licensed for narcolepsy only (MHRA).
Driving & the DVLA
SituationDrivingNotify the DVLA?
OSA without sleepiness that would impair drivingMay continue to driveNo need to notify
Mild OSAS with excessive sleepinessMust not drive until the sleepiness is satisfactorily controlledNotify only if not controlled within 3 months
Moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepinessMust not drive. May resume only once the sleep clinic confirms symptom control and documented CPAP complianceMust notify the DVLA
Group 2 (bus / lorry)The same standard, applied more strictly — licensing depends on confirmed control plus documented complianceAs above, and reviewed at least annually (Group 1: at least every 3 years)
Nobody with sleepiness likely to impair driving may drive, whatever the AHI — that rule sits above the table. Your duty is to advise. It is the patient who must notify the DVLA; your job is to tell them clearly, and to document that you did. You only inform the DVLA yourself if the patient continues to drive against that advice — after trying to persuade them and telling them you intend to do so. Prioritise the assessment where the person is a vocational driver or works in a vigilance-critical job — they are off the road until treated, so a routine waiting list costs them their living and keeps the risk in play.
⚠ Anaesthesia & sedation — OSA is a perioperative risk factor. Screen surgical patients — STOP-BANG is the standard pre-op tool (taught in the presentation note Snoring & Witnessed Apnoeas (OSA); not repeated here). Anticipate a difficult airway, and minimise long-acting opioids and sedatives — the same drugs this note flags as worsening pharyngeal collapse. Continue the patient's own CPAP peri- and post-operatively, with extended recovery monitoring. Day surgery is not automatically contraindicated.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Apnoea = ≥10 sec cessation. Severity by AHI: mild 5–14 · moderate 15–29 · severe ≥30.
Classic vignette: obese middle-aged man + loud snoring + partner witnesses apnoeas + daytime sleepiness
Epworth >10 = abnormal (screening tool — it cannot diagnose). The diagnosis is made on a sleep study: home respiratory polygraphy is the first-line UK study, with full polysomnography the reference standard, reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected other sleep disorders.
CPAP = mainstay for moderate-severe. Mandibular advancement device for mild / CPAP-intolerant.
Weight loss = most important modifiable factor. Avoid alcohol and sedatives (worsen pharyngeal collapse).
Never drive when sleepy — that rule sits above every tier. Whether the DVLA must be told depends on severity and control (see the driving table above); Group 2 (HGV/bus) is the strictest, and is reviewed at least annually.
Cardiovascular consequences: resistant hypertension (think OSA in any patient with poorly controlled BP), AF, ↑MI/stroke, cor pulmonale
Cross-ref: OSA sits in Group 3 pulmonary hypertension (hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction → cor pulmonale). OSA alone is an uncommon cause of significant PH, and any PH is usually mild — where it is marked, look for coexisting obesity hypoventilation, COPD or left heart disease.
CPAP adherence ≥4 h/night is the benchmark, and benefit is dose-dependent. Learn the four fixes: leak → re-fit / change interface; dry or blocked nose → heated humidification; claustrophobia → desensitisation; pressure intolerance → re-titration. Early failure is technical, not moral.
DVLA is tiered, not blanket. No impairing sleepiness = drive, no notification. Mild OSAS + sleepiness = stop driving, notify only if uncontrolled at 3 months. Moderate/severe OSAS + sleepiness = stop driving and must notify. You advise; you only tell the DVLA yourself if they keep driving anyway.
Flag OSA before theatre. STOP-BANG pre-op, anticipate a difficult airway, spare the long-acting opioids and sedatives, and bring the patient's own CPAP in with them for peri- and post-operative use.
RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessation:
NICE recommends offering a choice of effective quit aids alongside behavioural support: NRT, varenicline, cytisine, bupropion, and nicotine-containing e-cigarettes (vapes). The classic three pharmacological agents (a comparison) + two current additions (vaping and cytisine) + one special case: pregnancy (different rules apply). The universal cross-topic intervention — appears in COPD, IHD, lung cancer, PAD, OSA, and stroke prevention.
Very Brief Advice — The Front End of the Pathway

Every option below is offered alongside behavioural support — this is how the patient reaches it. Very Brief Advice (VBA) is a 30-second intervention delivered at every clinical contact, not only the ones that are about smoking.

1
ASKAsk about and record smoking status — current, ex- or never-smoker.
↓
2
ADVISEAdvise that the best way to stop is with support and medication — a statement of the most effective route, not a lecture on willpower.
↓
3
ACTAct on the response — opt-out referral to the stop-smoking service (referred unless they decline) plus an offer of a quit aid from the menu below.
What “behavioural support” actually is: the stop-smoking service provides weekly one-to-one or group sessions through the quit date, CO monitoring to verify abstinence, and supply of the medication. Support plus pharmacotherapy beats either alone — which is why the two are always prescribed together.
The Three Agents — Comparison Table
📷 Image placeholder — Exhaled carbon monoxide (CO) breath test — the handheld CO monitor and reading used to objectively confirm smoking status (CO >4 ppm) and motivate quitting.
NRT Varenicline (Champix) Bupropion (Zyban)
Mechanism Nicotine replacement — reduces withdrawal symptoms Nicotinic receptor partial agonist — reduces craving (agonist) + blocks nicotine reward (antagonist) Noradrenaline/dopamine reuptake inhibitor + nicotinic antagonist — reduces craving and withdrawal
When to start Supplied ahead; start the day before the quit date 1–2 weeks before quit date; continue for 12 weeks 1–2 weeks before quit date
Key side effects Nausea, headache, flu-like, local irritation (patch/gum) Nausea (commonest), insomnia, vivid/abnormal dreams, mood change Seizures (most important), insomnia, dry mouth, headache
Cautions / CI Caution in acute MI, unstable angina; remove patch before sleep if vivid dreams Caution: depression / history of self-harm; CI: pregnancy and breastfeeding; not for under-18s (NICE). Supply note: varenicline was withdrawn in 2021 over a nitrosamine impurity. Generic varenicline returned through NHS stop-smoking services in 2024 and the branded product followed in 2025 — it is a routine option again. CI: epilepsy (lowers seizure threshold); CI: pregnancy and breastfeeding; eating disorders, bipolar; not for under-18s (NICE)
Three distinguishing hooks: Varenicline = partial agonist + vivid dreams + mood caution  |  Bupropion = seizure risk + CI in epilepsy  |  NRT = combine patch + fast-acting for high dependence
NRT — Forms & Combination Therapy
Long-Acting (Baseline)
  • Transdermal patch (16h or 24h) — steady background level
  • 24h patch: remove before sleep if causing insomnia or vivid dreams
Short-Acting (Craving Relief)
  • Gum
  • Lozenge
  • Nasal spray
  • Inhalator
  • Sublingual tablet — faster absorption to manage acute cravings
Combination for High Dependence
  • Patch + short-acting agent — patch provides baseline nicotine, short-acting covers breakthrough cravings
  • More effective than either alone in highly dependent smokers
E-cigarettes (Vaping) & Cytisine — Current NICE-Endorsed Options
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram of the widened NICE first-line menu — NRT, nicotine vape, varenicline, cytisine, bupropion, each combined with behavioural support.
Nicotine-containing E-cigarettes (Vapes)
  • NICE: an effective quit aid — advise adults who smoke that a nicotine vape is one of the most effective options, alongside behavioural support
  • Backed by the national “Swap to Stop” scheme
  • Not for never-smokers or under-18s
  • Substantially less harmful than smoking but not risk-free
Cytisine (Cytisinicline)
  • Plant-derived nicotinic receptor partial agonist — same principle as varenicline (reduces craving + blocks reward)
  • NICE-recommended — comparable in effect, safety and cost to the other options, given as a short reducing course (~25 days)
  • Start while still smoking — set the quit date within the first 5 days of treatment, then complete the fixed 25-day course
  • CI in pregnancy/breastfeeding, advanced atherosclerosis and uncontrolled hypertension
  • Caution in ischaemic heart disease, heart failure and treated hypertension
  • Not for under-18s, and not for people aged 66 and over (NICE)
How they fit
  • Offer the person a choice from all effective options (NRT, vape, varenicline, cytisine, bupropion) + behavioural support
  • Vaping and cytisine have widened the first-line menu beyond the traditional three agents
After the Quit Date — Duration, Review & Relapse

Writing the prescription is the start of the intervention, not the end. NICE attaches the same instruction to every agent: reassess the person shortly before the prescription runs out — has the person stopped, are they tolerating the drug, and do they need a further supply?

Agent Typical course Then
NRT 8–12 weeks Stop; continue longer only if needed to stay off tobacco
Varenicline 12 weeks Reassess before the course ends
Bupropion 7–9 weeks Reassess before the course ends
Cytisinicline 25 days Fixed reducing schedule — quit date in the first 5 days
The NHS success metric: CO-validated abstinence at 4 weeks after the quit date — the person reports not smoking and an exhaled CO reading of <10 ppm confirms it. This is the outcome every UK stop-smoking service is judged on; it is a validation-of-quit measure taken at a fixed time point, not the threshold used to identify a smoker at screening.
Nicotine Withdrawal — What They Actually Feel
  • Craving — the core symptom
  • Irritability, anxiety, restlessness
  • Low mood, poor concentration
  • Increased appetite
  • Disturbed sleep
Withdrawal Timeline
  • Onset within hours of the last cigarette
  • Peaks at 24–72 hours
  • Largely settles over about 4 weeks — the same window as the phone call to the surgery asking whether the drug is working
  • This is what “reduces withdrawal symptoms” in the table above means
Weight Gain — Name It Before They Do
  • Averages 3–5 kg after stopping
  • Blunted by NRT (and by other pharmacotherapy)
  • One of the commonest stated reasons for refusing or abandoning a quit attempt — raise it, do not wait for it
  • Far outweighed by the cardiorespiratory benefit of stopping
Relapse is the norm, not failure. Most people who eventually stop need several attempts. A lapse (one cigarette) is not a relapse (back to regular smoking) — treat it as data, not defeat. The response to a failed attempt is to re-offer behavioural support and pharmacotherapy — including a different agent from the menu — never to discharge the patient as unmotivated.
Pregnancy — The Special Case
📷 Image placeholder — Flowchart of smoking cessation in pregnancy — CO screening at every antenatal visit → behavioural support for everyone, with NRT considered alongside it from the earliest opportunity → never varenicline/cytisinicline/bupropion.
Varenicline, cytisine and bupropion are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Step 1 — Objective Screening
  • CO (carbon monoxide) testing at every antenatal appointment — patients often under-report smoking
  • CO 4 ppm or above = active smoker
  • Also refer anyone who stopped in the past 2 weeks, or who was referred before but has not engaged
  • Objective, non-judgmental
Step 2 — Behavioural Support & Incentives (First-line)
  • CBT and motivational interviewing — first-line in pregnancy
  • Refer to specialist stop-smoking service
  • Offer the financial incentive (voucher) scheme — refer at the booking appointment or the next opportunity (NICE, NHS England)
Step 3 — NRT (alongside support)
  • Consider NRT alongside behavioural support, at the earliest opportunity — do not wait for support alone to fail (NICE)
  • Continue it after the birth if needed to prevent relapse
  • Remove 16h patch before sleeping
  • Safer than continuing to smoke
Pregnancy rule: behavioural support for everyone, with NRT considered alongside it from the earliest opportunity and continued after delivery if needed to prevent relapse → never varenicline, cytisinicline, or bupropion. If a pregnant woman is already using a vape to stay off cigarettes, NICE advises not to discourage it, though licensed NRT is preferred.
⚠️ Stopping Smoking Is Itself a Prescribing Event
It is the tar (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), not the nicotine, that induces CYP1A2 — so quitting, or switching to NRT or a vape, removes the induction just as completely. Levels then rise: theophylline (nausea, vomiting, tachyarrhythmia, seizures — a respiratory drug, so this is the limb to know here), clozapine and olanzapine; warfarin control is also altered. Review doses and monitor whenever a patient stops — classically on admission to a smoke-free ward. Clozapine monitoring itself is covered in the psychiatry and therapeutic drug monitoring notes.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Varenicline = nicotinic partial agonist. Start 1–2 weeks before quit date. Key SEs: vivid dreams + mood/behaviour change. Caution in depression/self-harm history.
Bupropion = seizure risk. CI in epilepsy (and eating disorders, bipolar). Start 1–2 weeks before quit date.
Varenicline, cytisine and bupropion: CI in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Pregnancy: CBT/motivational interviewing for all, NRT considered alongside it early (remove patch before sleep) → no varenicline/cytisine/bupropion ever. Use CO testing to screen objectively.
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) for high dependence — more effective than monotherapy
Varenicline and bupropion both start 1–2 weeks before the quit date to reach therapeutic effect; cytisinicline is likewise begun while still smoking, with the quit date in the first 5 days. NRT is the near-exception — no loading period, but have it in hand and start the day before the quit date.
The universal intervention: smoking cessation appears in COPD, IHD, lung cancer, PAD, OSA, stroke prevention — always mention it
Very Brief Advice = Ask → Advise → Act in 30 seconds at every contact: record status, advise that support + medication works best, then make an opt-out referral.
Course lengths: NRT 8–12 weeks · varenicline 12 weeks · bupropion 7–9 weeks · cytisinicline 25 days (quit date in the first 5 days). Reassess shortly before the prescription ends — for every agent.
Withdrawal peaks at 24–72 hours and settles over ~4 weeks; weight gain averages 3–5 kg and is blunted by NRT. The service outcome is CO-validated abstinence <10 ppm at 4 weeks after the quit date — and relapse is normal, so re-offer support rather than discharge.
Stopping smoking (or switching to NRT or a vape) removes CYP1A2 induction — it was the tar, not the nicotine. Theophylline, clozapine and olanzapine levels rise; warfarin control alters. Review doses on admission.
RESPIRATORY__Occupational Lung Disease:
Lung diseases caused by inhaled occupational dusts → inflammation and fibrosis. Most are restrictive / ILD pattern (cross-ref ILD). Examined as a trio: occupation → CXR signature → cancer/TB risk. Most are compensable industrial diseases (Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit) — note isolated pleural plaques are the exception and are not compensable.
Classification Tree
📷 Image placeholder — Classification of occupational lung disease — fibrotic pneumoconioses (coal, silica, asbestos) vs hypersensitivity vs airway/malignant disease.
Coal
  • Coal worker’s pneumoconiosis — simple, progressing to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
Silica
  • Silicosis — fibrotic pneumoconiosis, with a markedly increased TB risk.
Asbestos — a spectrum
  • Pleural plaques — benign; the commonest finding.
  • Asbestosis — lower-zone interstitial fibrosis.
  • Mesothelioma — can follow even minimal exposure.
  • Lung cancer — the commonest asbestos-related malignancy (not mesothelioma).
Airways — sensitisers
  • Occupational asthma — obstructive and potentially reversible.
  • Sensitiser-induced is the commonest reported work-related lung disease in the UK.
Master Comparison Table
DiseaseDust / OccupationCXR SignatureZoneCancer / TB Risk
Coal worker's pneumoconiosisCoal dust — mining, tunnellingSmall nodules (simple); PMF masses (progressive massive fibrosis)UpperCOPD risk; no ↑ lung cancer
SilicosisSilica — engineered/artificial stone worktops; sandblasting, quarrying, pottery, foundries, slateEgg-shell hilar node calcification; upper nodulesUpper↑↑ TB; ↑ lung cancer
Asbestos-related diseaseAsbestos — construction, shipyards, insulation, pipe-laggingBibasal fibrosis → honeycombing (asbestosis); pleural plaques are a separate benign marker of the same exposure, not part of asbestosisLower (asbestosis)Lung cancer — multiplicative with smoking; mesothelioma — independent of smoking
Asbestos is the odd one out: lower-zone fibrosis (all other pneumoconioses are upper), a benign-to-malignant spectrum, and very long latency.
Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (“Black Lung”)
Coal dust overwhelms macrophage clearance → macule formation → nodules → fibrosis. Upper-zone disease. No increased lung cancer risk (unlike silica and asbestos).
Simple CWP
  • Commonest form, often asymptomatic
  • Small coal-dust macules + nodules on CXR
  • ↑ COPD risk
  • Up to ~30% progress to PMF over years — mainly in higher radiographic-category disease (overall progression is lower)
PMF (Progressive Massive Fibrosis)
  • Nodules coalesce → large upper-lobe fibrotic masses (>1 cm)
  • Black sputum (melanoptysis), progressive dyspnoea, mixed obstructive/restrictive PFTs, cor pulmonale in advanced disease
Management
  • Remove from exposure
  • Smoking cessation (↓COPD progression)
  • Supportive (inhaled bronchodilators, O₂)
  • No specific treatment
  • Compensable (IIDB)
Silicosis
📷 Image placeholder — Silicosis imaging schematic — upper-zone nodularity, eggshell hilar node calcification, and progression to progressive massive fibrosis.
Inhalation of crystalline silica → macrophage activation → fibrotic nodule formation. Upper-zone disease. The most important risk is reactivation TB — silica impairs macrophage killing of mycobacteria.
Occupations
  • Engineered / artificial stone worktop fabrication and installation — dry cutting, grinding and polishing (the source of the current UK outbreak)
  • Sandblasting (highest historic risk), stone quarrying, slate working, pottery, foundries, tunnelling, glass manufacturing
CXR Signatures
  • Egg-shell calcification of hilar lymph nodes (classic/characteristic — also seen in sarcoidosis)
  • Upper-zone small round nodules
  • May progress to PMF-like confluent masses
Classic vs accelerated silicosis — the vignette has changed.
  • Classic silicosis follows decades of exposure in an older worker; crystalline silica content varies widely by stone — granite roughly 20–45%, and sandstone, gritstone and quartzite over 70% (HSE).
  • Accelerated silicosis is the current UK outbreak among engineered / artificial stone worktop fabricators and installers: the material is up to ~90% crystalline silica, and dry cutting, grinding and polishing generate very high respirable crystalline silica exposure → symptomatic within roughly 3–10 years, in workers in their 20s–40s, with faster progression to progressive massive fibrosis.
  • A student working from the old (historic) occupations list would never consider silicosis in a 32-year-old stonemason — which is exactly the vignette now appearing.
Key Risks
  • ↑↑ TB risk (most important — screen all silicosis patients with Mantoux/IGRA)
  • ↑ lung cancer risk
  • Progressive fibrosis even after exposure ceases
Management
  • Remove from exposure
  • screen and treat latent TB
  • Supportive care
  • No disease-modifying treatment
  • Compensable (IIDB)
Always screen silicosis patients for TB — Mantoux/IGRA + CXR. Silicosis + TB = silicotuberculosis, rapid deterioration.
Asbestos-Related Disease
📷 Image placeholder — Spectrum of asbestos-related disease with latency — benign pleural plaques → diffuse pleural thickening/asbestosis → mesothelioma, on one timeline.
Asbestos (crocidolite > chrysotile) causes a spectrum from benign to malignant. Unique: lower-zone fibrosis (unlike all other pneumoconioses). Very long latency — often decades. Occupations: construction, shipbuilding, insulation, pipe-lagging, naval engineering.

The Spectrum — Benign to Malignant

ConditionKey FactsExam Points
Pleural plaquesCommonest asbestos disease. Discrete fibrous/calcified pleural thickenings. Latency 20–40 years. Often asymptomatic incidental CXR finding.Benign — no malignant potential. No routine radiological follow-up or referral. Marker of past exposure only. Does NOT become mesothelioma. But investigate unexplained symptoms or new signs — the same exposure carries a mesothelioma and lung-cancer risk.
Diffuse pleural thickeningMore extensive than plaques; may restrict lung expansion → restrictive PFTs; dyspnoea.Distinguish from plaques (diffuse vs discrete); both benign.
AsbestosisLower-zone interstitial fibrosis. Dose-dependent (proportional to cumulative exposure). Latency 15–30 years. Progressive dyspnoea, bibasal end-inspiratory crackles, clubbing, restrictive PFTs + ↓TLCO.Dose-dependent. Same PFT/HRCT pattern as IPF but lower zone. Honeycombing on HRCT.
MesotheliomaPleural malignancy. Even minimal/brief asbestos exposure can cause it. Latency up to 45 years. Progressive dyspnoea, chest wall pain, weight loss, ± pleural effusion (very common, ~75–90%).No safe threshold — even brief or low-level exposure can cause it. Not caused by smoking. Pemetrexed + cisplatin, or nivolumab + ipilimumab immunotherapy (NICE first-line, unresectable); poor prognosis (~12 months).
Lung cancerCommonest asbestos-related malignancy (not mesothelioma). Multiplicative/synergistic risk with smoking.Classic exam trap. Smoking cessation is critical to reduce this risk.

Key Discriminators

Asbestosis vs Mesothelioma
  • Asbestosis = dose-dependent (cumulative exposure needed)
  • Mesothelioma = no safe threshold — brief or low-level exposure can be enough
  • Different mechanisms — fibrosis vs malignant transformation of mesothelium
Lung Cancer vs Mesothelioma
  • Lung cancer = commonest asbestos malignancy (not mesothelioma)
  • Smoking + asbestos = multiplicative risk for lung cancer
  • Mesothelioma risk is independent of smoking
Pleural Plaques vs Asbestosis
  • Plaques = pleural only, benign, asymptomatic
  • Asbestosis = parenchymal interstitial fibrosis, symptomatic, progressive
  • Both can coexist
  • Plaques do NOT progress to asbestosis

Investigation & Management

Investigations
  • CXR (pleural plaques, bibasal fibrosis)
  • HRCT (honeycombing, plaques, thickening)
  • PFTs (restrictive + ↓TLCO in asbestosis)
  • thoracoscopic biopsy for mesothelioma
  • Pleural fluid cytology
Asbestosis Management
  • Remove from exposure
  • No specific disease-modifying treatment routinely (nintedanib may be considered if a progressive fibrosing ILD phenotype develops)
  • Supportive: O₂, pulmonary rehab
  • Monitor PFTs
  • Compensable (IIDB)
Mesothelioma Management
  • Pemetrexed + cisplatin (chemotherapy) or nivolumab + ipilimumab immunotherapy (NICE-recommended first-line in unresectable disease)
  • Surgery in highly selected cases
  • Palliative MDT
  • O₂, analgesia
  • Poor prognosis (~12 months median survival)
Smoking cessation is the most important intervention for anyone with asbestos exposure — it substantially reduces the multiplicative lung-cancer risk.
Occupational Asthma — The Airway Branch
Not every occupational lung disease is fibrotic. Occupational asthma is the most frequently reported work-related lung disease in the UK — an airway disease (obstructive, not restrictive) and the one branch of the tree that is potentially reversible. It belongs on the classification tree alongside the pneumoconioses.
Recognise it — pointer, not a re-teach
  • High-molecular-weight agents — flour (bakers), latex, grain dust, animal proteins → IgE-mediated
  • Low-molecular-weight agents — isocyanates (spray painters), colophony (soldering flux) → non-IgE
  • Diagnosis rests on the serial peak-flow diary: worse on working days, better on days off and holidays
  • The agents and the PEF diary are taught in full in the Asthma and Lung Function notes — this section covers only what is specific to occupational duty of care
  • Refer early to a specialist with an interest in occupational lung disease — suspicion alone warrants referral, and delay is what costs the recovery
  • Confirm it objectively before anyone is moved off the job. Removal from exposure is the treatment, but it can cost a livelihood — do not act on a story alone
Prognosis — why speed matters
  • Early removal from exposure offers the best chance of complete recovery
  • The longer exposure continues after symptom onset, the more likely symptoms and bronchial hyperresponsiveness become permanent
  • Only about a third of workers recover fully
  • Bronchial hyperresponsiveness can persist for up to a decade after removal from exposure
“Remove from exposure” means two different things. In the fibrotic pneumoconioses removal does not halt progression — silicosis progresses even after exposure ceases (see above), so removal prevents further insult rather than curing anything. In sensitiser-induced occupational asthma removal is potentially curative if it is early. Same three words in every management box; opposite prognostic weight.
After the Diagnosis — Duties, Benefits and Compensation
“Compensable (IIDB)” is a label, not a plan. Once the diagnosis is made there are four separate strands: report it, help the patient claim a benefit, point them at compensation, and protect the workers still exposed.
1 · Report — RIDDOR & SWORD
  • The employer makes the RIDDOR report, not you — but it is triggered by your written diagnosis given to the worker and employer
  • Currently reportable respiratory diseases include occupational asthma (where the work involves significant or regular exposure to a known respiratory sensitiser) and occupational cancer (which captures mesothelioma and asbestos-related lung cancer)
  • SWORD / THOR — the physician-facing voluntary reporting scheme that chest and occupational physicians report to; it generates UK incidence data and is not a legal duty
2 · Benefit — IIDB
  • IIDB is a claim the patient makes to the DWP for a “prescribed disease” — the hospital does not arrange it; your job is to advise and to write a clear diagnosis letter
  • Prescribed diseases include diffuse mesothelioma, pneumoconiosis (including asbestosis and silicosis), unilateral or bilateral diffuse pleural thickening, asbestos-related primary lung carcinoma, occupational asthma, extrinsic allergic alveolitis and byssinosis
  • General threshold is ≥14% disablement, but pneumoconiosis and byssinosis are assessable from 1%, and diffuse mesothelioma is assessed at 100%
3 · Compensation — lump sums
  • For those who cannot trace an employer or its insurer: the Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers’ Compensation) Act 1979 and the Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme 2014
  • A claimant takes one or the other — not both
  • Separately, a civil claim against a negligent employer or its insurer remains open and is usually the larger sum
⚠ RIDDOR and the pneumoconioses — teach the current position. Silicosis and asbestosis were removed from RIDDOR in 2013 and are under review. As things stand they are not RIDDOR-reportable — do not state that they are — but flag it as under review.
Isolated pleural plaques are not a prescribed disease; diffuse pleural thickening is. Both are benign asbestos-related pleural changes, but only diffuse thickening restricts lung expansion and produces measurable disablement, so only it attracts IIDB. A real and examinable discrimination — and the reason most, not all, occupational lung disease is compensable.
A death attributable to an industrial disease must be reported to the coroner. This is not a formality: the inquest usually provides the evidence of occupational causation that benefit and civil claims rely on, so omitting the referral can seriously prejudice the family’s claim. Genuinely examinable and practically consequential.

4 · The Occupational Health Arm — What “Remove from Exposure” Actually Requires

Refer to occupational health
  • Redeployment or reasonable adjustments — substituting the process, improving control, or moving the worker to a different role
  • Not automatic job loss — the fear that it is why workers conceal symptoms and present late
Inform the employer — with consent
  • You do not notify the employer yourself. With the patient’s consent the employer is informed — in practice by giving the written diagnosis to the worker to pass on. Occupational reporting duties do not override medical confidentiality
  • So that exposure is controlled at source and other exposed workers are reviewed
  • This is the public-health step that distinguishes occupational from general respiratory medicine — one index case implies a whole workforce
  • If consent is refused, explain the risk to co-workers and revisit it. Disclosure without consent is only justifiable in the rare public-interest case — a decision to take with senior and occupational-health advice, not alone
Health surveillance
  • Questionnaire plus spirometry under COSHH for workers exposed to respiratory sensitisers and Schedule 6 substances
  • This is why asymptomatic pneumoconiosis is detected at all — nobody presents with a chest that feels normal
Exam Pearls
Caplan syndrome: rheumatoid arthritis + pneumoconiosis (coal/silica) → multiple well-defined peripheral pulmonary nodules.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (e.g. farmer’s / bird-fancier’s lung) is the other key occupational exposure — upper/mid-zone; see the ILD topic.
CXR signatures: coal = PMF masses · silica = egg-shell hilar calcification · asbestos = pleural plaques
Zone: coal & silica = upper; asbestos = lower — the only lower-zone pneumoconiosis (other lower-zone fibrosis: IPF, CTD-ILD, drugs — see ILD)
Silica → ↑↑ TB (silica particles impair macrophage killing of mycobacteria)
Commonest asbestos malignancy = lung cancer, NOT mesothelioma — classic exam trap. Smoking + asbestos is multiplicative.
Pleural plaques = benign, no malignant potential, no routine follow-up — but investigate unexplained symptoms or new signs. Latency 20–40 yrs — marker of past exposure only.
Asbestosis = dose-dependent (cumulative exposure — intensity × duration). Mesothelioma = no safe threshold — brief or low-level exposure can be enough.
Coal PMF → black sputum (melanoptysis); up to ~30% of simple pneumoconiosis progresses to PMF (mainly higher radiographic-category disease)
Most occupational lung diseases are compensable industrial diseases (IIDB) — isolated pleural plaques are the exception. Document occupational history carefully.
Mesothelioma latency ~45 years; pemetrexed + cisplatin chemotherapy; poor prognosis (~12 months median)
Engineered/artificial stone worktops (up to ~90% silica) → accelerated silicosis — symptomatic in 3–10 years in workers in their 20s–40s. Consider silicosis in a young stonemason.
RIDDOR is reported by the employer, triggered by your written diagnosis. Currently reportable: occupational asthma and occupational cancer; the pneumoconioses were removed in 2013 and are under review. SWORD/THOR = voluntary physician reporting. An industrial-disease death must go to the coroner — omitting the referral can seriously prejudice the family’s claim.
IIDB = the patient’s own DWP claim for a “prescribed disease”, not a hospital referral. General threshold ≥14% disablement; pneumoconiosis and byssinosis from 1%; diffuse mesothelioma at 100%. Diffuse pleural thickening is prescribed; isolated pleural plaques are not.
“Remove from exposure” has two meanings. Pneumoconioses: progression continues regardless. Sensitiser-induced occupational asthma: early removal offers the best chance of complete recovery — but only about a third recover fully, and hyperresponsiveness can persist for a decade.
RESPIRATORY__Bronchiectasis:
Overview

Bronchiectasis is permanent, irreversible dilatation of bronchi → impaired secretion clearance → recurrent infection and inflammation. Unlike COPD (obstruction) or asthma (reversible narrowing), bronchiectasis is defined by dilated, mucus-pooling airways.

The spine: Everything in bronchiectasis — why sputum is copious, why it progresses, and why management targets clearance and infection — is explained by the vicious cycle.
The Vicious Cycle — Conceptual Centrepiece
📷 Image placeholder — Cole’s vicious cycle as a circular diagram — initial insult → impaired mucociliary clearance → bacterial colonisation → neutrophilic inflammation → airway wall damage → (back to impaired clearance).
💥
Bronchial injury — infection, inflammation
↓
🔥
Airway + elastin damage — neutrophil elastase destroys wall
↓
📏
Permanent dilatation — irreversible bronchial widening
↓
🟤
Impaired mucociliary clearance — mucus pools in dilated airways
↓
🦠
Recurrent infection — bacteria colonise static mucus
↺ the cycle repeats
Neutrophil elastase also drives mucus hypersecretion — explaining the copious, purulent sputum. Management targets both arms: break the cycle by clearing mucus and treating infection.
Aetiology
📷 Image placeholder — Overview of causes grouped as post-infective, obstructive, immunodeficiency, genetic (CF, PCD/Kartagener) and ABPA.
Common Causes
  • Post-infectious — most common: childhood pneumonia, whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis), TB. Always ask about recurrent childhood LRTIs.
  • Cystic fibrosis — the key genetic cause; bilateral, upper lobe predominance, Pseudomonas colonisation
  • COPD (frequent coexistence)
  • Idiopathic (~50% in adults)
High-Yield Named Causes
  • Kartagener's syndrome — bronchiectasis + situs inversus + sinusitis, caused by primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia)
  • ABPA (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis) — asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis
  • Immunodeficiency — HIV, hypogammaglobulinaemia (check Ig levels)
  • Obstruction — foreign body, enlarged TB lymph nodes (e.g. in children)
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Finger clubbing — bulbous fingertips with loss of the nail-bed angle; a classic sign in bronchiectasis (and other chronic suppurative lung disease).
Symptoms
  • Chronic cough + copious purulent sputum — the cardinal feature
  • Recurrent chest infections
  • Haemoptysis — can be massive and life-threatening (eroded bronchial artery)
  • Progressive breathlessness, wheeze, fatigue
Examination
  • Coarse crackles — typically at the bases (or wherever disease is located)
  • Clubbing (chronic suppurative lung disease)
  • Wheeze (from airway oedema)
  • Signs of cor pulmonale in advanced disease
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated HRCT of bronchiectasis — the signet-ring sign (dilated airway wider than its adjacent artery) and tram-track / bronchial wall thickening.
🖥️
HRCT Chest — Gold Standard
Signet ring sign: airway lumen wider than its accompanying artery. Bronchial wall thickening, lack of airway tapering, mucus plugging, cysts.
🩻
CXR
May be normal or show "tramtrack" lines (thickened parallel bronchial walls). Insensitive — HRCT always needed to confirm.
🧫
Sputum MC&S
Essential in exacerbation. Common organisms: H. influenzae (commonest), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (persistent green sputum), S. aureus.
🧬
Cause Workup
In everyone (the baseline bundle): FBC with differential white count · serum immunoglobulins IgG, IgA, IgM (hypogammaglobulinaemia) · ABPA screen — total IgE plus Aspergillus-specific IgE/skin prick · sputum culture, including mycobacteria. Selected patients only: sweat test + CFTR genetics if young or CF features · nasal nitric oxide — the first-line PCD test (biopsy and genetics come later, in specialist centres) · HIV, rheumatoid serology, anti-pneumococcal antibody titres if indicated. (BTS)
Management — Break the Vicious Cycle
Airway Clearance — Mainstay (targets the mucus arm)
  • Chest physiotherapy — active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT), postural drainage; taught and reviewed by a respiratory physiotherapist
  • Oscillatory PEP devices — Flutter / Acapella (vibration loosens mucus)
  • Mucolytics (hypertonic saline nebulisation) — not recombinant human DNase, see below
  • Regular, daily — not just during exacerbations
Treat / Prevent Infection (targets the infection arm)
  • Prompt antibiotics for exacerbations (↑cough, ↑sputum volume, purulence) — how to prescribe them is in the block below
  • S. aureus → flucloxacillin
  • Persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → oral ciprofloxacin (the first-line oral agent — but eradication and suppression are different jobs: see the Pseudomonas block below); if severe or ciprofloxacin fails, IV anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (ceftazidime or piperacillin/tazobactam) — adding an aminoglycoside only for resistant strains, not routinely
  • Prophylactic azithromycin (≥3 exacerbations/year) — check ECG (QT), LFTs and hearing, and exclude non-tuberculous mycobacteria first (macrolide monotherapy in undiagnosed NTM breeds resistance and wrecks later treatment; macrolides are also ototoxic long term)
What is NOT used in bronchiectasis — the classic transfer errors: recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) helps in cystic fibrosis but is harmful in non-CF bronchiectasis — more exacerbations and faster FEV1 decline — so do not use it. Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine either, unless there is coexisting asthma, COPD or ABPA. (BTS)
Acute Exacerbation — Getting the Prescription Right
  • What counts as one: deterioration in ≥3 of — ↑cough, ↑sputum volume or purulence, breathlessness, haemoptysis, fatigue/malaise — persisting >48 h and needing a change of treatment
  • Send sputum for MC&S before the first dose — then start empirically without waiting for the result. Choose the empirical drug from previous culture results, and modify it once sensitivities return. This is exactly why the Investigations panel calls sputum MC&S essential in exacerbation.
  • 14 days is the standard course (BTS expert consensus) — not the 5-day CAP course students reflexively prescribe. Always 14 days if P. aeruginosa-infected; 7–10 days only in mild disease with a rapid response. NICE licenses a 7–14 day range — but 14 days is the safe exam answer, and 5 days is wrong under either.
  • Empirical first-line: amoxicillin — it covers H. influenzae, the commonest organism. Doxycycline or clarithromycin are the other first-choice orals (and the answer in penicillin allergy); then organism-directed as opposite (S. aureus → flucloxacillin, Pseudomonas → ciprofloxacin)
Pseudomonas — Eradication vs Suppression (two different situations)
  • First isolation → attempt eradication. Systemic antibiotics (typically oral ciprofloxacin) for 2 weeks, followed by inhaled antibiotics for 3 months. A first Pseudomonas isolate is a reason to act, not to observe.
  • Chronic infection → you cannot eradicate it, so suppress it. Long-term nebulised antibiotics are used if exacerbations remain frequent (≥3 per year), chosen and started by the specialist service.
  • Consultant-initiated — eradication regimens and long-term inhaled antibiotics are started in secondary care, not in primary care
  • Same number, two drugs: ≥3 exacerbations/year is the trigger for long-term nebulised antibiotics in chronic Pseudomonas — and for azithromycin prophylaxis in those without it
Supportive / Other
  • Smoking cessation
  • Influenza (annual), pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccination
  • Bronchodilators if dyspnoeic
  • No routine inhaled corticosteroid — only if coexisting asthma, COPD or ABPA
  • Treat underlying cause (CF, ABPA, immunodeficiency)
  • Surgery — localised resectable disease or end-stage transplant
Follow-Up, Rehabilitation & Referral
Keeping Patients Well Between Exacerbations
  • Airway clearance taught by a respiratory physiotherapist — technique (ACBT, postural drainage, oscillatory PEP device) is assessed, taught and reviewed; it is a trained daily skill, not a vague instruction to "do some physio"
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation if MRC ≥2 — any breathlessness that limits function, from “short of breath hurrying on the flat or up a slight hill” upwards. A lower threshold than in COPD (MRC 3+) — do not import the COPD number. Supervised exercise + education.
  • Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), smoking cessation, and treatment of the underlying cause continue lifelong
Monitoring & When to Refer
  • Monitor: symptoms and exacerbation frequency (the number driving every long-term antibiotic decision) · sputum culture (has Pseudomonas appeared?) · spirometry
  • Spirometry — typically an obstructive pattern (FEV₁/FVC <0.7); repeated to track decline, not to make the diagnosis (that is HRCT)
  • Refer to secondary care if: frequent exacerbations, a new Pseudomonas isolation, or when long-term antibiotics are being considered — all consultant-initiated
  • Also refer for rapidly declining lung function, massive haemoptysis, or possible surgery / transplant assessment
Complications
  • Massive haemoptysis — life-threatening
  • Pneumonia, empyema
  • Pneumothorax
  • Respiratory failure
  • Cor pulmonale
  • Metastatic abscess (e.g. cerebral)
  • Non-TB mycobacteria colonisation
  • Aspergillus colonisation / ABPA
Massive haemoptysis (>200 mL/24 h, or any bleeding compromising the airway or circulation) is an airway emergency: bleeding side down, protect the airway, correct clotting, IV antibiotics guided by the patient’s known sputum microbiology (infection is usually the driver) and consider tranexamic acid; urgent CT angiography → bronchial artery embolisation, the first-line intervention if bleeding persists. Involve respiratory, interventional radiology and thoracic surgery early (BTS). Full algorithm in the Haemoptysis note.
⭐ Exam Pearls
HRCT = gold standard; the same airway, two planes — signet ring end-on (airway > adjacent artery) and tram-track along its length (parallel, non-tapering walls), plus bronchi within 1 cm of the pleura. CXR may show tramlines/ring shadows but is insensitive
DNase helps in CF, harms in non-CF bronchiectasis — never transfer it across; ICS only if coexisting asthma, COPD or ABPA
Cardinal feature: copious purulent sputum + chronic cough + clubbing
Commonest cause = post-infectious (ask about childhood LRTIs); CF the key genetic cause
Commonest organism = H. influenzae; persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → oral ciprofloxacin (IV dual therapy if severe)
Kartagener's = bronchiectasis + situs inversus + sinusitis (caused by primary ciliary dyskinesia)
ABPA = asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis
Mainstay = airway clearance physio + treat infection (break the vicious cycle)
Azithromycin prophylaxis if ≥3 exacerbations/yr — check QT + LFTs first
Haemoptysis can be massive and life-threatening
Exacerbation antibiotics run for 14 days, not the 5-day CAP course — and send sputum before the first dose, but never wait for it before starting
First Pseudomonas isolate → eradicate (2 weeks oral ciprofloxacin, then 3 months inhaled); chronic infection → suppress with long-term nebulised antibiotics if ≥3 exacerbations/yr
Pulmonary rehabilitation if MRC ≥2; airway clearance is taught by a respiratory physiotherapist; spirometry (obstructive) tracks decline, HRCT makes the diagnosis
RESPIRATORY__Acute Bronchitis:
Overview

Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) — inflammation of the trachea and major bronchi → oedematous large airways + increased sputum. Usually viral. The cough commonly lasts 3–4 weeks.

Organisms: >90% viral — rhinovirus commonest, also influenza, coronavirus, RSV and adenovirus. Bacterial causes are uncommon, chiefly Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Bordetella pertussis (whooping cough — covered in the Paediatrics note, not re-taught here).

Two things matter: (1) distinguish from pneumonia and (2) apply the NICE three-tier antibiotic decision (default: no antibiotic). Most cases are managed supportively.
Anatomy Overview
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Cough — dominant symptom; may or may not be productive
  • Sore throat, rhinorrhoea
  • Wheeze (from airway inflammation)
  • Low-grade or no fever
  • Systemic features (malaise, myalgia) often absent
Examination
  • Chest exam normally CLEAR — the key finding
  • ± Mild wheeze; ± low-grade fever
  • No focal chest signs — no dullness, no bronchial breathing, no localised persistent crackles. Scattered coarse crackles or rhonchi that shift or clear after coughing are compatible with bronchitis
Bronchitis vs Pneumonia
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side comparison graphic — clear chest + no systemic upset (bronchitis) vs focal signs + consolidation on CXR (pneumonia).
Feature Acute Bronchitis Pneumonia
Chest exam Usually normal Focal signs — dullness, bronchial breathing, ↓BS, crackles
Systemic features Often absent Present — fever, rigors, malaise, myalgia
Observations Normal — afebrile or low-grade, HR <100, RR <24, SpO₂ ≥94% Fever >38°C · HR >100 · RR >24 · SpO₂ <94% ± confusion
CXR Normal — not needed if observations are normal and the chest is clear Consolidation ± air bronchograms
Course Self-limiting; cough commonly 3–4 weeks Needs antibiotic treatment
Exam line: Clear chest + no systemic upset = bronchitis. Focal signs + systemic illness = pneumonia.
Do I need a CXR? Normal observations + a clear chest → pneumonia unlikely, no CXR needed. Any of fever >38°C · HR >100 · RR >24 · SpO₂ <94% · new focal chest signs · confusion → think pneumonia and request a CXR. Point-of-care CRP is the tie-breaker for residual uncertainty after clinical assessment — it does not replace the examination and the observations.
Management — The Three-Tier Antibiotic Decision

Supportive care is the mainstay — analgesia, fluids, reassurance that it is self-limiting. NICE self-care advice for the cough: honey (first choice in adults/children >1 yr), or an OTC cough medicine (e.g. guaifenesin) or pelargonium.

NICE — the three tiers. Do not routinely offer an antibiotic for an acute cough associated with an upper respiratory tract infection or acute bronchitis. Every case lands in one of three tiers.
1 · No antibiotic + self-care
  • The default — an otherwise well adult or child
  • Explain the expected course, give self-care advice, and safety-net
2 · Back-up (delayed) prescription
  • Consider for people at higher risk of complications — NICE allows an immediate or a back-up prescription here; in a well patient, back-up
  • Handed over to hold, and started only if things change
3 · Immediate antibiotic
  • Systemically very unwell → offer an immediate antibiotic
  • Symptoms or signs of a more serious illness or condition (pneumonia, sepsis, PE, lung cancer) → refer to hospital or seek specialist advice — not simply a prescription
Higher risk of complications — the definable list
  • Pre-existing significant heart, lung, renal, liver or neuromuscular disease
  • Immunosuppression
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Young children born prematurely
  • Over 65 with 2+, or over 80 with 1+, of: hospitalisation in the previous year · type 1 or type 2 diabetes · congestive heart failure · current use of oral corticosteroids

Within that framework, where uncertainty remains after clinical assessment, point-of-care CRP is used as the tie-breaker:

Situation / CRP Action
Systemically unwell / significant comorbidities Consider antibiotics regardless of CRP
CRP <20 mg/L No antibiotic
CRP 20–100 mg/L Delayed / back-up prescription
CRP >100 mg/L Immediate antibiotic
Antibiotic Choice
  • First choice in adults: doxycycline — 200 mg day 1, then 100 mg OD × 4 days (5-day course)
  • Alternative first choices: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 days, or clarithromycin × 5 days
  • Doxycycline avoided in children under 12 and in pregnancy → use amoxicillin instead
  • Penicillin allergy — relevant where amoxicillin would otherwise be used: a macrolide, clarithromycin (or erythromycin in pregnancy)
What You Actually Say to the Patient
The duration message is the consultation. Tell them the cough commonly lasts 3–4 weeks, and that an antibiotic would shorten it by around half a day. Setting that expectation up front is the main defence against inappropriate antibiotic pressure.
Why it lingers
  • The virus clears early, but post-viral airway hyperreactivity keeps the cough going for weeks
  • So a cough still there at week 3 is not treatment failure — and not a reason to add an antibiotic
Back-up prescription — the words to use
  • “Take this to the pharmacy, but do not start it yet.”
  • “Start it if you get significantly worse at any time, or if you are not starting to improve after the time we agree (commonly 3–5 days).”
  • Agree that interval out loud and document it
Safety-net — come back urgently if: rapid or significant worsening · breathlessness · pleuritic chest pain · haemoptysis · confusion · persistent fever · feeling systemically very unwell.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Clear chest + no systemic features = bronchitis (vs pneumonia's focal signs)
>90% viral; self-limiting, but the cough commonly lasts 3–4 weeks — antibiotics shorten it by ~half a day
CRP <20 → none / 20–100 → delayed / >100 → immediate
Doxycycline first choice in adults; amoxicillin in children under 12 and in pregnancy
Mostly supportive — do not over-treat
Default = no antibiotic. Higher risk of complications → consider a back-up (or immediate) script; immediate if systemically very unwell; refer if a more serious illness is suspected
Over 65 with 2+ / over 80 with 1+ of: admission in the past year · type 1 or 2 diabetes · CHF · oral steroids → higher risk of complications
Normal obs + clear chest → no CXR. Fever >38°C · HR >100 · RR >24 · SpO₂ <94% · focal signs · confusion → CXR
RESPIRATORY__Pneumonia:
Overview & Classification
📷 Image placeholder — Lobar pneumonia vs bronchopneumonia vs interstitial pattern — distribution of consolidation on a lung schematic.

Pneumonia = infection of the lung parenchyma → inflammation + alveolar exudate + consolidation. The topic is three reference tables: causative organisms, CURB-65, and antibiotics by severity.

Type Definition Key point
CAPDevelops outside hospitalS. pneumoniae commonest
HAP>48 h after hospital admissionEarly-onset often the same organisms as CAP; late-onset and higher-resistance-risk are Gram-negatives, Pseudomonas and MRSA — hence broader cover
AspirationForeign material → bronchial treeRight lower lobe (wider, more vertical R main bronchus) — superior segment of RLL / posterior segment of RUL if aspirated lying down, basal segments if upright; risk: ↓consciousness, dysphagia, poor dental hygiene
Causative Organisms — The MCQ Clues
Atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Coxiella, Chlamydia psittaci) → don't respond to penicillins — Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall; Legionella, Coxiella and Chlamydia/Chlamydophila are intracellular and/or lack classic peptidoglycan → need a macrolide or doxycycline.
Organism The Classic Clue Extra features / Treatment
S. pneumoniae Commonest CAP — any severity Lobar consolidation, rust-coloured sputum. Treat: amoxicillin
H. influenzae COPD Also common in elderly. Treat: amoxicillin / co-amoxiclav
Staph aureus CF; post-influenza Bilateral patchy infiltrates, cavitation. Treat: flucloxacillin
Klebsiella pneumoniae Alcoholic Red-currant jelly sputum, upper lobe, bulging fissure sign, cavitation. Treat: co-amoxiclav or a cephalosporin, guided by sensitivities
Legionella Air-con / water cooling systems Hyponatraemia (SIADH) + lymphopenia, deranged LFTs. Urinary antigen test. Notifiable — notify UKHSA on clinical suspicion, before confirmation (source investigation). Treat: macrolide; levofloxacin if severe
Mycoplasma Young adults, walking pneumonia Cold agglutinins → haemolytic anaemia; erythema multiforme; neurological complications. Treat: macrolide/doxycycline
Chlamydophila pneumoniae School-age child Mild + wheeze; biphasic illness. Treat: macrolide
Coxiella (Q fever) Farmer / animal bodily fluids Hepatitis + endocarditis risk. Treat: doxycycline
Chlamydia psittaci Parrot / bird owner Psittacosis — flu-like, splenomegaly. Treat: doxycycline
PCP (P. jirovecii) HIV / CD4 <200 Dry cough, exertional desaturation, clear chest on auscultation, bilateral perihilar haze on CXR. Treat: co-trimoxazole + steroids if hypoxic (PaO₂ <9.3 kPa on air, or SpO₂ <92%). Prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole if CD4 <200
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Productive cough ± haemoptysis
  • Fever, rigors, malaise
  • Pleuritic chest pain (pleural irritation)
  • Breathlessness, ↓sats
  • Confusion — especially in the elderly
Signs of Consolidation (focal triad)
  • Dullness to percussion over the affected lobe
  • Bronchial breathing (harsh, same quality as tracheal)
  • Focal coarse crackles
  • ↑vocal resonance / tactile vocal fremitus — solid lung transmits sound better. Contrast a pleural effusion, where both are REDUCED
  • Focal signs + systemic upset = pneumonia (vs clear chest = bronchitis)

CRB-65 — the primary-care score: same criteria minus urea (no bloods needed). Different disposition bands from CURB-65: 0 → primary care with safety-netting · 1 → primary care with safety-netting or referral (virtual ward, SDEC, hospital-at-home, hospital) · ≥2 → consider referral to hospital (NICE). Investigations
Do NOT delay antibiotics — give within 4 hours of diagnosis (or of presentation to hospital). Within 1 hour if sepsis is suspected and the patient meets any high-risk criterion (NICE). Do not wait for investigation results.
🩻
CXR
Consolidation + air bronchograms. Silhouette sign. A follow-up film is not routine (NICE) — consider a CXR at 6 weeks only if there are risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease (e.g. smokers, over 50), as a shared decision.
🧪

↑WCC/neutrophilia. CRP may lag (can rise next day despite improvement); may be normal in immunocompromised.

Urea for CURB-65. Hyponatraemia in Legionella (SIADH).

Before antibiotics in moderate/severe — must NOT delay treatment for this.
🫘

Pneumococcal antigen in moderate/high severity — its job is to let you de-escalate to a narrower antibiotic. Legionella antigen where there are Legionella risk factors (travel, hotel/spa, air-con or water systems, outbreak) or high-severity disease. Do not routinely test in low-severity CAP (NICE).
💨
