If SpO₂ low or severe disease. Assesses type 1/2 respiratory failure. Target sats 94–98% — but 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD and similar) pending gases (BTS).
Antibiotic Treatment by Severity
Severity / Type Antibiotic Duration
Low CAP (CURB 0–1) Oral amoxicillin (penicillin-allergic: doxycycline or clarithromycin — doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and in children under 12; use erythromycin in pregnancy) 5 days
Moderate CAP (CURB 2) Oral amoxicillin, add clarithromycin if atypicals are suspected (erythromycin in pregnancy). Penicillin-allergic: doxycycline or clarithromycin 5 days (review at 5 days; extend if not improving)
High CAP (CURB ≥3) IV or oral co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin — oral first-line if they can swallow and IV is not required (levofloxacin if penicillin-allergic — avoid combining a fluoroquinolone with the corticosteroid used in high-severity CAP: tendinitis / tendon rupture risk (MHRA); discuss with microbiology). Local protocols may substitute ceftriaxone, or tazocin where Pseudomonas is a risk 5 days, then review — extend only if not clinically stable
HAP — mild Oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg 5 days, then review
HAP — severe IV tazocin (piperacillin/tazobactam) 4.5 g TDS 5 days, then review — extend if not clinically stable
Aspiration IV/oral co-amoxiclav (covers anaerobes) 5 days, then review — extend if not improving or if abscess/empyema
PCP (HIV/immunocompromised) Co-trimoxazole + prednisolone if hypoxic 21 days
Corticosteroids in high-severity CAP — a recent change in NICE guidance. For adults in hospital with high-severity CAP, consider a corticosteroid in addition to antibiotics, for 4–7 days or until discharge if sooner. Consider starting with IV hydrocortisone, or an alternative such as dexamethasone if hydrocortisone is unsuitable. This is one of the named important changes to practice in the current NICE pneumonia guidance. Note this is separate from the steroid given in PCP — steroids in pneumonia are no longer a PCP-only answer.
Step down from IV to oral when apyrexial >24h, improving, tolerating orally.
Not Getting Better — the 48–72 h Review
The trigger: by 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics the patient should be turning the corner. Fever that persists, a CRP that is not falling, or a worsening oxygen requirement means stop and re-assess from first principles — do not simply reach for a broader antibiotic. Decide which of the five forks below you are in.
Fork What to think of Action
Complication Empyema, lung abscess, necrotising pneumonia — the commonest reason a treated pneumonia stalls Repeat CXR, thoracic ultrasound and a pleural tap of any collection (pH, glucose, LDH, MC&S). CT chest if abscess or necrosis suspected
Wrong bug Atypical organism not covered, a resistant organism, or TB Atypical screen (Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen, Mycoplasma serology/PCR, respiratory viral PCR), sputum AFB × 3 and TB culture, and an HIV test; chase blood and sputum cultures and re-check sensitivities
Wrong host Undiagnosed immunosuppression — HIV, haematological malignancy, steroids/biologics, asplenia — and PCP HIV test and CD4 count, immunoglobulins, medication review. If dry cough with exertional desaturation and a relatively clear chest → treat as PCP (induced sputum or BAL)
Obstruction Endobronchial tumour or an inhaled foreign body — suspect if the same lobe is repeatedly involved or a lobe has collapsed CT chest, then bronchoscopy
Wrong diagnosis It was never pneumonia: PE, pulmonary oedema, lung cancer, organising pneumonia CTPA or CT chest as the story dictates; echo and BNP if heart failure is plausible; refer for consideration of steroids/biopsy in suspected organising pneumonia
↪ Confirmed pleural infection is managed differently from CAP — different antibiotic principles, a different course length, and drainage. See Pleural Effusion → Parapneumonic Effusion & Empyema for the full regimen.
Complications
General Complications
  • Sepsis / septic shock
  • Respiratory failure — type 1, and type 2 if the patient tires or has underlying COPD
  • Parapneumonic pleural effusion → empyema
  • Lung abscess (foul sputum, air-fluid level on CXR — exclude malignancy)
  • Death
Parapneumonic effusion → empyema: the drainage decision

Drain on ANY ONE of these — they do not have to co-exist:

  • Frank pus = empyema — drain, no further tests needed
  • Organisms on Gram stain, or a positive culture — drain
  • pH <7.2 in non-purulent fluid (bacteria respire → lactic acid) = complicated parapneumonic effusion — drain

Supporting, not deciding: glucose <2.2 mmol/L (bacteria consume glucose), LDH >1000 U/L (cell destruction). A simple effusion — clear, pH >7.2, no organisms — needs antibiotics alone.

After the Pneumonia — Recovery, Safety-Netting & Discharge
“When will I be back to normal?” is the question patients actually ask, and the one students are least able to answer. The BTS recovery milestones below are a genuinely useful thing to say at discharge — recovery is measured in months, not days.
~1 week
Fever should have resolved
~4 weeks
Chest pain and sputum production substantially reduced
~6 weeks
Cough and breathlessness substantially reduced
~3 months
Most symptoms resolved — but fatigue may persist
~6 months
Back to normal
Safety-netting — come back if…
  • Breathlessness worsens or new/worsening pleuritic chest pain
  • Fever returns after settling, or has not settled by about a week
  • Haemoptysis, or sputum turning foul-smelling (think abscess/empyema)
  • Confusion or drowsiness, or unable to keep fluids down — reassess for sepsis
  • Symptoms not improving at all by ~3 weeks, or a cough persisting beyond 6 weeks
  • Give the milestones above and these triggers — safety-netting only works if the patient knows what “normal recovery” looks like
Follow-up CXR — risk-stratified (NICE)
  • Do not routinely offer a follow-up chest X-ray after discharge — this replaces the old universal “6-week film”
  • Consider one at 6 weeks for people with risk factors for lung cancer or other underlying respiratory disease — e.g. smokers, people over 50
  • Frame it as a shared decision: discuss what a repeat film can and cannot show
  • Imaging during the illness is a different question — a patient who is not improving is imaged straight away (see the 48–72 h review above)
  • A shadow that persists after adequate treatment = obstructing lesion until proven otherwise → CT chest ± bronchoscopy
✅ The discharge bundle
  • Vaccination: check pneumococcal (a single dose at 65, or from age 2 in a clinical risk group — asplenia, CKD, immunosuppression, chronic heart/lung/liver disease, diabetes, cochlear implant, CSF leak) and annual influenza status before they leave, and arrange whatever is outstanding — full indications and schedule in Vaccinations & Immunisation Schedule
  • Smoking cessation: an admission with pneumonia is one of the highest-yield moments to offer it — see Smoking Cessation
  • Recurrent pneumonia, or the same lobe twice → look for an underlying cause: bronchial obstruction (tumour, foreign body), bronchiectasis, aspiration / an unsafe swallow, and immunodeficiency (HIV, myeloma, hypogammaglobulinaemia)
  • Warn about persistent fatigue and advise a graded return to work and activity — it is expected, not a relapse
