RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and Oxygen Supp:
Respiratory support follows an escalation ladder: oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula → non-invasive ventilation → mechanical ventilation → ECMO. Two anchors examined most: oxygen saturation targets (which patient gets what %) and the CPAP vs BiPAP distinction (Type 1 vs Type 2 respiratory failure).
The Escalation Ladder
📷 Image placeholder — Respiratory support escalation ladder — supplemental O₂ → high-flow nasal cannula → NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) → invasive ventilation → ECMO.
  1. Supplemental O₂
    • Nasal cannula / simple mask / non-rebreather / Venturi
  2. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) — up to 60 L/min + gentle PEEP
  3. Non-invasive respiratory support
    • CPAP — Type 1 respiratory failure (one constant distending pressure: it recruits alveoli and offloads work of breathing, but does not ventilate, so strictly it is not NIV)
    • BiPAP — Type 2 respiratory failure
  4. Invasive mechanical ventilation — ETT + sedation
  5. ECMO — specialist centres; reversible failure
Oxygen Targets — Highest-Yield Point
💊 Oxygen is a drug — and it has to be prescribed. These target ranges are not just numbers to know; they are what you write on the drug chart. BTS requires oxygen to be prescribed against a written target saturation range, with the device recorded, signed for at every drug round, and titrated by nursing staff to keep the patient in range.
  • Prescribe a target range, not a fixed flow — the flow is whatever it takes to stay in the range
  • SpO₂ below range → step the device up. SpO₂ above range → step it down and wean. Being above the target is a prescribing error too, not a job well done
  • In an emergency (peri-arrest, critically unwell) give high-concentration oxygen immediately, then prescribe it retrospectively — never delay oxygen to find a drug chart
“Oxygen prescribed to a target range” is a classic OSCE and prescribing-exam mark.
Most Acutely Ill Patients
  • Target SpO₂ 94–98%
  • Titrate O₂ to achieve and maintain this range
Patients at Risk of Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure
  • COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, severe kyphoscoliosis, bronchiectasis, CF
  • Target SpO₂ 88–92% via a 24–28% Venturi mask, pending blood gases — the risk sets the target, not a gas that has already proved hypercapnia. If the gas shows a normal PaCO₂ and pH, change the target to 94–98% — unless there is a history of hypercapnic respiratory failure that needed NIV or ventilation, when 88–92% stays. Recheck the gas after 30–60 minutes (BTS)
  • Controlled oxygen avoids worsening hypercapnia — mainly by not undoing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (see below)
  • Drive nebulisers with air, not O₂ — if only oxygen is available, limit it to 6 minutes
Critically Ill (Shock, Arrest, Anaphylaxis)
  • Start 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask — hypoxia kills acutely
  • Titrate down once stabilised
  • Never withhold O₂ in a crashing patient
Rule: High-flow O₂ in the critically ill. Controlled O₂ in CO₂ retainers (COPD) — the single most examined O₂ prescribing point.
Avoid hyperoxia: oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness — do not give it to a non-hypoxic patient (SpO₂ already ≥94%). Routine O₂ in acute MI or stroke without hypoxia is not recommended and may be harmful.
🧠 Why oxygen raises CO₂ — and why “hypoxic drive” is only part of the answer. The old teaching is that oxygen switches off the hypoxic respiratory drive. That mechanism is real but minor. BTS ranks the mechanisms, and the top one is different:
  • 1. V/Q mismatch (the main mechanism). Diseased lung units are poorly ventilated, so the body diverts blood away from them by hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Give high-concentration oxygen and that vasoconstriction relaxes — blood floods back into units that cannot clear CO₂, and PaCO₂ rises
  • 2. Reduced ventilatory drive — the classic “hypoxic drive”, genuine but a smaller contributor
  • 3. The Haldane effect — oxygenated haemoglobin carries less CO₂, so saturating the blood releases CO₂ into the plasma
Why it matters practically: if it were purely about drive, the fix would be to withhold oxygen. It is not. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient for fear of CO₂ retention — treat the hypoxaemia with a controlled device, then manage the CO₂ with NIV if the pH falls.
📉 When the saturation probe lies. Everything above is built on the SpO₂ reading — so you need to know when that number cannot be trusted. If the clinical picture and the oximeter disagree, believe the patient and get an ABG.
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning — the dangerous one. Carboxyhaemoglobin is read as if it were oxyhaemoglobin, so the SpO₂ looks normal or high while the patient is profoundly hypoxic. Needs a blood gas with co-oximetry (CO poisoning)
  • Poor peripheral perfusion — shock, cold peripheries, vasoconstriction: the trace is damped and unreliable or absent
  • Methaemoglobinaemia — the reading drifts toward ~85% and stops tracking the true saturation
  • Darker skin pigmentation — oximeters overestimate true saturation, so occult hypoxaemia can be missed. Have a lower threshold for an ABG
  • Nail varnish, dirt, motion artefact — mechanical causes of a poor or false signal
And the conceptual limit that catches people out: SpO₂ measures oxygenation only, never ventilation. A patient can sit at 92% with a rising PaCO₂ and a falling pH while the monitor looks reassuring — only a blood gas shows you the CO₂.
Oxygen Delivery Devices
📷 Image placeholder — Illustrated oxygen delivery devices — nasal cannula, simple (Hudson) mask, non-rebreather with reservoir bag, and colour-coded Venturi valves with their FiO₂ values.
DeviceFiO₂FlowKey Notes
Nasal cannula ~24–50% 1–6 L/min Comfortable; patient can talk/eat; variable FiO₂ (affected by breathing pattern). Above ~6 L/min they are drying and uncomfortable without adding useful FiO₂
Simple face mask (Hudson) 40–60% 5–10 L/min Mild-moderate hypoxia; variable FiO₂; must run ≥5L (avoid CO₂ re-breathing)
Non-rebreather mask (reservoir) ~60–80% 15 L/min Severe/critically ill; variable FiO₂ (entrains air around the mask, and the delivered FiO₂ falls as inspiratory flow rises); the highest FiO₂ of the simple masks
Venturi mask 24–60% Per valve colour Fixed/precise FiO₂ → use in COPD / CO₂ retainers. Colour-coded valves: blue 24% · white 28% · yellow 35% · red 40% · green 60%
Venturi = fixed performance (precise FiO₂) — the fixed-performance device among the standard oxygen masks; cannulae, simple masks and reservoir masks are all variable performance. (High-flow nasal oxygen and a ventilator also deliver a set FiO₂.) The caveat: it only delivers the marked concentration if total flow exceeds the patient’s inspiratory flow, so turn the flow up above the figure printed on the valve if the patient is very tachypnoeic.
PEEP — The Unifying Concept
  • Prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration
  • ↓Atelectasis
  • Improves oxygenation
  • ↓Work of breathing
  • Recruits collapsed lung units
Added by: HFNC (small amount), CPAP/BiPAP (controlled), mechanical ventilator (precise titration)
High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC)
How It Works
  • Delivers up to 60 L/min of warmed, humidified oxygen via wide-bore nasal prongs
  • Generates low-level PEEP, washes out nasopharyngeal dead space, reduces work of breathing
Role
  • Bridge between standard O₂ and NIV — for patients failing standard O₂ who aren't yet in Type 2 failure
  • Well-tolerated, allows talking and eating
  • Mainly for Type 1 respiratory failure
Non-Invasive Ventilation — CPAP vs BiPAP
📷 Image placeholder — CPAP vs BiPAP diagram — CPAP single constant pressure (Type 1 RF) vs BiPAP dual iPAP/ePAP actively assisting ventilation (Type 2 RF).
CPAPBiPAP
Pressure Constant single pressure throughout breathing cycle Two pressures — higher iPAP (inspiration) + lower ePAP (expiration)
Action Splints airways and alveoli open; improves oxygenation; reduces work of breathing Actively assists ventilation — iPAP supports inspiration → ↓CO₂, ↑tidal volume
Failure type Type 1 RF (↓O₂, normal CO₂) Type 2 RF (↓O₂ + ↑CO₂); NIV is for the acute, uncompensated form — the one with a respiratory acidosis
Indications Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (including acute decompensation of chronic heart failure), OSA AECOPD with respiratory acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy (pH <7.35, PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa), neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation
The exam rule: CPAP = oxygenation problem (Type 1)  |  BiPAP = ventilation/CO₂ problem (Type 2). COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy → BiPAP (pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa). A pH <7.25 is not a contraindication — it predicts a higher chance of NIV failure, so deliver NIV in HDU/ICU with immediate access to intubation and a documented escalation plan.
Starting NIV — Contraindications, Settings & the 1-Hour Gas
Choosing CPAP or BiPAP is the exam question; what you do in the hour after starting it is the ward question. NIV is a treatment with a deadline — if it is not working, that has to be recognised early, not at the next ward round.
🚫 Contraindications — check before the mask goes on
  • Untreated pneumothorax — positive pressure can convert it to a tension pneumothorax. Drain it first
  • Vomiting, or a high aspiration risk — a tight mask over a vomiting patient is dangerous
  • Facial trauma or burns, or recent upper airway / upper GI surgery — no seal, or a dehisced anastomosis
  • Cannot protect the airway — reduced consciousness, copious secretions, fixed upper airway obstruction
  • Haemodynamic instability or cardiac arrest — these patients need intubation, not a mask
⚙️ Typical starting settings
  • CPAP: a single pressure, usually 5–10 cmH₂O, with FiO₂ titrated to the target range
  • BiPAP: start iPAP 15 cmH₂O over ePAP 3–5 cmH₂O, then up-titrate the iPAP in increments of 2–5 cmH₂O as tolerated, guided by the pH, the CO₂ and patient tolerance (BTS/ICS)
  • It is the gap between iPAP and ePAP that does the ventilating — so if the CO₂ is not falling, increase the iPAP, not the oxygen
  • Treat the underlying cause in parallel — NIV buys time, it does not fix the pneumonia, the oedema or the exacerbation
⏱️ Repeat the gas at 1 hour
  • Recheck the ABG about an hour after starting, and after any significant settings change
  • Working: pH rising toward normal, PaCO₂ falling, respiratory rate settling, patient more comfortable
  • Failing: pH static or falling, CO₂ unchanged or climbing, worsening drowsiness, exhaustion, mask intolerance
  • Monitor continuously in between — SpO₂, respiratory rate and conscious level. A patient who is getting sleepy on NIV is deteriorating, not settling
😷 The problems NIV itself causes: pressure sores over the nose bridge (the commonest reason patients refuse to continue), dry eyes and dry mouth, gastric distension, and aspiration. Also decide the ceiling of care before you start — if NIV fails, is this patient for intubation, or is NIV itself the ceiling? (covered in the COPD note).
📎 Device set-up, Venturi valve flow rates and the full oxygen-prescribing detail are covered in Oxygenation & Respiratory Support under Lung Function.
Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
Indications
  • NIV failed/contraindicated
  • GCS ≤8 (can't protect airway)
  • Refractory hypoxia
  • Haemodynamic instability
  • Cardiac arrest
Access
  • Endotracheal tube (ETT) for short-term
  • tracheostomy for prolonged ventilation
  • Requires sedation ± paralysis
Key Settings
  • FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume (~6 mL/kg ideal body weight — lung protective), PEEP, I:E ratio
  • Aim: shortest duration possible
⚠️ Complications
  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia — risk rises with every day tubed; the reason the aim is the shortest duration possible
  • Barotrauma / volutrauma — over-distension causes pneumothorax and lung injury. This is why tidal volumes are kept at ~6 mL/kg
  • Hypotension — positive pressure raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and preload. the induction agents add vasodilation and negative inotropy. A patient who drops their blood pressure right after intubation is usually showing you this rather than a new diagnosis — but exclude a tension pneumothorax and hypovolaemia if it does not respond
  • Sedation-related delirium, ICU-acquired weakness, and pressure/VTE risk from immobility
🔽 Getting off the ventilator
  • Weaning starts the day it begins — every day of unnecessary ventilation adds risk
  • Daily sedation hold, then a spontaneous breathing trial on minimal support to test whether they can do the work themselves
  • Extubate when the cause is improving, oxygenation is adequate on low settings, they are awake enough to protect the airway, and can cough
  • Tracheostomy if ventilation is prolonged or weaning repeatedly fails — easier weaning, less sedation, better mouth care
  • Watch for post-extubation stridor from laryngeal oedema, and the risk of reintubation
ECMO — The Top Rung
  • Blood removed → oxygenated + CO₂ removed → returned
  • Specialist ECMO centres only
  • Reversible respiratory failure only
  • Bridge to recovery / transplant
Indicated when all other measures have failed and the underlying cause is potentially reversible (e.g. severe ARDS, viral pneumonitis). Not a long-term solution.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Oxygen is a drug: prescribe it to a target range on the drug chart, not a fixed flow. In an emergency give it first and prescribe after.
O₂ raises CO₂ mainly via V/Q mismatch (losing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), not by switching off hypoxic drive. Never withhold O₂ from a hypoxic patient — use a controlled device.
SpO₂ lies in CO poisoning (reads normal/high), poor perfusion, methaemoglobinaemia and darker skin (overestimates). It never tells you the CO₂ — get an ABG.
Repeat the ABG ~1 hour after starting NIV. Not improving, or getting drowsy → failing. If the CO₂ is not falling, raise the iPAP, not the FiO₂.
Untreated pneumothorax contraindicates NIV — positive pressure can tension it. Drain first. Also: vomiting, facial trauma, and no airway protection.
Hypotension straight after intubation = positive pressure reducing venous return and preload. Ventilator harms: VAP, barotrauma, and this.
O₂ targets: 94–98% most patients · 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD and similar) via a 24–28% Venturi · 15L NRB for critically ill
Venturi = fixed/precise FiO₂ (the fixed-performance standard mask) → use in COPD. Cannula/mask/NRB = variable performance.
CPAP = Type 1 RF (oxygenation — pulmonary oedema, OSA). BiPAP = Type 2 RF (ventilation — COPD + hypercapnia).
BiPAP in COPD: use when pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa despite optimal medical therapy. pH <7.25 → still NIV, but delivered at HDU/ICU level with immediate access to intubation and a documented escalation plan — it predicts NIV failure, it does not contraindicate NIV. pH ≥7.35 → medical treatment first and repeat the gas.
PEEP = prevents alveolar collapse, recruits lung, improves oxygenation. Added by HFNC, CPAP/BiPAP, and mechanical ventilator.
In COPD exacerbation: drive nebulisers with air not O₂ (avoids worsening hypercapnia)
Escalation ladder: O₂ → HFNC → NIV → mechanical ventilation → ECMO — but the rung is chosen by the clinical problem, not climbed in order: a COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis goes straight to BiPAP, and a patient who cannot protect their airway straight to intubation.
ECMO = reversible failure only, specialist centres. Not a long-term solution — bridge to recovery or transplant.
RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Failure & ARDS:
Respiratory failure = the lungs fail to oxygenate and/or remove CO₂, defined on ABG. The central fork: Type 1 (oxygenation failure) vs Type 2 (ventilation failure) — drives the cause, the management, and which form of non-invasive support to use.
Type 1 vs Type 2 — The Spine
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram contrasting Type 1 (oxygenation failure — ↓PaO₂, normal CO₂ → CPAP) and Type 2 (ventilation failure — ↓PaO₂ + ↑PaCO₂ → BiPAP) respiratory failure with example causes.
Type 1Type 2
Definition ↓PaO₂ (<8 kPa), normal or low CO₂ ↓PaO₂ + ↑PaCO₂ (>6 kPa)
Problem Oxygenation failure (V/Q mismatch — blood not oxygenated) Ventilation failure (can't blow off CO₂)
Causes Pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, asthma (early), ILD COPD (commonest), severe asthma (late/tiring), neuromuscular disease (GBS, MND), opiates, obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OSA alone does not cause type 2 failure — it is the daytime hypoventilation that does), chest wall deformity
Non-invasive support CPAP (splints alveoli open and improves oxygenation — it does not ventilate, so it is not strictly NIV) BiPAP — the true NIV (actively ventilates, ↓CO₂)
O₂ target 94–98% — unless also at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall or neuromuscular disease), when 88–92% still applies. The risk sets the target, not the failure type (BTS) 88–92% (controlled — avoid worsening hypercapnia)
⚠️ Neuromuscular Type 2 failure does not announce itself on the blood gas. In GBS, myasthenia and MND the patient ventilates adequately until the muscles abruptly fail, so a normal ABG is falsely reassuring and hypoxia and hypercapnia are late signs. Monitor with serial FVC, not gases, and escalate on a falling trend (the 20/30/40 rule is covered in the Guillain-Barré syndrome note).
The tie-in rule: Type 1 → CPAP (oxygenation problem)  |  Type 2 → BiPAP (ventilation problem). Neither is safe in an undrained pneumothorax — drain it first (BTS/ICS). Cross-ref respiratory support notes.
The Danger Sign — Tiring Type 1
Type 1 RF — ↓PaO₂, low/normal CO₂ (hyperventilating to compensate)
↓
Patient tires → respiratory muscles fail → can no longer hyperventilate
↓
CO₂ starts to rise → normal or rising CO₂ = danger signal
↓
Progresses to Type 2 RF → exhaustion → arrest
In acute asthma: a normal PCO₂ = life-threatening (patient should be blowing off CO₂; normalisation = exhaustion). Cross-ref asthma management.
Clinical Features
Hypoxia (both types)
  • Dyspnoea
  • Tachypnoea
  • cyanosis
  • Confusion/agitation
  • Tachycardia
  • Use of accessory muscles
Hypercapnia (Type 2 specific)
  • CO₂ retention flap (asterixis — outstretched hands)
  • Bounding pulse
  • Warm peripheries (vasodilation)
  • Headache
  • Drowsiness → coma ("CO₂ narcosis")
Management Principles
Type 1 — Oxygenation
  • Oxygen titrated to target — 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. If critically ill, start with a reservoir mask at 15 L/min and titrate down as soon as saturations are reliable. Oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness — do not give it to a normoxic patient (BTS)
  • CPAP if not responding
  • Treat the cause (e.g. antibiotics for pneumonia, diurese pulmonary oedema)
  • Consider HFNC
  • Escalate to critical care if oxygenation cannot be maintained on CPAP or HFNC, or the patient is tiring — intubation is the next step unless a ceiling of care has been agreed
Type 2 — Ventilation
  • Controlled O₂ (88–92%)
  • BiPAP (NIV) for respiratory acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy (pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6 kPa) — pH 7.25–7.35 is the band usually managed on a respiratory ward
  • Treat the cause (bronchodilators for COPD, reverse opiates with naloxone)
  • pH <7.25 does not rule NIV out — it predicts a higher chance of NIV failure, so NIV is delivered in HDU/ICU with a documented escalation plan. Intubate if NIV fails, is contraindicated, or the patient deteriorates — unless NIV has been agreed as the ceiling of care
ARDS = severe Type 1 respiratory failure caused by increased alveolar-capillary permeability → protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → atelectasis, ↓compliance, refractory hypoxia. The heart is fine — the capillaries are leaky.
Aetiology — The Inflammatory Insults
Direct (pulmonary)Indirect (extra-pulmonary)
  • Pneumonia
  • Aspiration of gastric contents
  • COVID-19
  • Sepsis (commonest overall)
  • Massive transfusion (TRALI)
  • Major trauma / burns
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass
Unifying theme: a massive inflammatory insult (pulmonary or systemic) → diffuse alveolar damage → capillary leak → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Clinical Features
  • Acute severe dyspnoea
  • Tachypnoea
  • Refractory hypoxia (doesn't correct with O₂)
  • Bilateral fine crackles
  • Low SpO₂ despite high FiO₂
Refractory hypoxia = hallmark of ARDS — hypoxia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen alone (distinguishes from most other causes of Type 1 RF).
🧠 Why it is refractory — the word is doing real work. Flooded alveoli are perfused but not ventilated: that is a right-to-left intrapulmonary shunt. Shunted blood never meets alveolar gas, so raising the FiO₂ cannot oxygenate it — you can only enrich the blood passing alveoli that still work. That is the difference from ordinary V/Q mismatch, which does respond to oxygen.
  • It explains the entire management strategy: if oxygen cannot fix a shunt, you have to re-open the alveoli — hence PEEP and prone positioning, which recruit lung rather than adding oxygen
  • It also explains why chasing a normal saturation with ever-higher FiO₂ is futile — it buys oxygen toxicity, not oxygenation
(Shunt vs V/Q mismatch is covered in Foundations of the Respiratory System.)
Berlin Criteria — Diagnostic Definition
📷 Image placeholder — CXR of ARDS — diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates ("white-out") with air bronchograms, not explained by effusion or cardiac failure.
1. Acute Onset
  • Within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms
2. Bilateral Infiltrates
  • CXR or CT — bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, lobar collapse, or nodules
  • Resembles pulmonary oedema + air bronchograms
3. Non-Cardiogenic
  • Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
  • Echo or wedge pressure if doubt
  • See the comparison table below
4. PaO₂/FiO₂ Ratio ≤300 mmHg (≤40 kPa)
  • Mild: >200 to ≤300 mmHg, Moderate: >100 to ≤200 mmHg, Severe: ≤100 mmHg
  • Lower ratio = worse disease
  • Measured with PEEP or CPAP ≥5 cmH₂O
2023 update: a new global definition of ARDS broadened the Berlin criteria to include patients on high-flow nasal oxygen (≥30 L/min) and to allow SpO₂/FiO₂ (≤315) — valid only when the SpO₂ is 97% or below — and ultrasound where ABGs/CT are unavailable — recognising ARDS earlier and in non-intubated/resource-limited settings. Berlin remains the classic exam definition.
⚖️ ARDS vs cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — the distinction criterion 3 actually asks you to make. Both give a breathless patient with bilateral infiltrates and crackles, and the treatments pull in opposite directions: the cardiogenic patient needs offloading with diuretics; the ARDS patient needs the cause treated and lung-protective ventilation. Diuresing a septic ARDS patient into hypoperfusion does harm.
ARDSCardiogenic pulmonary oedema
MechanismLeaky capillaries — protein-rich exudateHigh hydrostatic pressure — protein-poor transudate
HistoryA preceding insult — sepsis, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, transfusionCardiac history, ischaemic chest pain, arrhythmia, fluid overload, missed dialysis
ExaminationJVP normal or low; peripheries often warm (sepsis); no gallopRaised JVP, S3 gallop, peripheral oedema, cool peripheries
CXRPeripheral, patchy, bilateral infiltrates; normal heart size; effusions uncommonCardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, perihilar “bat’s wing”, effusions
BNP / NT-proBNPTypically low — a low BNP argues against a cardiac causeRaised
EchoGood LV function, normal filling pressuresImpaired LV function and/or raised filling pressures
Response to diuresisLittle improvement in oxygenation; risk of hypoperfusionImproves, often quickly
⚠️ They can coexist. A septic patient with poor ventricles can have both — and criterion 3 says the failure must not be fully explained by cardiac failure, not that the heart must be normal. Echo is the practical arbiter; the pulmonary artery wedge pressure is now largely historical.
Management — Supportive (No Specific Cure)
📷 Image placeholder — Prone positioning in ventilated ARDS — improved dorsal lung recruitment and V/Q matching; and a lung-protective ventilation schematic (low tidal volume + PEEP).
Treat the Cause
  • Antibiotics for sepsis/pneumonia, amylase monitoring for pancreatitis, stop offending transfusion (TRALI)
  • Treating the cause addresses the underlying disease process — but it is not the only thing that changes outcome: lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning in moderate-to-severe ARDS and corticosteroids in some ARDS all carry a mortality benefit
Lung-Protective Ventilation
  • Low tidal volume (~6 mL/kg predicted body weight) — PBW is calculated from height and sex, not actual weight; avoids volutrauma
  • Plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O — the pressure limit that goes with the volume limit; if it exceeds 30, reduce the tidal volume further
  • Adequate PEEP — prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening (atelectrauma)
  • Permissive hypercapnia acceptable — tolerate a high CO₂ and low pH rather than injure the lung to normalise them
Prone Positioning
  • 12–16 hours/day — promotes uniform lung inflation, ↓dorsal atelectasis, improves V/Q matching
  • Mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS — in practice a P/F ratio below 150 mmHg (20 kPa) (ICS)
Supportive / ITU
  • Corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone) have a mortality benefit in some ARDS (including COVID-19 ARDS)
  • Conservative fluid balance (avoid further oedema)
  • Vasopressors
  • Renal support
  • ECMO if refractory
  • High mortality (30–60%)
📏 Low volumes and low pressures — two halves of the same idea. ARDS lungs are small, not uniformly stiff: the aerated volume left is child-sized (the “baby lung”), so a normal tidal volume over-distends it. ARDSNet showed 6 mL/kg versus 12 mL/kg cut mortality from ~40% to ~31% — one of the few things in ARDS that changes outcome.
  • Plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O is the safety ceiling. It is measured at an inspiratory pause and reflects alveolar pressure, unlike peak pressure, which also includes airway resistance
  • These limits are why permissive hypercapnia is accepted: protect the lung and let the CO₂ ride
After ARDS — What Happens to Survivors
The note quotes a mortality of 30–60%. The other half of that statistic is that most survivors do not simply return to normal — and the lungs usually recover better than the patient does. The lasting disability is typically neuromuscular and psychological rather than respiratory.
🫁 The lungs mostly recover
  • Lung function improves over 6–12 months and is often near-normal by a year
  • A reduced transfer factor (TLCO) is the commonest persisting abnormality
  • Some are left with fibrotic change on CT, more likely after prolonged high-pressure ventilation
💪 The body often does not
  • ICU-acquired weakness — profound proximal weakness from critical illness myopathy and neuropathy
  • Marked fatigue and exercise limitation outlasting the lung recovery, often for years
  • Weight loss, deconditioning, and difficulty returning to work
🧠 Post-intensive care syndrome
  • New or worsened cognitive impairment — memory, attention, executive function
  • Anxiety, depression and PTSD — the last strongly linked to delirium and to delusional ICU memories
  • Affects families and carers too (PICS-F)
  • Follow-up, rehabilitation and explanation matter — survivors are often discharged with no idea why they feel like this
⭐ Exam Pearls
Refractory hypoxia = shunt — flooded alveoli are perfused but not ventilated, so more FiO₂ cannot fix it. You have to recruit lung: PEEP and proning.
Plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O goes with 6 mL/kg — a volume limit and a pressure limit.
ARDS vs cardiogenic oedema: normal JVP, no gallop, normal heart size, low BNP, good LV on echo — and it does not improve with diuresis.
Neuromuscular Type 2 failure: monitor FVC, not the ABG. In GBS/MND hypoxia and hypercapnia are late — a normal gas is falsely reassuring.
ARDS survivors: lungs largely recover by a year (↓TLCO the commonest residue); the lasting problems are ICU-acquired weakness, fatigue and post-intensive care syndrome.
Type 1 = hypoxia alone (oxygenation failure, normal/low CO₂) → CPAP. Type 2 = hypoxia + ↑CO₂ (ventilation failure) → BiPAP.
Tiring Type 1 → rising CO₂ = danger sign (exhaustion). Normal CO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening.
88–92% is the target for anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall or neuromuscular disease) — the risk sets the target, and the ABG then confirms or releases it — if the PaCO₂ is normal, move to 94–98%, unless there is a history of hypercapnic respiratory failure that needed NIV or ventilation, when 88–92% stays. Recheck the gas after 30–60 minutes. Everyone else: 94–98%. Never give high O₂ freely to CO₂ retainers.
CO₂ retention flap (asterixis) = hypercapnia. Bounding pulse + warm peripheries = vasodilation from ↑CO₂.
ARDS = non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — leaky capillaries, heart is fine. Severe Type 1 RF.
Berlin criteria: acute (<1 wk) + bilateral infiltrates + non-cardiogenic + PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤300 mmHg
ARDS causes: sepsis/pneumonia (commonest), pancreatitis, aspiration, TRALI, trauma
ARDS Rx: low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) + PEEP + prone positioning; treat cause; ITU. No specific cure.
Refractory hypoxia = ARDS hallmark. Doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ alone.
Prone positioning: 12–16h/day — mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS (improved V/Q, ↓dorsal atelectasis)
RESPIRATORY__Upper Respiratory Tract Epi:
Overview — Respiratory Epithelium

The conducting airway (nose, sinuses, pharynx, larynx and — strictly lower tract — trachea/bronchi) is lined mostly by respiratory epithelium — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (often abbreviated PCCE). Its job is to condition inspired air (warm, humidify, filter) and to run the mucociliary escalator that clears trapped debris.

🔬 Image slot — respiratory epithelium — pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells on a thick basement membrane
Where it is found
  • Respiratory epithelium (PCCE): most of the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx (below the vocal cords), trachea and bronchi.
  • Stratified squamous where there is abrasion/airflow stress: nasal vestibule (keratinised), oropharynx, and the true vocal cords.
  • Olfactory epithelium (specialised) in the roof of the nasal cavity.
“Respiratory epithelium” and “pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells” are the same thing — the exam-classic lining of the conducting airways.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power respiratory epithelium showing cilia, goblet cells and nuclei at different levels
  • Pseudostratified — every cell touches the basement membrane, but the nuclei sit at different levels, giving a false impression of layering.
  • Cilia form a fuzzy pink border on the apical surface (taller than microvilli).
  • Goblet cells — pale/clear, cup-shaped, mucin at the top and the nucleus squashed to the base.
  • A characteristically thick (hyaline) basement membrane below the epithelium.
  • Underlying lamina propria is vascular with seromucous glands.
Pseudostratified vs truly stratified: if you can trace every cell down to the basement membrane it is pseudostratified; in true stratified epithelium the surface cells do not reach it.
The Cell Types of Respiratory Epithelium
CellFeature & role
Ciliated columnarMost numerous; ~200–300 cilia each; drive the mucociliary escalator toward the pharynx
Goblet cellUnicellular gland; secretes mucins (the gel layer of mucus); PAS/Alcian-blue positive
Basal cellStem/reserve cell sitting on the basement membrane; regenerates the other cell types (does not reach the surface)
Brush cellColumnar cell with blunt microvilli; a sensory receptor with a nerve ending at its base (chemosensory)
Small granule (neuroendocrine / Kulchitsky) cellPart of the DNES; contains dense-core granules (serotonin, bombesin); origin of carcinoid / small-cell carcinoma
The epithelium looks pseudostratified because it contains cells of different heights (short basal, intermediate, tall ciliated/goblet), so nuclei sit at several levels — yet every cell reaches the basement membrane. Basal cells (markers p63/CK5) are the stem cells.
The Mucociliary Escalator
🔬 Image slot — mucociliary escalator — gel + sol (periciliary) layers and the direction of ciliary beat
The mucus blanket
  • Sol (periciliary) layer — watery; cilia beat within it
  • Gel layer on top — sticky mucus (goblet cells + glands) that traps particles & microbes
Ciliary beat
  • Fast forward power stroke tips the gel layer toward the pharynx; slow recovery stroke within the sol
  • Mucus is swallowed or expectorated
Cilium ultrastructure
  • “9 + 2” axoneme — nine peripheral microtubule doublets + a central pair.
  • Dynein arms use ATP to slide doublets → bending; anchored by a basal body.
  • Defective dynein → dysmotile cilia (see clinical box).
  • Contrast the non-motile primary cilium (9+0, no central pair/dynein) and stereocilia (long actin microvilli, e.g. epididymis/hair cells).
Regional Epithelia of the Upper Tract
🔬 Image slot — sagittal nasal cavity showing vestibule / respiratory / olfactory regions
RegionEpithelium
Nasal vestibuleStratified squamous keratinised + hairs (vibrissae) & sebaceous glands
Respiratory region (most of nasal cavity, sinuses, nasopharynx, trachea, bronchi)Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
Olfactory region (roof)Specialised olfactory epithelium (bipolar receptor neurons continuously replaced from basal stem cells, sustentacular, basal; Bowman’s glands secrete serous fluid dissolving odorants)
Oropharynx & true vocal cordsStratified squamous non-keratinised (abrasion) — but the false (vestibular) cords above are respiratory PCCE (a squamous “sandwich”)
EpiglottisSquamous on the lingual/upper surface → respiratory on the lower
The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous epithelium to withstand vibration — a favourite exam contrast with the respiratory epithelium above and below them.
Lamina Propria & Air-Conditioning
  • Seromucous glands in the lamina propria/submucosa add watery & mucous secretion — humidification.
  • Rich venous plexuses / swell bodies in the nasal conchae warm the air and cause the alternating nasal cycle (and blockage in rhinitis).
  • Vibrissae and the mucus blanket filter particles.
  • Waldeyer’s ring (pharyngeal/palatine/tubal/lingual tonsils) — MALT; the adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil) is uniquely covered by respiratory PCCE (vs squamous palatine/lingual tonsils). Dimeric IgA is secreted into mucus via the poly-Ig receptor.
Three functions to remember for the nose: warm, humidify, filter — delivered by vasculature, glands and the mucociliary blanket respectively.
Stains
  • H&E — cilia, goblet cells and the thick basement membrane.
  • PAS / Alcian blue — goblet-cell & gland mucins (magenta / blue); highlights goblet-cell density.
  • Immunohistochemistry — chromogranin / synaptophysin for neuroendocrine (small granule) cells; cytokeratins for epithelial tumours.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Squamous metaplasia
Smoking replaces ciliated/goblet epithelium with stratified squamous → loss of clearance; a step toward dysplasia & SCC
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect → dysmotile cilia (dx: low nasal NO). Kartagener triad = situs inversus + sinusitis + bronchiectasis (+ infertility in PCD).
Allergic rhinitis
Type I hypersensitivity → oedema, eosinophils, goblet-cell & gland hypersecretion
Nasal polyps
Oedematous inflamed respiratory mucosa; Samter’s triad/AERD (asthma + polyps + aspirin sensitivity); polyps in a child → think CF; unilateral → exclude tumour.
Sinusitis
Impaired drainage/ciliary clearance → infection of sinus respiratory mucosa
Epistaxis
Anterior (Little’s area/Kiesselbach, ~90%) — pinch/cautery; posterior (sphenopalatine/Woodruff’s, older/anticoagulated) — packing/ligation.
Nasopharyngeal / laryngeal carcinoma
NPC: undifferentiated SCC, EBV, endemic S. Chinese, neck node. Laryngeal SCC: smoking+alcohol, glottic → early hoarseness.
Other sinonasal lesions
Inverted papilloma (unilateral, ~10% → SCC), esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory), juvenile angiofibroma (teen males, epistaxis), GPA → saddle nose.
Metaplasia is adaptive but costly: squamous cells resist smoke but cannot clear mucus, so smokers accumulate secretions and infections — and squamous change can progress to carcinoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells. Every cell touches the basement membrane.
Five cell types: ciliated (most), goblet, basal (stem), brush (sensory microvilli), small-granule/neuroendocrine.
Basal cells are the stem cells and the reason it looks “stratified”.
Cilia have a 9 + 2 axoneme moved by dynein; the escalator sweeps mucus to the pharynx.
True vocal cords & oropharynx = stratified squamous (abrasion); nasal vestibule = keratinised squamous.
Nose functions: warm (venous plexus), humidify (glands), filter (vibrissae + mucus).
Smoking → squamous metaplasia → lost clearance → dysplasia/SCC.
Kartagener (dynein defect): situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis + infertility.
RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronchioles:
Overview — The Conducting Tree

Below the trachea the airway branches repeatedly, and its wall changes in a predictable, graded way at each level. Knowing the trend lets you place any airway on a slide.

🔬 Image slot — airway tree — trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal → respiratory bronchiole
1
BronchiMain → lobar → segmental; have cartilage plates + glands
2
Bronchioles≤1 mm; no cartilage, no glands; prominent smooth muscle
3
Terminal bronchioleLast purely conducting airway; club cells; no goblet cells
4
Respiratory bronchioleWall interrupted by alveoli → gas exchange begins
The four trends going distal: epithelium gets shorter (columnar → cuboidal), cartilage & glands disappear, goblet cells disappear, and smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent.
How to Place an Airway on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — side-by-side bronchus (cartilage + glands) vs bronchiole (no cartilage, thick smooth muscle)
It is a BRONCHUS if…
  • Cartilage plates in the wall
  • Submucosal seromucous glands
  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
  • A discrete band of smooth muscle between mucosa & cartilage
It is a BRONCHIOLE if…
  • No cartilage, no glands
  • Smooth muscle looks relatively thick for the wall
  • Epithelium simple ciliated columnar → cuboidal; club cells; few/no goblet cells
  • Often a folded (scalloped) lumen from muscle contraction
The single best discriminator: cartilage & glands = bronchus; their absence = bronchiole.
Bronchi — Wall Layers
🔬 Image slot — bronchus cross-section — mucosa, smooth-muscle band, seromucous glands, cartilage plate
LayerFeatures
MucosaPseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells; thin lamina propria rich in elastic fibres
MuscularisContinuous spiral band of smooth muscle (separates mucosa from submucosa — more prominent than in the trachea)
SubmucosaSeromucous glands (mucus for the escalator)
CartilageIrregular plates/islands of hyaline cartilage (replace the C-shaped tracheal rings) — keep the airway patent
AdventitiaFibroelastic CT binding the bronchus to lung parenchyma; carries vessels & nerves
As bronchi enter the lung the ring cartilage of the trachea breaks into plates that encircle the now-intrapulmonary airway, and a complete smooth-muscle layer appears.
Bronchioles — Muscle Without Cartilage
🔬 Image slot — bronchiole — simple columnar/cuboidal epithelium over a prominent smooth-muscle layer, no cartilage
  • ≤1 mm diameter; no cartilage, no glands, no goblet cells in the terminal bronchiole.
  • Epithelium: simple ciliated columnar proximally → simple cuboidal (often ciliated) distally.
  • Relatively thick smooth-muscle layer (Reisseissen’s muscle) — controls airway calibre and, because there is no cartilage to splint them open, bronchioles are the airways that collapse/constrict in asthma.
  • Held open by radial traction (elastic recoil of the surrounding alveoli), not by cartilage.
  • Terminal bronchiole = the last conducting airway; each supplies one pulmonary acinus (a secondary pulmonary lobule = the septum-bounded HRCT unit fed by 3–5 terminal bronchioles).
Because their patency depends on smooth-muscle tone and elastic traction rather than cartilage, small airways are the critical site of obstruction in asthma and COPD.
Club (Clara) Cells
🔬 Image slot — club (Clara) cell — dome-shaped non-ciliated cell bulging into the bronchiolar lumen
  • Dome-shaped, non-ciliated cells that bulge into the lumen; increase in number distally.
  • Secrete a surfactant-like material & club-cell secretory protein (CC16) → reduce surface tension & protect the small-airway lining.
  • Detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via cytochrome P450.
  • Act as progenitor (stem) cells that regenerate bronchiolar epithelium.
Think of the club cell as the bronchiolar all-rounder: serous secretion (no mucin) + detoxification + stem cell — the small-airway counterpart of the goblet cell (which it replaces). Goblet-cell metaplasia can still appear in bronchioles in smokers/asthma.
Neuroepithelial bodies = innervated clusters of pulmonary neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells at bronchiolar bifurcations — hypoxia chemoreceptors (serotonin/bombesin); the origin of carcinoid & small-cell carcinoma.
Level-by-Level Comparison
FeatureBronchusBronchioleTerminal bronchioleRespiratory bronchiole
EpitheliumPCC + gobletCiliated columnar→cuboidalCiliated cuboidal + clubCuboidal, interrupted by alveoli
CartilageYes (plates)NoNoNo
GlandsYesNoNoNo
Goblet cellsYesFew→noneNoneNone
Smooth musclePresentProminentPresentBands between alveoli
Club cellsNoYesYes (many)Yes
Gas exchange?NoNoNo (last conducting)Yes (first respiratory)
Respiratory Bronchiole — the Hand-off
  • The first airway where gas exchange occurs: its cuboidal wall is interrupted by scattered alveoli.
  • Leads on to alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli (covered in the alveoli note).
  • Everything from the respiratory bronchiole distal to one terminal bronchiole = the pulmonary acinus, the functional gas-exchange unit.
Boundary to memorise: the terminal bronchiole ends the conducting zone; the respiratory bronchiole begins the respiratory zone.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Asthma
Smooth-muscle hyperplasia & hypertrophy, bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, eosinophils, subepithelial BM fibrosis & goblet metaplasia; Curschmann spirals + Charcot–Leyden crystals. Reversible; atopic/IgE; beware ABPA.
Chronic bronchitis
Clinical: productive cough ≥3 months/yr for ≥2 yrs. Histology: gland hypertrophy (↑Reid index >0.4) + goblet-cell hyperplasia.
Bronchiectasis
Permanent bronchial dilatation (destroyed muscle/cartilage). Causes: post-infective, CF, PCD, obstruction, ABPA. CT: signet-ring & tram-track.
Bronchiolitis
RSV in infants. Constrictive/obliterative (irreversible fibrosis — transplant rejection, RA, fumes) vs organising pneumonia (BOOP, intraluminal Masson bodies, steroid-responsive).
COPD / emphysema
Small-airway remodelling; lost radial traction → expiratory collapse (equal-pressure point). Centriacinar (smoking, upper) vs panacinar (α1-antitrypsin def, lower + liver).
Carcinoid / small-cell carcinoma
From neuroendocrine cells. Carcinoid: low-grade, chromogranin+, better prognosis. Small-cell: central, smoking, aggressive, paraneoplastic (SIADH, ACTH, Lambert–Eaton).
Reid index = gland thickness ÷ total wall thickness (bronchus). It is increased (>0.4) in chronic bronchitis — a classic histological measure of gland hypertrophy.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cartilage + glands = bronchus; neither = bronchiole. The one distinction that answers most questions.
Going distal: epithelium shortens, cartilage/glands/goblet cells disappear, smooth muscle becomes relatively prominent.
Terminal bronchiole = last conducting airway; respiratory bronchiole = first gas exchange (alveoli in the wall).
Club (Clara) cells replace goblet cells distally: secretion + P450 detox + stem cell.
Bronchioles have no cartilage → held open by elastic radial traction; they collapse/constrict in asthma & COPD.
The acinus (distal to one terminal bronchiole) is the gas-exchange unit; the secondary lobule (HRCT unit) is fed by several (3–5) terminal bronchioles.
Chronic bronchitis = ↑ Reid index (gland hypertrophy); asthma = smooth-muscle hypertrophy + mucus + eosinophils.
Bronchial neuroendocrine cells → carcinoid / small-cell carcinoma.
RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-Air Barrier:
Overview — The Gas-Exchange Surface

Alveoli are the thin-walled air sacs where gas is exchanged. There are ~300 million of them, giving a total surface area of ~70 m² — the whole design is built to make diffusion large in area and short in distance.

🔬 Image slot — lung parenchyma at low power — thin-walled alveoli opening off alveolar ducts & sacs
  • Alveoli open off respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs.
  • Adjacent alveoli share an interalveolar septum containing the capillary network.
  • Gas exchange obeys Fick’s law: rate ∝ (area × Δpressure) ÷ thickness — so the barrier is kept huge and thin.
Everything about the alveolus is optimised for diffusion: a massive surface area, an ultra-thin (~0.2 µm) blood–air barrier, and a dense capillary bed.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — interalveolar septum — flat type I pneumocytes, plump type II cells, septal capillary with RBCs
  • Empty, thin-walled air spaces separated by delicate septa.
  • Septa contain capillaries packed with red cells — the pink profiles in the wall.
  • Type I pneumocytes — you mostly see their flat nuclei bulging into the space (cytoplasm too thin to resolve).
  • Type II pneumocytes — rounded, cuboidal cells at septal corners, with foamy/vacuolated cytoplasm.
  • Alveolar macrophages — large cells free in the airspace, often with brown/black particulate.
On routine H&E you usually identify type I cells only by their nuclei; the gas-exchange cytoplasm is below the resolution of the light microscope.
The Interalveolar Septum
ComponentRole
Type I pneumocyteSimple squamous; covers ~95% of surface; the gas-exchange cell; cannot divide
Type II pneumocyteCuboidal; surfactant (lamellar bodies); stem cell for both types; ~5% of area but more numerous
Capillary endotheliumContinuous endothelium of the dense septal capillary network
Fused basement membranesPneumocyte & endothelial basal laminae fuse on the thin (exchange) side
InterstitiumElastic + collagen fibres + fibroblasts (thick side) — elastic recoil for expiration
Alveolar macrophage (dust cell)Fetal-derived, self-renewing tissue-resident (monocytes recruited only in inflammation); patrols airspace & interstitium
The septum has a thin side (fused basement membranes → efficient gas exchange) and a thick side (interstitium with fluid/elastic → structural support & fluid handling).
The Blood–Air Barrier
🔬 Image slot — blood-air barrier ultrastructure (EM) — type I pneumocyte, fused basal lamina, capillary endothelium

To reach haemoglobin, oxygen crosses just three thin layers (total ~0.2–0.5 µm):

1
Type I pneumocyte+ surfactant film lining the alveolus
2
Fused basement membranePneumocyte & endothelial basal laminae fused
3
Capillary endotheliumThen plasma → RBC membrane → haemoglobin
Anything that thickens this barrier (oedema, fibrosis, hyaline membrane) or reduces its area (emphysema) lowers the DLCO (transfer factor). CO is diffusion-limited (basis of DLCO); O₂ is normally perfusion-limited but becomes diffusion-limited when the barrier thickens or in exercise. Alveolar hypoxia triggers hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction to preserve V/Q (chronic → pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale).
Type I vs Type II Pneumocytes
Type I (membranous)
  • Simple squamous, extremely thin
  • ~95% of surface area, ~40% of cell number
  • The gas-exchange cell; type I and type II are joined by tight junctions (barrier integrity)
  • Cannot divide — if killed, replaced by type II
Type II (granular)
  • Cuboidal, at septal corners; lamellar bodies
  • ~5% of area, ~60% of cell number
  • Make & secrete surfactant
  • Stem cell — regenerate type I and type II
Full detail is in the dedicated Type I & II Pneumocytes note — here, remember: I = thin gas exchange, II = surfactant + repair.
Surfactant — Keeping Alveoli Open
  • A phospholipid–protein film (chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC, + surfactant proteins A–D) made by type II cells and stored in lamellar bodies.
  • Lowers surface tension at the air–liquid interface → prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at end-expiration and reduces the work of breathing.
  • Laplace’s law (P = 2T/r): small alveoli would empty into large ones; surfactant lowers T more in small alveoli → keeps them stable.
  • Appears ~24 weeks, adequate by ~35 weeks. Fetal maturity: amniotic lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio >2 + phosphatidylglycerol. Accelerated by antenatal steroids/stress; delayed by maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia).
  • ~90% of surfactant is recycled by type II cells (the rest cleared by macrophages).
Surfactant proteins A & D are also innate-immune opsonins (collectins); B & C spread the lipid film.
Alveolar Macrophages & Pores of Kohn
🔬 Image slot — alveolar macrophage (dust cell) free in the airspace; pore of Kohn between adjacent alveoli
Alveolar macrophage (dust cell)
  • Fetal-derived & locally self-renewing (GM-CSF-dependent); phagocytoses dust, microbes & spent surfactant
  • Migrate up the mucociliary escalator or into lymphatics
  • In pulmonary congestion become heart-failure cells (haemosiderin-laden)
Pores of Kohn
  • Small holes connecting adjacent alveoli → collateral air flow
  • Also let macrophages, fluid & infection spread between alveoli
Stains
  • H&E — thin septa, capillaries, pneumocyte nuclei, macrophages; hyaline membranes as glassy pink lining in DAD.
  • Elastic stains (EVG) — the septal elastic network (lost in emphysema).
  • Perls’ Prussian blue — haemosiderin in heart-failure cells (blue).
  • TTF-1 (IHC) — marks type II pneumocytes & lung adenocarcinoma.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Neonatal RDS
Surfactant deficiency (prematurity; worse in maternal diabetes) → atelectasis + hyaline membranes; CXR ground-glass + air bronchograms. Prevent with antenatal maternal steroids; treat with exogenous surfactant + CPAP. Cx: BPD, PDA, IVH, ROP.
ARDS (diffuse alveolar damage)
Type I death, protein-rich exudate, hyaline membranes; hypoxaemia is from intrapulmonary shunt/V-Q mismatch (refractory to O₂, needs PEEP). Sepsis/aspiration/pancreatitis; Berlin P/F ratio; DAD exudative→proliferative→fibrotic.
Emphysema
Septal destruction → loss of surface area & elastic recoil → impaired exchange
Pulmonary oedema
Fluid in the interstitium/airspaces thickens the barrier → impaired diffusion
Pulmonary fibrosis
Septal collagen deposition widens the barrier → restrictive defect, low DLCO
Heart-failure cells
Haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in chronic pulmonary venous congestion
Alveolar proteinosis
Anti-GM-CSF impairs macrophage clearance → alveoli fill with PAS+ lipoproteinaceous surfactant; Rx whole-lung lavage.
Alveolar haemorrhage
Goodpasture (anti-GBM vs the fused basement membrane) & vasculitis; DLCO is raised (alveolar blood binds CO).
Hyaline membranes (glassy eosinophilic alveolar lining of dead cells + plasma protein) are the shared histological signature of ARDS and neonatal RDS.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The blood–air barrier = type I pneumocyte → fused basement membrane → capillary endothelium (~0.2–0.5 µm).
Type I = 95% of surface, gas exchange, can’t divide; Type II = surfactant + stem cell (regenerate type I).
Surfactant (DPPC, from type II lamellar bodies) lowers surface tension → prevents atelectasis; adequate by ~35 weeks.
By Laplace, surfactant stabilises small alveoli so they don’t empty into large ones.
Hyaline membranes = ARDS & neonatal RDS; both involve barrier injury.
Dust cells = alveolar macrophages; haemosiderin-laden ones = heart-failure cells (Perls’ positive).
Pores of Kohn allow collateral airflow — and spread of infection/exudate.
Barrier disease: thicken it (oedema/fibrosis) or lose area (emphysema) → hypoxaemia.
RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneumocytes:
Overview — Two Cells, One Lining

The alveolar surface is lined by a continuous epithelial sheet of just two cells, sealed by tight junctions that keep the alveolus dry:

🔬 Image slot — type I (flat, squamous) vs type II (cuboidal, granular) pneumocytes side by side in an alveolar wall
Type I — the surface
  • Thin squamous cell for gas exchange
  • Covers most of the area; terminally differentiated
Type II — the caretaker
  • Surfactant, fluid clearance, defence
  • The alveolar stem cell — repairs the lining
One-line division of labour: Type I = thin gas-exchange surface; Type II = surfactant + stem cell + housekeeping.
How to Recognise Each ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power alveolar wall labelling a flat type I nucleus vs a cuboidal foamy type II cell at the corner
Type I
  • Only the flattened nucleus is visible, bulging into the airspace
  • Cytoplasm too thin (~0.1–0.2 µm) to resolve on light microscopy
  • Lines the long, smooth stretches of septum
Type II
  • Rounded / cuboidal, sits in septal corners/niches
  • Foamy, vacuolated cytoplasm (dissolved lamellar-body lipid)
  • Apical surface bulges (“dome”); may look like a fried egg
On EM the diagnosis is easy: type II cells contain lamellar bodies (whorled, osmiophilic) and apical microvilli; type I cells are a thin rim with pinocytotic vesicles.
Type I Pneumocyte (Membranous)
  • Simple squamous; ~95% of alveolar surface but only ~40% of cell number.
  • Extremely attenuated cytoplasm forms the thin side of the blood–air barrier; rich in pinocytotic vesicles & caveolae (fluid/solute handling).
  • Joined to neighbours by occluding tight junctions → a barrier that keeps fluid out of the airspace.
  • Terminally differentiated — essentially cannot divide. When killed it is replaced by a proliferating type II cell (a facultative progenitor) that differentiates into type I.
  • Markers: AQP5 (aquaporin-5), podoplanin (T1α), caveolin-1.
Because it cannot divide and is so thin, the type I cell is the vulnerable cell of the alveolus — the first to die in diffuse alveolar damage.
Type II Pneumocyte (Granular)
🔬 Image slot — type II pneumocyte ultrastructure — apical microvilli, RER/Golgi, lamellar bodies
  • Cuboidal with short apical microvilli (a.k.a. granular/septal/great alveolar cell); ~5% of area but ~60% of cell number (the more numerous cell).
  • Abundant RER & Golgi and the diagnostic lamellar bodies (osmiophilic whorls storing surfactant — lysosome-related organelles; the ABCA3 transporter loads their lipid, and ABCA3 loss causes fatal neonatal surfactant deficiency).
Four jobs
Surfactant — synthesise, secrete & recycle it
Stem cell — self-renew & differentiate into type I (repair)
Fluid clearance — ENaC + Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump fluid out (type I cells also help, covering most of the area)
Defence — secrete innate-immune SP-A/SP-D (xenobiotic P450 detox is mainly the club cell’s job)
Lineage markers: SP-B/SP-C. The diagnostic IHC panel for lung adenocarcinoma is TTF-1 + Napsin A (Napsin A = an aspartic protease) — TTF-1 is negative in squamous (p40/p63+) but positive in small-cell & thyroid, so pair it with Napsin A.
The Surfactant Life-Cycle
🔬 Image slot — surfactant pathway — RER → Golgi → lamellar body → tubular myelin → surface film
1
SynthesisLipid & SP made in RER → Golgi
2
StoragePackaged into lamellar bodies
3
SecretionExocytosis into the alveolar lining fluid
4
Tubular myelinLattice (needs SP-A + SP-B + Ca²⁺) feeds the film
5
Recycle / clearRe-uptaken by type II; excess cleared by macrophages
ComponentRole
DPPC (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine)Main lipid — the surface-tension-lowering molecule (~90% of surfactant is lipid)
SP-A & SP-D (hydrophilic collectins)Innate immunity (opsonisation); SP-A regulates secretion & tubular myelin
SP-B & SP-C (hydrophobic)Spread & stabilise the lipid film; SP-B (with SP-A) forms tubular myelin; SP-B deficiency is lethal in neonates (autosomal recessive)
Injury & Repair
🔬 Image slot — type II hyperplasia lining a damaged alveolus (reparative response)
  • Because type I cells cannot divide, repair depends on type II proliferation → transdifferentiation into type I.
  • Acute injury therefore shows type II (pneumocyte) hyperplasia — a plump cuboidal lining replacing the flat one.
  • Aberrant / repeated repair drives fibrosis (fibroblast recruitment) rather than clean re-epithelialisation.
Reactive type II hyperplasia can mimic malignancy on cytology — a known diagnostic pitfall after ARDS or infection.
Quick Comparison
FeatureType IType II
ShapeSquamous (flat)Cuboidal (with microvilli)
% surface area~95%~5%
% cell number~40%~60%
Main roleGas exchangeSurfactant, repair, fluid clearance, defence
Divide?NoYes (stem cell)
Key organellePinocytotic vesicles / caveolaeLamellar bodies
MarkersAQP5, podoplanin (T1α)SP-B/C, TTF-1, Napsin A
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Neonatal RDS
Immature type II cells → surfactant deficiency → atelectasis + hyaline membranes. Fatal genetic forms: SP-B & ABCA3 (autosomal recessive).
ARDS / diffuse alveolar damage
Type I necrosis → hyaline membranes, then reactive type II hyperplasia in the organising phase
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Repeated AT2 injury/aberrant repair → UIP (fibroblastic foci, temporal heterogeneity, subpleural/basal honeycombing). Familial: SFTPC/telomerase (TERT/TERC), MUC5B. Rx antifibrotics (pirfenidone/nintedanib).
Lung adenocarcinoma
Type II/club-cell lineage; TTF-1 + Napsin A+. Lepidic growth along septa (former BAC) = adenocarcinoma-in-situ — mimics reactive type II hyperplasia. Drivers: EGFR, ALK.
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Defective macrophage clearance (anti-GM-CSF) → alveoli fill with PAS-positive surfactant material
Oxygen toxicity
High FiO₂ → free-radical injury to type I cells → DAD (a cause of ARDS)
Pattern to hold: injury kills the fragile type I cell; the type II cell both cleans up (surfactant, fluid, defence) and rebuilds the lining — and its hyperplasia or dysregulated repair underlies fibrosis and adenocarcinoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Type I = 95% surface, gas exchange, squamous, cannot divide. Type II = 60% of cells, cuboidal, surfactant + stem cell.
Lamellar bodies are the EM signature of the type II cell (store surfactant).
Repair = type II proliferate → transdifferentiate to type I; hence type II hyperplasia marks alveolar injury.
Surfactant is ~90% lipid (DPPC) + SP-A–D; SP-B forms tubular myelin and its deficiency is lethal in neonates.
SP-A/D = innate immunity (collectins); SP-B/C = spread the film.
TTF-1 & Napsin A mark type II cells and lung adenocarcinoma.
Type II cells clear alveolar fluid via ENaC + Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — keeping the alveolus dry.
Alveolar proteinosis = PAS-positive surfactant filling alveoli from defective (anti-GM-CSF) macrophage clearance.
RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & Cilia:
Overview — The Two Partners of Mucociliary Clearance

Airway defence rests on a partnership: goblet cells make the sticky mucus that traps particles, and cilia move it toward the pharynx. Together they form the mucociliary escalator — the airway’s primary innate defence.

🔬 Image slot — respiratory epithelium showing ciliated cells and interspersed goblet cells (the escalator team)
Goblet cell = the flypaper
  • Unicellular gland secreting gel-forming mucins
  • Traps inhaled particles, microbes & irritants
Cilia = the conveyor
  • Motile apical projections
  • Beat in coordinated waves to sweep mucus out
Break either partner and clearance fails: bad cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia) or bad mucus (cystic fibrosis) both cause recurrent infection & bronchiectasis.
How to Recognise Them ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power view — pale cup-shaped goblet cells beside the eosinophilic ciliary fringe
Goblet cell
  • Pale / clear, cup-shaped (“goblet”) profile
  • Apical theca distended with mucin; nucleus squashed to the base
  • PAS-magenta / Alcian-blue positive
Cilia
  • Fuzzy eosinophilic fringe on the apical surface
  • A dark line of basal bodies just beneath (the terminal-web level)
  • Taller than microvilli; motile
Both sit at the apical pole, but the goblet cell is a secretory cell (no cilia) while the ciliated cell carries the motile fringe — they alternate along the epithelium.
Goblet Cell — Structure & Secretion
🔬 Image slot — goblet cell ultrastructure — basal RER/Golgi/nucleus and an apical theca of mucinogen granules
  • A unicellular exocrine gland: narrow base with the nucleus + abundant RER & Golgi, widening into an apical theca packed with mucinogen granules.
  • Secretes gel-forming mucins (chiefly MUC5AC; submucosal glands add MUC5B) by merocrine exocytosis.
  • Mucins are huge glycoproteins that swell 100–1000× on hydration to form the sticky gel layer.
  • Secretion is up-regulated by irritants & inflammation (smoke, infection) → more mucus.
  • Goblet cells are numerous in the trachea/bronchi and disappear by the bronchioles (club cells take over).
The mucus blanket also carries antimicrobials — lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins and secretory IgA (dimeric IgA transcytosed via the poly-Ig receptor → secretory component) — chemical as well as physical defence.
Mucin chemistry: gel-forming/secreted (MUC5AC, MUC5B; gut MUC2) vs membrane-tethered (MUC1/MUC16, glycocalyx/tumour markers). PAS = neutral mucin (magenta); Alcian blue = acid mucin (pH 2.5 sialo+sulfo; pH 1.0 sulfo only). Goblet cells also line the gut (MUC2, depleted in ulcerative colitis).
The Cilium — Axoneme Architecture
🔬 Image slot — cilium cross-section (EM) — 9+2 axoneme with outer & inner dynein arms, radial spokes, nexin
  • “9 + 2” axoneme: nine peripheral doublets (a complete A tubule, 13 protofilaments + an incomplete B tubule) around a central pair (which, with radial spokes, coordinates the planar beat).
  • Dynein arms (outer & inner, ODA/IDA) project from the A tubule — the ATPase motors that drive beating.
  • Radial spokes link doublets to the central sheath; nexin (dynein-regulatory) links tie adjacent doublets together.
  • Anchored by a basal body (nine microtubule triplets, derived from a centriole) with a ciliary rootlet.
  • ~200–300 cilia per cell, each ~5–10 µm long.
Compare the basal body (9 triplets, 9×3, no central pair) with the axoneme (9 doublets + 2, 9×2 + 2) — a classic exam contrast.
Not all cilia are 9+2 motile: the solitary primary cilium is 9+0, non-motile & sensory (renal mechanosensor via polycystin → defect → PKD; also Hedgehog signalling). Embryonic nodal cilia are 9+0 but MOTILE (rotational), setting L–R asymmetry. Cilia are built by intraflagellar transport (kinesin-2 anterograde, dynein-2 retrograde); their disorders = “ciliopathies” (PCD, ADPKD, Bardet–Biedl, nephronophthisis).
How Cilia Beat & Move Mucus
🔬 Image slot — metachronal wave — rows of cilia beating in sequence to sweep the gel layer toward the pharynx
  • Dynein arms walk toward the minus (basal) end of the adjacent B tubule using ATP; because nexin (N-DRC) restrains sliding, the doublets bend instead.
  • Biphasic beat: a fast, stiff power stroke (tip engages the gel layer) then a slow, curled recovery stroke within the watery sol.
  • Neighbouring cilia beat slightly out of phase → a metachronal wave that propels mucus at ~1 cm/min toward the pharynx (frequency ~12–15 Hz).
  • Beating needs a normal periciliary (sol) depth — dehydrated mucus (CF) collapses the cilia and clearance stalls even when the cilia are structurally normal.
Two layers must be right: cilia beat within the watery sol and their tips grip the overlying sticky gel. Get the hydration wrong and the escalator jams.
Cilia vs Microvilli vs Stereocilia
FeatureCiliaMicrovilliStereocilia
CoreMicrotubules (9+2)ActinActin (long microvilli)
Motile?YesNoNo
LengthLong (~5–10 µm)ShortVery long
Main jobMove mucus / fluid↑ absorptive surfaceAbsorption / sensory (epididymis, ear)
MotorDyneinNoneNone
Only cilia are motile and microtubule-based; microvilli & stereocilia are non-motile actin projections (“stereocilia” are misnamed — they are giant microvilli, not cilia).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Autosomal recessive; most often a dynein-arm defect (DNAH5) but also radial-spoke/central-pair/N-DRC → dyskinetic cilia; neonatal distress. Screen low nasal NO; confirm video/EM.
Kartagener syndrome
PCD subset: situs inversus + bronchiectasis + chronic sinusitis (± infertility, otitis media)
Cystic fibrosis
CFTR defect (AR, ΔF508) → dehydrated thick mucus; cilia normal but escalator jams. Sweat chloride >60; infertility = CBAVD (obstructive, not axonemal); CFTR modulators.
Goblet-cell hyperplasia / metaplasia
Chronic irritation (smoking, chronic bronchitis) or asthma (Th2/IL-13-driven) → more/ectopic goblet cells & MUC5AC hypersecretion
Smoking & ciliary loss
Smoke paralyses & strips cilia and triggers squamous metaplasia → impaired clearance, morning cough
Male infertility
The sperm flagellum shares the 9+2 axoneme, so PCD often causes immotile sperm
PCD vs CF vs Young: all give bronchiectasis & sinusitis. PCD = ciliary (motor) defect; CF = mucus (hydration/CFTR) defect with normal cilia; Young syndrome = bronchiectasis + sinusitis + obstructive azoospermia with normal cilia.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Goblet cell = unicellular gland; apical mucin theca, basal nucleus; PAS/Alcian-blue positive; secretes MUC5AC.
Goblet cells are plentiful in trachea/bronchi and absent by the bronchioles (club cells replace them).
Cilium = 9 + 2 axoneme; dynein arms are the ATPase motors; nexin converts sliding into bending.
Basal body = 9 triplets (like a centriole); axoneme = 9 doublets + 2.
Cilia beat with a power + recovery stroke as a metachronal wave (~1 cm/min toward the pharynx).
PCD (Kartagener) = dynein defect → immotile cilia + situs inversus, bronchiectasis, sinusitis, infertility.
CF = normal cilia but dehydrated mucus (CFTR) → escalator jams; contrast with PCD.
Only cilia are motile microtubule (9+2) projections; microvilli/stereocilia are non-motile actin.
RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma:
Overview — Putting the Lung Together

Parenchyma = the functional gas-exchange tissue (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs & alveoli), held in an elastic connective-tissue framework and served by a dual blood supply. This note assembles the individual cells & airways of the earlier notes into the organ.

🔬 Image slot — low-power lung — vast pale airspaces, delicate septa, a bronchovascular bundle and the pleural edge
  • Conducting portion (no exchange): trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles.
  • Respiratory portion / parenchyma (exchange): respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli.
  • Everything is embedded in an elastic stroma and wrapped by the pleura.
Two design themes to carry through: the lung is built for elastic recoil (to drive expiration) and for maximal thin-walled surface area (to drive diffusion).
How to Read Lung Architecture ⭐
🔬 Image slot — bronchovascular bundle — a bronchiole travelling with its accompanying pulmonary artery branch
  • Vast pale airspaces with delicate, capillary-rich septa = alveolar parenchyma.
  • A bronchovascular bundle: an airway always travels with a branch of the pulmonary artery of similar calibre — find one, the other is beside it.
  • Pulmonary veins run alone, out in the interlobular septa (not with the airway).
  • The pleura is the thin mesothelium-covered edge of the section.
  • Scattered black specks = anthracotic (carbon-laden) macrophages.
Artery-with-airway, vein-apart: the pulmonary artery accompanies the bronchus/bronchiole; the pulmonary vein sits at the periphery of the lobule — a reliable orientation clue.
The Organisational Units
UnitDefinitionWhy it matters
AcinusEverything distal to one terminal bronchiole (respiratory bronchioles → alveoli)The functional gas-exchange unit
Secondary lobuleSeptum-bounded unit fed by several (3–5) terminal bronchioles (many acini)Unit of HRCT interpretation; septa carry veins & lymphatics
Bronchopulmonary segmentRegion supplied by a segmental bronchus + its own arterySurgically resectable unit (segmentectomy)
🔬 Image slot — diagram of a pulmonary lobule / bronchopulmonary segment with interlobular septa
Distribution of disease follows these units: centriacinar vs panacinar emphysema; lobar vs lobular (broncho) pneumonia. On HRCT: centrilobular (bronchiole-centred — HP, centriacinar emphysema) vs perilymphatic (septa/pleura — sarcoid, lymphangitic carcinomatosis).
The Pleura
🔬 Image slot — pleura — a single layer of flat mesothelial cells over subserosal elastic connective tissue
  • A serous membrane of simple squamous mesothelium over a thin elastic connective-tissue layer.
  • Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the chest wall; the potential pleural cavity between them holds a film of serous fluid (lubrication).
Visceral pleura
  • Blood: bronchial (+pulmonary); nerves: autonomic → insensate to pain
Parietal pleura
  • Blood: systemic; nerves: somatic (intercostal, phrenic) → pain-sensitive
Pleuritic chest pain comes from the parietal pleura (somatic innervation); the visceral pleura is insensitive — and mesothelium is the cell of origin of mesothelioma (asbestos).
A Dual Blood Supply
🔬 Image slot — dual circulation schematic — pulmonary (gas exchange) vs bronchial (nutritive) vessels
Pulmonary circulation
  • Deoxygenated blood for gas exchange
  • Low pressure, high flow (whole cardiac output)
  • Arteries run with the airways (bronchovascular bundle); veins return in interlobular septa
Bronchial circulation
  • Systemic, oxygenated blood that nourishes airways, vessels & pleura
  • Small, high-pressure branches of the aorta
The lung is unusual: the vessels doing the work (pulmonary) carry deoxygenated blood, while a separate bronchial supply keeps the tissue alive — which is why pulmonary emboli rarely infarct the (dually-supplied) lung unless the bronchial supply is also compromised.
Bronchial arteries supply airways to the respiratory bronchiole; ~half their venous return drains into the pulmonary veins (a normal physiological shunt). When bronchial supply is inadequate (CHF), PE causes a wedge-shaped subpleural haemorrhagic infarct.
Elastic Framework, Interstitium & Lymphatics
  • A continuous elastic-fibre network runs from the pleura through the septa around airways & vessels → provides recoil and holds bronchioles open by radial traction.
  • Interstitium = the connective tissue of the septa: a thin (exchange) side and a thick side with collagen, elastin, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells and occasional lymphocytes.
  • Lymphatics form two plexuses — a superficial (pleural) and a deep (bronchovascular) network — draining to hilar nodes; there are no lymphatics in the alveolar wall itself.
  • BALT (bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue) guards the airways.
Two failure modes of the framework: lose elastin → emphysema (floppy, over-inflated); expand the interstitium with collagen → fibrosis (stiff, restricted).
Stains
  • H&E — overall architecture; airspaces, septa, bronchovascular bundles, pleura.
  • Elastic stains (Verhoeff–van Gieson / orcein) — the elastic framework & pleural elastica; shows destruction in emphysema and helps stage pleural invasion by tumour.
  • Masson trichrome — interstitial collagen / fibrosis (blue) — used in ILD.
  • Calretinin / WT-1 (IHC) — mesothelial markers (mesothelioma vs adenocarcinoma).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Emphysema
Elastin destruction & alveolar-wall loss → permanent airspace enlargement, ↓ recoil (centriacinar = smoking; panacinar = α1-antitrypsin)
Interstitial lung disease
IPF: interstitial collagen → honeycombing (UIP), restrictive, low DLCO. Granulomatous ILD: sarcoid (non-caseating, perilymphatic, ↑ACE) vs TB (caseating, Ghon complex).
Pneumonia
Lobar (S. pneumoniae): congestion → red → grey hepatisation → resolution. Bronchopneumonia (patchy, lobular; Staph/Klebsiella, elderly).
Pneumothorax
Air in the pleural cavity → lung recoils/collapses. Primary (tall thin young males, apical bleb) vs secondary (COPD/CF); tension = emergency (mediastinal shift → needle decompression).
Mesothelioma
Malignancy of pleural mesothelium (asbestos, long latency); calretinin/WT-1/CK5-6/D2-40 positive (adeno: TTF-1/Napsin/MOC-31); BAP1 loss favours malignant.
Pleural effusion
Transudate (CHF, cirrhosis) vs exudate (infection, malignancy) by Light’s criteria (pleural/serum protein >0.5, LDH >0.6).
Anthracosis / pneumoconioses
Anthracosis = harmless carbon. Coal (CWP, PMF), silica (upper-zone nodules, eggshell nodes, ↑TB), asbestos (lower-zone fibrosis, ferruginous bodies, plaques, mesothelioma+lung ca).
Obstructive vs restrictive at the tissue level: emphysema destroys the elastic parenchyma (obstructive, air-trapping); fibrosis stiffens the interstitium (restrictive) — opposite architectural failures.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Parenchyma = gas-exchange tissue (respiratory bronchiole → alveoli); the rest is conducting/stroma.
Bronchovascular bundle: airway travels with the pulmonary artery; the pulmonary vein runs alone in interlobular septa.
Acinus = distal to one terminal bronchiole (gas exchange); lobule (secondary) = several (3–5) terminal bronchioles, septum-bounded (many acini); bronchopulmonary segment = resectable unit.
Pleura = simple squamous mesothelium; parietal pleura is pain-sensitive (somatic), visceral is insensate.
Dual supply: pulmonary (deoxygenated, exchange) + bronchial (systemic, nutritive) — why PE rarely infarcts the lung.
Elastic framework gives recoil; lose elastin → emphysema, expand interstitium with collagen → fibrosis.
No lymphatics in the alveolar wall; two plexuses (pleural + bronchovascular) drain to hilar nodes.
Mesothelioma (asbestos) is calretinin/WT-1 positive; anthracosis = harmless carbon.
RESPIRATORY__Haemoptysis:
Haemoptysis — coughing up blood from the lungs or airways — is a red-flag symptom: cancer, TB and PE until proven otherwise.
  • First confirm it really is haemoptysis — not haematemesis (from the gut) or pseudohaemoptysis (from the nose / mouth).
  • Then the one thing that changes everything — is it massive? Massive haemoptysis is a life-threatening airway emergency.
  • For non-massive bleeding: a chest X-ray then CT chest leads the work-up, with bronchoscopy to localise or treat. For the broader approach when there is no blood, see Cough.
🚨Massive haemoptysis (roughly >200 mL in 24 h, or any bleeding that threatens the airway or the circulation) kills by asphyxiation, not exsanguination — protect the airway, lie the patient with the bleeding side DOWN, correct clotting, and arrange urgent CT angiography and bronchial artery embolisation (± thoracic surgery). Any haemoptysis in a person aged 40 or over needs urgent (2-week-wait) imaging/referral for lung cancer regardless of smoking (smoking and weight loss raise the risk further); and haemoptysis with haematuria is a pulmonary-renal syndrome (vasculitis / Goodpasture) until excluded.

1Characterise it
🩸Is it really haemoptysis?
  • Bright red, frothy, alkaline, mixed with sputum, coughed up → haemoptysis
  • Dark / coffee-ground, acidic, contains food, vomited, ± melaena → haematemesis (upper GI)
  • Blood from the nose, gums or mouth without a cough → pseudohaemoptysis
🚨Massive or non-massive? (this changes everything)
  • Massive: >200 mL / 24 h, or airway / haemodynamic compromise → emergency (resus, side down, embolisation)
  • Non-massive: smaller volume, stable → investigate the source (CXR → CT → bronchoscopy)
🎯The big three to exclude
  • Lung cancer — smoker >40, chronic cough, weight loss, hoarse voice
  • Tuberculosis — night sweats, weight loss, fever, risk factors
  • Pulmonary embolism — pleuritic pain, breathlessness, VTE risk factors
🫁Other airway & lung causes
  • Bronchiectasis — copious daily purulent sputum, recurrent infections
  • Pneumonia / lung abscess — fever, productive cough, consolidation
  • Aspergilloma — a fungal ball in an old TB / cavity
🩺The systemic clues — don’t miss these
  • Haemoptysis + haematuria / AKI (± sinusitis, saddle nose) → vasculitis (GPA) / anti-GBM (Goodpasture)
  • Malar flush + mid-diastolic murmur → mitral stenosis
  • Anticoagulation / bleeding disorder → a coagulopathy unmasking or worsening a bleed
🚩Red flags
  • Massive haemoptysis → airway emergency (asphyxiation risk)
  • Haemoptysis, age ≥40 → lung cancer — urgent CT & 2WW (regardless of smoking)
  • Haemoptysis + haematuria → pulmonary-renal syndrome — urgent
Two questions come first: is it truly haemoptysis (vs haematemesis or a nosebleed), and is it massive (an airway emergency)? Everything after that is finding the source — and in an adult smoker, that means excluding lung cancer, TB and PE.
